messages.subject: Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.subject_clean: Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Hi STAN users,

   I'm trying to transition a somewhat complicated modeling exercise from JAGS to STAN, in hopes that STAN can do a better job of exploring posterior distributions of some complex relationships between variables and datasets. Essentially, I'm trying to conduct a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off rates in water, combining data from many experiments in the literature. Traditionally, this has been modeled like so:

ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)-k_i*t, sigma_C)

k_i~Normal(k_20*exp(lambda*(T_i-20)), sigma_k)

Where C(t)_i is the concentration of organisms at time t in experiment i, C(0)_i is the initial concentration, k_i is the geometric rate of die-off, k_20 is the mean rate of die-off at a reference temperature of 20 degrees Celsius, T_i is the temperature at which experiment i was conducted, and lambda is a coefficient for geometric increases in the rate of decay with temperature.

What I'm eventually trying to accomplish is an extension of this model to a typical non(log) linear decay pattern. For many microbes, a tailing off of the rate of die-off is common, giving the appearance of two distinct populations decaying at separate rates. This type of biphasic decay is usually modeled as a sum of two exponential decay functions:

ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)+ln(a_i*exp(-k1_i*t)+(1-a_i)*exp(-k2_i*t)), sigma_C)

k1_i~Normal(k1_20*exp(lambda1*(T_i-20)), sigma_k1)
k2_i~Normal(k2_20*exp(lambda2*(T_i-20)), sigma_k2)

where k1 is the decay rate for the more sensitive subpopulation, k2 is the decay rate for the more resistant subpopulation, and a is the proportion of organisms belonging to the sensitive population subject to k1.

In the context of a meta-analysis, there is the added challenge to the second model that some data exhibit biphasic decay and some do not. To cope with this, I'm pursuing the assumption that the temperature dependencies of k1 and k2 underlie the temperature dependency of monophasic decay, following from the idea that monophasic data can represent either the case where only the sensitive or resistant subpopulations were present, or both populations were present, but poor resolution/measurement errors resulted in an inability to resolve the biphasic decay. My model for combining biphasic and monophasic data would use biphasic experiments to estimate the temperature responses of k1 and k2, then, for monophasic experiments, use a discrete categorical variable to assign monophasic rate constant k to either the temperature-dependent distribution of k1 or k2, in which case a=1 or a=0 and the monophasic data impact the posterior distribution of the biphasic temperature response functions. Alternatively, k can be assigned to a third category, in which case it is drawn from a diffuse, non-temperature dependent prior distribution, and a is estimated between 0 and 1 based on the relative values of k, and k1 and k2 at the given temperature. In this case, the monophasic data are not used to estimate temperature dependency of k1 and k2. Is it reasonable to pursue this model in STAN, or is this sort of dynamic inclusion of data for parameter estimates incompatible with STAN's form of inference?

On Tuesday, May 17, 2016 at 12:03:35 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>

The 9th attachment is the STAN model. What showed up in the email? Sorry for all the confusion around this, I'm still not sure what's going on...

>
> You really need to consider the non-centered parameterizations for
> efficiency if there are small data sizes int he groups.
>

Thank you for suggesting this. I'm struggling somewhat to understand how centered vs. non-centered parameterizations work. Basically the sampling of the estimated parameters is independent from the likelihood estimation in the NCP? In the case of the above model, if for example I wanted to have a non-centered parameterization for K1, would I declare it like so?

Centered:
model{
K1~normal(mu_K1, sigma_K1)
mu_K1~normal(0,100)
sigma_K1~cauchy(0,15)
}

Non-centered:
transformed parameters{
K1<-mu_K1+sigma_K1*z_K1
}

model{
mu_K1~normal(0,100)
sigma_K1~cauchy(0,15)
z_K1~normal(0,1)

}

> And you don't want super-diffuse gamma priors (I didn't try to
> figure out how to inspect your data).

The gamma distribution estimated from the known variances is not very diffuse, I think. Parameters are .4 and .54, tails don't get out beyond ~25.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-NlZLOYmpZ8c/V05RnX4mWCI/AAAAAAAAAAM/CwKPy1hyoBQYryDRJTHPASstVgO1kzF7gCLcB/s1600/Rplot01.png>

> And you can just mode scales
> directly --- Stan doesn't use any conjugacy information.
>

Meaning I should go ahead and draw samples of the sigma parameters directly, rather than worrying about doing it through the variances?

> Is this right:
>
> >    mu_ln_Conc0~normal(ln_Conc0, sigma_ln_Conc0);
>
> sigma and ln_Conc0 are vectors, but mu_ln_Conc0 isn't, so you're
> modeling mu_ln_Conc0 Nobs times.
>
> - Bob
>

ln_Conc0 and sigma_ln_Conc0 are single values in this model, whereas ln_Conc and sigma_ln_Conc are vectors. mu_ln_Conc0 is only sampled once per iteration.

>
> > At any rate, I was able to improve things a bit by creating dynamic constraints for the parameters of the model that vary according to properties of each dataset I want to run the model for. I also was able to get a bit better performance by making the prior distributions for variance and mean parameters a bit less flat. Examining trace plots of problematic runs, I noticed that periods where sampling efficiency of a chain was very poor seemed to correspond to times when a couple of key variance parameters were simultaneously very close to 0. Placing constraints on these parameters so that they could not take on values below 1E-6 seemed to prevent the worst of the inefficient mixing behavior.
>
> If lower=1e-6 makes a difference, then you have a problem with estimates
> near the boundary and adding that lower bound is just going to mask that.
>
> What do the posteriors look like?
>
> - Bob
>

Ah, I was afraid that might be a bit cheaty. I'll rerun the models overnight with all parameters saved and post some posterior distributions (I assume you were interested in the scale parameters?) tomorrow.

Thanks again,

   Philip

We usually just model sigma directly (with a prior).
The reason it's easier than variance or precision is that
it's on the natural scale of the data, so easier to formulate
reasonable priors for.

Stan samples everything jointly, though --- so you never sample
sigma directly all by itself.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] initial values for a Bayesian mixture model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] initial values for a Bayesian mixture model
messages.body_plain:
You need to track down where the log density goes off
the rails.  You can use print statements to track it as
it goes and to evaluate inputs and outputs to make sure
everything's well defined before being called.

But I'd really suggest starting with a simpler working
model and building up.  That way, you can see where things
go wrong.  It's hard to debug a complicated program that
doesn't work.

Stan should have finite log densities for any input meeting
the constraints of the parameters.

You almost never need initial values in Stan.  It can
solve some problems, but it's rare.

What you're calling weakly informative are very diffuse
priors.  We don't recommend the gamma(0.001, 0.001) things
anywhere, or really even normal(0, 100) when you expect
the result to have order 1.

I couldn't follow your model.  Lots of pieces of it
look problematic (like dividing by a log_sum_exp)
and it looks like you're redefining things
for which there are built-in functions.

You really don't want to do this for efficiency:

> transformed data {
>
>   // covariance matrix for alpha & beta
>
>   matrix[K+1, K+1] Sigma;
>
>   Sigma <- diag_matrix(rep_vector(10000, K+1));
>
> }

>   gamma ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0, K+1), Sigma);

You can just use the vectorized form

  gamma ~ normal(0, 100);

which should be orders of magnitude faster.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Well, at least 5GB is an upper bound.

The only reason we haven't built servers for a Stan server
is that we have no way to pay for the hosting.  It should be easy to
set up a server-based version of Stan that operates via HTTP
or some other form of socket.  We wouldn't need Docker for that,
though that might be a dev ops friendly solution.

- Bob

> On May 31, 2016, at 7:42 AM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> To answer Bob's question, the current rstan image is quite large at about 5gb.   It's built on top of the hadleyverse image from Dirk Eddelbuettel's rocker project (https://github.com/rocker-org/rocker), which has a base R install plus all the Hadley Wickham packages as well as a working TeX installation. I think the TeX stuff accounts for a lot of the bloat. Then I added pandoc and cURL and some extra LaTeX fonts. So there's definitely room to pare it down, especially for a stand-alone Stan-machine, particularly if it just ran cmdstan.
>
> Allen's point about running as privileged by default (b/c it needs direct access to the linux kernel) is definitely a sticking point, particularly for working in any kind of HPC environment.
>
> One interesting use case for folks who don't want to run locally that this could help to solve could be to create a server image that runs Stan-as-a-service, potentially taking models and data via an HTTP request and returning a link to the results. It might also be possible to link it to dropbox for something a bit more seamless from the user end? If it was well-packaged, a lab group could download it to a local server with minimal config.
>
> I was thinking it might be easiest for me to write up a 3-part series (Makefiles, Docker, and Gitlab CI) on my relatively lightly-trafficked blog, and then you guys can either link to or post a synopsis or carbon copy of those on the big blog?
>
> -Jon

This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:

> > >
> > > 1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Soft constraints, not hard constraints: We need to write some little article just making this point.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Soft constraints, not hard constraints: We need to write some little article just making this point.
messages.body_plain:
This isn't what's going on Andrew.  They don't want to
set to a fixed value, they want to cap the evolution of
the time series so that inter-day, there's a 0.01 sd on
the probability scale.  Same for starting values, which they're
trying to coax to a very narrow range.  It's probably not
necessary --- I'd actually fit that SD rather than hard
coding it.

It's all in Jackman's paper.  Luke's just trying to implement
Jackman's model, which is the source of all of these
modeling decisions.

I think they can and should all be relaxed, and to the
extent possible, estimated rather than hard-coded.

But the whole model's defective in that it doesn't
constraint proportions to (0, 1).

- Bob

> On May 31, 2016, at 3:28 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Just very quickly:  if you want to set a parameter to a fixed value, we recommend specifying it as data rather than giving it a very sharp prior.
> A
>> On May 31, 2016, at 4:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>>
>>> On May 31, 2016, at 10:34 AM, Luke Mansillo <lukema...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> When I thought I was embarrassing myself horribly with my utter ignorance, I emailed Bob. I am very thankful for his assistance given how stumped I have been. Below highlighted is my text responding to his comments.
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> This model's going to be fast and easy to fit in Stan.
>>>
>>> I took a look at the model, and indeed the error scale is observed (it comes with the poll).  Jackman uses that same hacked uniform(0.4, 0.6) on the initial state.  You shouldn't need an extreme measure like that in Stan --- in fact, as Andrew pointed out, we actively discourage it (if estimates are near boundaries, the constraint dominates and the truncation chops off probability mass and has an extreme effect on posterior means;  if not, you don't need the interval constraint).
>>>
>>> Also, the whole model is degenerate if you want to assume alpha[i] in (0,1).  You either need to put that constraint on alpha OR you need to work on the logit scale, where the time series is log odds in (-inf, inf), and you use inverse-logit to transform back to (0,1).  That's the usual GLM approach to general models for variables constrained to lie in (0,1).
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> I could put the constraint on alpha between 0.32 and 0.65 which is well within my polling data and would be intuitive. But that being said the initial state is an election outcome, so ought to start at 0.5363 given that is the observed measured election result.
>>
>> This is *not* a good idea.  Remember that we're doing Bayesian
>> statistics here, not point estimation.  Given that we have a time
>> series, that original alpha could be anything and isn't constrained
>> to be near the initial value.
>>
>> Also, the constraint between 0.32 and 0.65 is arbitrary --- we only
>> know the value has to be between 0 and 1.  So what we're recommending
>> is only constraining between 0 and 1, and then if you want, including
>> something like a beta prior that's concentrated between 0.3 and 0.7 if
>> you know that's what's reasonable.
>>>
>>> It would be appropriate to have a hard constraint on alpha[1] as it is the known election result.
>>>
>>> alpha [1] ~ normal(0.5363, 0.001);
>>
>> This is a bad idea for the same reason.  I know it was in Jackman's
>> original model.
>>>
>>> The Stan model's going to look something like this (I took the liberty of eliminating the hacks to intervals and converted the precision variable to a scale):
>>>
>>>
>>> I am unsure what the difference between a precision and a scale. Could you please elaborate on what the scale entails.
>>
>> "Scale" is the name of the "standard deviation" parameter.
>> In general, variance = sd^2,  precision = 1 / sd.
>>
>> So I just mean parameterize in terms of scale.
>>
>>>
>>> I am unsure how to approach what Andrew suggested regarding specifying my observed values and defining the times as random variables during the periods between the measured values.
>>

> > Hi STAN users,
> >
> >    I'm trying to transition a somewhat complicated modeling exercise from JAGS to STAN, in hopes that STAN can do a better job of exploring posterior distributions of some complex relationships between variables and datasets. Essentially, I'm trying to conduct a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off rates in water, combining data from many experiments in the literature. Traditionally, this has been modeled like so:
> >
> > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)-k_i*t, sigma_C)
> >
> > k_i~Normal(k_20*exp(lambda*(T_i-20)), sigma_k)
> >
> > Where C(t)_i is the concentration of organisms at time t in experiment i, C(0)_i is the initial concentration, k_i is the geometric rate of die-off, k_20 is the mean rate of die-off at a reference temperature of 20 degrees Celsius, T_i is the temperature at which experiment i was conducted, and lambda is a coefficient for geometric increases in the rate of decay with temperature.
> >
> > What I'm eventually trying to accomplish is an extension of this model to a typical non(log) linear decay pattern. For many microbes, a tailing off of the rate of die-off is common, giving the appearance of two distinct populations decaying at separate rates. This type of biphasic decay is usually modeled as a sum of two exponential decay functions:
> >
> > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)+ln(a_i*exp(-k1_i*t)+(1-a_i)*exp(-k2_i*t)), sigma_C)
> >
> > k1_i~Normal(k1_20*exp(lambda1*(T_i-20)), sigma_k1)
> > k2_i~Normal(k2_20*exp(lambda2*(T_i-20)), sigma_k2)
> >
> > where k1 is the decay rate for the more sensitive subpopulation, k2 is the decay rate for the more resistant subpopulation, and a is the proportion of organisms belonging to the sensitive population subject to k1.
> >
> > In the context of a meta-analysis, there is the added challenge to the second model that some data exhibit biphasic decay and some do not. To cope with this, I'm pursuing the assumption that the temperature dependencies of k1 and k2 underlie the temperature dependency of monophasic decay, following from the idea that monophasic data can represent either the case where only the sensitive or resistant subpopulations were present, or both populations were present, but poor resolution/measurement errors resulted in an inability to resolve the biphasic decay. My model for combining biphasic and monophasic data would use biphasic experiments to estimate the temperature responses of k1 and k2, then, for monophasic experiments, use a discrete categorical variable to assign monophasic rate constant k to either the temperature-dependent distribution of k1 or k2, in which case a=1 or a=0 and the monophasic data impact the posterior distribution of the biphasic temperature response functions. Alternatively, k can be assigned to a third category, in which case it is drawn from a diffuse, non-temperature dependent prior distribution, and a is estimated between 0 and 1 based on the relative values of k, and k1 and k2 at the given temperature. In this case, the monophasic data are not used to estimate temperature dependency of k1 and k2. Is it reasonable to pursue this model in STAN, or is this sort of dynamic inclusion of data for parameter estimates incompatible with STAN's form of inference?

messages.subject: Timeline on experimental use of GMO?
messages.subject_clean: Timeline on experimental use of GMO?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

We're doing some planning on scaling up our modeling, and I wanted
to get an idea if/when there was a timeline for an alpha version of
GMO (is that what Andrew calls the method in the EP as a way of
life paper?)  in Stan?

For context, we model customer behaviour. Most of our clients are in the
2-70k customers range.  For training purposes we randomly
sample these, drawing 100-500 customers' full histories, and train our models using
HMC. The small sample size, around 20 observations per customer, is adequate
given our models are reasonably small, with 1-200 parameters.
After estimating, we simulate posterior predictions for all customers'
futures. All models are tested by estimating on simulated data to
recapture known parameters. They perform well out of sample.

A couple of upcoming clients have much larger customer books
(1-5M customers). We'd like to make use of the richer data
by segmenting customers (say, by geography/product) and estimate
our current models with segment-varying parameters. We're a
business and don't really have 2-3 days to wait around between
model runs. I've tried to recover known parameters for our models
using ADVI without much luck (more a function of our models
than ADVI I suspect).

One approach that I'm partial to is to

1. Estimate a pooled model on a random subset of the data.
2. Segment the full data, split it, and estimate the pooled
model on each segment taking group-level parameters from
(1) as priors.

This would scale pretty easily, and I can continue using HMC,
which I trust. As to whether my intuition is off about using priors
in stage (2) here, I have no idea. The aim is to get something
approximating a partial pooling model.

But this is all to say that if there is a method that a) I know can recover
known parameters, b) I can parallelize, and c) runs quickly,
we'd be be happy to collaborate during experimentation phase.

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I'm still having trouble with the jargon.

If the inclusion is based on data alone, then no problem.
If the inclusion is based on parameter values, then you're really looking at a mixture model and you should look at the section on marginalizing discrete parameters.

Daniel

On Wed, Jun 1, 2016 at 12:59 PM, <pcoll...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Krzyzsztof and Daniel,
>
>    Thanks for the replies and sorry for the confusing question. I'll work on figuring out the joint probability function. What I meant by dynamic inclusion of data was that if the categorical variable assigns a set of monophasic data to either of the temperature dependent probability distributions for the biphasic rate parameters, then the data influences the estimation of those temperature-dependent probability distributions. If the experiment is assigned to the third (intermediate) category, then the data doesn't influence the underlying temperature dependent probability distributions.
>
> Phil
>
> On Wednesday, June 1, 2016 at 5:15:40 AM UTC-7, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > I was inclined to give a similar answer---mixture model with a few complications. K
> >
> > On Wednesday, June 1, 2016 at 12:37:17 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > Hi. That question was really hard to follow, so short answer, yes.
> > >
> > > The long answer: yes. But I don't see what part of this has "dynamic inclusion of data"? What does that mean? If you can write down a (log) joint probability function for the data and the parameters, then this is straightforward.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Daniel
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tue, May 31, 2016 at 8:57 PM, <pcoll...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > > Hi STAN users,
> > > >
> > > >    I'm trying to transition a somewhat complicated modeling exercise from JAGS to STAN, in hopes that STAN can do a better job of exploring posterior distributions of some complex relationships between variables and datasets. Essentially, I'm trying to conduct a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off rates in water, combining data from many experiments in the literature. Traditionally, this has been modeled like so:
> > > >
> > > > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)-k_i*t, sigma_C)
> > > >
> > > > k_i~Normal(k_20*exp(lambda*(T_i-20)), sigma_k)
> > > >
> > > > Where C(t)_i is the concentration of organisms at time t in experiment i, C(0)_i is the initial concentration, k_i is the geometric rate of die-off, k_20 is the mean rate of die-off at a reference temperature of 20 degrees Celsius, T_i is the temperature at which experiment i was conducted, and lambda is a coefficient for geometric increases in the rate of decay with temperature.
> > > >
> > > > What I'm eventually trying to accomplish is an extension of this model to a typical non(log) linear decay pattern. For many microbes, a tailing off of the rate of die-off is common, giving the appearance of two distinct populations decaying at separate rates. This type of biphasic decay is usually modeled as a sum of two exponential decay functions:
> > > >
> > > > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)+ln(a_i*exp(-k1_i*t)+(1-a_i)*exp(-k2_i*t)), sigma_C)
> > > >
> > > > k1_i~Normal(k1_20*exp(lambda1*(T_i-20)), sigma_k1)
> > > > k2_i~Normal(k2_20*exp(lambda2*(T_i-20)), sigma_k2)
> > > >
> > > > where k1 is the decay rate for the more sensitive subpopulation, k2 is the decay rate for the more resistant subpopulation, and a is the proportion of organisms belonging to the sensitive population subject to k1.
> > > >
> > > > In the context of a meta-analysis, there is the added challenge to the second model that some data exhibit biphasic decay and some do not. To cope with this, I'm pursuing the assumption that the temperature dependencies of k1 and k2 underlie the temperature dependency of monophasic decay, following from the idea that monophasic data can represent either the case where only the sensitive or resistant subpopulations were present, or both populations were present, but poor resolution/measurement errors resulted in an inability to resolve the biphasic decay. My model for combining biphasic and monophasic data would use biphasic experiments to estimate the temperature responses of k1 and k2, then, for monophasic experiments, use a discrete categorical variable to assign monophasic rate constant k to either the temperature-dependent distribution of k1 or k2, in which case a=1 or a=0 and the monophasic data impact the posterior distribution of the biphasic temperature response functions. Alternatively, k can be assigned to a third category, in which case it is drawn from a diffuse, non-temperature dependent prior distribution, and a is estimated between 0 and 1 based on the relative values of k, and k1 and k2 at the given temperature. In this case, the monophasic data are not used to estimate temperature dependency of k1 and k2. Is it reasonable to pursue this model in STAN, or is this sort of dynamic inclusion of data for parameter estimates incompatible with STAN's form of inference?

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Timeline on experimental use of GMO?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, GMO is gradient-based marginal optimization.  We currently have an R package for GMO that Dustin wrote; I haven't fully explored it myself.  My original GMO idea did not involve data partitioning, but Dustin has implemented a data partitioning version of GMO that he says is very fast.  We should have a clean draft of the paper soon.  It would be great to try it out on your example.
Andrew

> On Jun 1, 2016, at 11:00 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi all -
>
> We're doing some planning on scaling up our modeling, and I wanted
> to get an idea if/when there was a timeline for an alpha version of
> GMO (is that what Andrew calls the method in the EP as a way of
> life paper?)  in Stan?
>
> For context, we model customer behaviour. Most of our clients are in the
> 2-70k customers range.  For training purposes we randomly
> sample these, drawing 100-500 customers' full histories, and train our models using
> HMC. The small sample size, around 20 observations per customer, is adequate
> given our models are reasonably small, with 1-200 parameters.
> After estimating, we simulate posterior predictions for all customers'
> futures. All models are tested by estimating on simulated data to
> recapture known parameters. They perform well out of sample.
>
> A couple of upcoming clients have much larger customer books
> (1-5M customers). We'd like to make use of the richer data
> by segmenting customers (say, by geography/product) and estimate
> our current models with segment-varying parameters. We're a
> business and don't really have 2-3 days to wait around between
> model runs. I've tried to recover known parameters for our models
> using ADVI without much luck (more a function of our models
> than ADVI I suspect).
>
> One approach that I'm partial to is to
>
> 1. Estimate a pooled model on a random subset of the data.
> 2. Segment the full data, split it, and estimate the pooled
> model on each segment taking group-level parameters from
> (1) as priors.
>
> This would scale pretty easily, and I can continue using HMC,
> which I trust. As to whether my intuition is off about using priors
> in stage (2) here, I have no idea. The aim is to get something
> approximating a partial pooling model.
>
> But this is all to say that if there is a method that a) I know can recover
> known parameters, b) I can parallelize, and c) runs quickly,
> we'd be be happy to collaborate during experimentation phase.
>
> Jim

> > For context, we model customer behaviour. Most of our clients are in the
> > 2-70k customers range.  For training purposes we randomly
> > sample these, drawing 100-500 customers' full histories, and train our models using
> > HMC. The small sample size, around 20 observations per customer, is adequate
> > given our models are reasonably small, with 1-200 parameters.
> > After estimating, we simulate posterior predictions for all customers'
> > futures. All models are tested by estimating on simulated data to
> > recapture known parameters. They perform well out of sample.
> >
> > A couple of upcoming clients have much larger customer books
> > (1-5M customers). We'd like to make use of the richer data
> > by segmenting customers (say, by geography/product) and estimate
> > our current models with segment-varying parameters. We're a
> > business and don't really have 2-3 days to wait around between
> > model runs. I've tried to recover known parameters for our models
> > using ADVI without much luck (more a function of our models
> > than ADVI I suspect).
> >
> > One approach that I'm partial to is to
> >
> > 1. Estimate a pooled model on a random subset of the data.
> > 2. Segment the full data, split it, and estimate the pooled
> > model on each segment taking group-level parameters from
> > (1) as priors.
> >
> > This would scale pretty easily, and I can continue using HMC,
> > which I trust. As to whether my intuition is off about using priors
> > in stage (2) here, I have no idea. The aim is to get something
> > approximating a partial pooling model.
> >
> > But this is all to say that if there is a method that a) I know can recover
> > known parameters, b) I can parallelize, and c) runs quickly,
> > we'd be be happy to collaborate during experimentation phase.
> >

I've updated the gist to include the stan file for a new version of the model where, instead of trying to derive the mean function of a GP in the transformed parameters section, I explicitly model a noiseless latent GP that is then sampled with noise to create the data. The resulting posterior on the latent function seems much more reasonable as a predictive band:

However, this new model samples rather slowly :O\ At least, I think it does. The above plot certainly looks nice and smooth, but it's from a 4-chain run of iter=2e3 where each chain took about 10 minutes and the resulting ESS for the GP parameters are fairly low (eta=68, rho=39, noise=16).

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, June 2, 2016 at 12:48:15 AM UTC-4, Jyoti Shankar wrote:
> I tried computing the SD from the posterior summaries but my answer does not match up with the output of the print() function.

The output of the print() function for the group-level covariance is not "correct". In particular, the reported standard deviations are the square roots of the posterior means of the variances rather than the posterior means of the square roots of the variances. We do not actually store what would be needed to directly calculate stuff like this directly, so it is conceptually better to do what you did ...

> However, if I calculate the standard deviations of these terms from the posterior samples as follows:
> ##########
> # extract posterior samples
> mat = as.matrix(modelresults)
>
> # get the random effect columns
> group_cols <- grep("^b", colnames(mat), value = T)
> group_posteriors <- mat[, group_cols]
>
> # example variable slope term: b[var1_scaled donor:donor1]
> variable_names <- unique(gsub("b\\[(.*)\\s.*", "\\1", colnames(group_posteriors)))
>
> # for each variable, compute its SD at each MCMC iteration
> var_group_summary <- sapply(variable_names, function(vname){
>     var_group_posteriors <- group_posteriors[, grep(vname, colnames(group_posteriors), value = T)]
>     group_sd <- sapply(1:nrow(var_group_posteriors), function(crow){
>       out <- sd(var_group_posteriors[crow, ])
>       return(out)
>       })
>     group_summary <- c(mean = mean(group_sd), quantile(x = group_sd, probs = c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975)))
>     return(group_summary)
>     })
>   return(var_group_summary)
>   }
> ##########

However, the standard deviation of some unknown across groups at each MCMC iteration could be a noisy estimate if the number of levels of that grouping variable is small.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can STAN handle probabilistic inclusion of data in subsets used for parameter estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Exactly.  If the inclusion depends on parameters then you
naively require some latent categorical variable which would
require integer-valued states in the Markov chain which is
not allowed in Stan.  But you can include all possible
configurations of data at once with a mixture model, using
Stan to explore the (continuous) mixing weights.

On Jun 2, 2016, at 4:55 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Hi Phil,
>
> I'm still having trouble with the jargon.
>
> If the inclusion is based on data alone, then no problem.
> If the inclusion is based on parameter values, then you're really looking at a mixture model and you should look at the section on marginalizing discrete parameters.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Wed, Jun 1, 2016 at 12:59 PM, <pcoll...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > Hi Krzyzsztof and Daniel,
> >
> >    Thanks for the replies and sorry for the confusing question. I'll work on figuring out the joint probability function. What I meant by dynamic inclusion of data was that if the categorical variable assigns a set of monophasic data to either of the temperature dependent probability distributions for the biphasic rate parameters, then the data influences the estimation of those temperature-dependent probability distributions. If the experiment is assigned to the third (intermediate) category, then the data doesn't influence the underlying temperature dependent probability distributions.
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > On Wednesday, June 1, 2016 at 5:15:40 AM UTC-7, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > I was inclined to give a similar answer---mixture model with a few complications. K
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, June 1, 2016 at 12:37:17 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > > Hi. That question was really hard to follow, so short answer, yes.
> > > >
> > > > The long answer: yes. But I don't see what part of this has "dynamic inclusion of data"? What does that mean? If you can write down a (log) joint probability function for the data and the parameters, then this is straightforward.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Daniel
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, May 31, 2016 at 8:57 PM, <pcoll...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > > > Hi STAN users,
> > > > >
> > > > >    I'm trying to transition a somewhat complicated modeling exercise from JAGS to STAN, in hopes that STAN can do a better job of exploring posterior distributions of some complex relationships between variables and datasets. Essentially, I'm trying to conduct a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off rates in water, combining data from many experiments in the literature. Traditionally, this has been modeled like so:
> > > > >
> > > > > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)-k_i*t, sigma_C)
> > > > >
> > > > > k_i~Normal(k_20*exp(lambda*(T_i-20)), sigma_k)
> > > > >
> > > > > Where C(t)_i is the concentration of organisms at time t in experiment i, C(0)_i is the initial concentration, k_i is the geometric rate of die-off, k_20 is the mean rate of die-off at a reference temperature of 20 degrees Celsius, T_i is the temperature at which experiment i was conducted, and lambda is a coefficient for geometric increases in the rate of decay with temperature.
> > > > >
> > > > > What I'm eventually trying to accomplish is an extension of this model to a typical non(log) linear decay pattern. For many microbes, a tailing off of the rate of die-off is common, giving the appearance of two distinct populations decaying at separate rates. This type of biphasic decay is usually modeled as a sum of two exponential decay functions:
> > > > >
> > > > > ln(C(t)_i)~Normal(ln(C(0)_i)+ln(a_i*exp(-k1_i*t)+(1-a_i)*exp(-k2_i*t)), sigma_C)
> > > > >
> > > > > k1_i~Normal(k1_20*exp(lambda1*(T_i-20)), sigma_k1)
> > > > > k2_i~Normal(k2_20*exp(lambda2*(T_i-20)), sigma_k2)
> > > > >
> > > > > where k1 is the decay rate for the more sensitive subpopulation, k2 is the decay rate for the more resistant subpopulation, and a is the proportion of organisms belonging to the sensitive population subject to k1.
> > > > >
> > > > > In the context of a meta-analysis, there is the added challenge to the second model that some data exhibit biphasic decay and some do not. To cope with this, I'm pursuing the assumption that the temperature dependencies of k1 and k2 underlie the temperature dependency of monophasic decay, following from the idea that monophasic data can represent either the case where only the sensitive or resistant subpopulations were present, or both populations were present, but poor resolution/measurement errors resulted in an inability to resolve the biphasic decay. My model for combining biphasic and monophasic data would use biphasic experiments to estimate the temperature responses of k1 and k2, then, for monophasic experiments, use a discrete categorical variable to assign monophasic rate constant k to either the temperature-dependent distribution of k1 or k2, in which case a=1 or a=0 and the monophasic data impact the posterior distribution of the biphasic temperature response functions. Alternatively, k can be assigned to a third category, in which case it is drawn from a diffuse, non-temperature dependent prior distribution, and a is estimated between 0 and 1 based on the relative values of k, and k1 and k2 at the given temperature. In this case, the monophasic data are not used to estimate temperature dependency of k1 and k2. Is it reasonable to pursue this model in STAN, or is this sort of dynamic inclusion of data for parameter estimates incompatible with STAN's form of inference?

Ben

messages.subject: Problem recapturing values from simulated data
messages.subject_clean: Problem recapturing values from simulated data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all —

I’m working on a hierarchical model of timing of leafout for trees, could use help figuring out why my fitted values differ so much from my (simulated) data in some simple parameters. I don’t know exactly where I went wrong in the model specification, so could use some help from this group.

The set up is that I have multiple species, and within species I have multiple individual trees. Each tree has branches taken from it and exposed to different experimental conditions; we measure day of leaf expansion. So there are random intercepts at the species and tree level, and random slopes as well for the effects of the experimental conditions.

I’m generating simulated data to test the model with an overall day of leafout of 35 days, then variation around that for species-level intercepts, and variation around each of those at the individual level. I'm not simulating variation of the slopes at species or individual level.

The surprising thing is that the fitted values come up with an overall day of leafout (“a_0” in the model) of 70 days. All the other intercepts at the species and individual level vary the way I expect, but around this higher value. The slopes follow the simulated values well.

My problem is in figuring out why the fitted intercepts are so high, and here I’m hoping this group can help me! I’m attaching the stan model, as well as a figure from a posterior predictive check, showing the shift in intercept up for the fitted values, and associated R code for those interested.

Any thoughts would be most welcome!

Dan

Mike L, I just looked at your gp_fit_2.stan. My guess is that the low ESS/second may be a function of the centered parameterization that you're using for f. With a non-centered parameterization for f, I get something like 400 ESS on 1000 post-warmup samples from NUTS for rho, eta and noise. The reparameterized model is attached with some fatter (default) half-cauchy(0, 2.5) priors on rho, eta and noise.

Given that you're increasing the number of parameters from 3 to around 170, it's not especially surprising that the wall-time for running a single chain should increase.

Betancourt, I do get some posterior correlation between log(rho) and log(eta), but I'm not getting the banana plots that I'm used to for non-identifiable models.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
I went quiet yesterday as I tried out the various suggestions and tweaks thereon:

Andrew suggested a more concentrated prior on the lengthscale. I had the GP coded as in the manual where rho=1/lengthscale, which I find more intuitive as the values from 0-1 imply near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1), making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for simpler functions.

That said, switching from rho~student_t(4,0,1) to rho~normal(0,1) indeed improved things quite a bit such that when I ran 4 chains at iter=2e3 they were about 5 mins each, had ESS for the noise & eta parameters in the thousands and rho >100.

Curiously, the 2.5%ile-97.5%ile ribbon of the posterior samples on f (the noiseless latent GP) didn't differ considerably from the earlier example with low ESS on the parameters. Indeed, I did a lot of fiddling (inc. using rho~weibull(2,1), setting the lower bound of rho to 1, using cauchy(0,2.5) for all priors, bumping the iter=2e4, etc) and while ESS and wall time varied fairly considerably, the aforementioned ribbon didn't really vary, so possibly ESS/Rhat aren't useful metrics in this case?

I also tried Rob's non-centered version which takes more wall time but indeed has a higher ESS. However, the ribbon on f came out very different this time, seemingly far too smooth.

Sitting here generating GPs with various values for rho, it strikes me that it may be better to sample it on the log-scale as the increase in wiggliness caused by going from rho=10 and rho=100 seems about the same as the increase in wiggliness caused by going from rho=100 and rho=1000. Or should the behaviour of the sampler account for this?

I found the following syntax to obtain the posterior central tendency (mu) and dispersion (sigma) paramenters using a normal distribution. I tried to change it to obtain these parameters using t-distribution. I couldn't do that following the posts above. Could someone help me with this?

Thank you very much!

Danilo

model <- "
// Inferring the Mean and Standard Deviation of a t-distribution
  data {
    int<lower=0> J;

real y[J]; // estimated treatment effects
real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of effect estimates
}
parameters {
real theta[J];
real mu;
real<lower=0> tau;
}
model {
theta ~ normal (mu, tau);
for (j in 1:J)
y[j] ~ student_t (4,theta[j], sigma[j]);

}#x <- c(1.1, 1.9, 2.3, 1.8)
x <- sample(dados$A, 100)
n <- length(x)

data <- list(x=x, n=n) # to be passed on to Stan
myinits <- list(
  list(mu=0, sigma=1))

# parameters to be monitored:
parameters <- c("mu", "sigma")

# The following command calls Stan with specific options.
# For a detailed description type "?rstan".
samples <- stan(model_code=model,
                data=data,
                init=myinits,  # If not specified, gives random inits
                pars=parameters,
                iter=10000,
                chains=1,
                thin=1,
                # warmup = 100,  # Stands for burn-in; Default = iter/2
                # seed = 123  # Setting seed; Default is random seed
                )
# Now the values for the monitored parameters are in the "samples" object,
# ready for inspection.

mu <- extract(samples)$mu
sigma <- extract(samples)$sigma
summary(samples)

> >> To answer Bob's question, the current rstan image is quite large at about 5gb.   It's built on top of the hadleyverse image from Dirk Eddelbuettel's rocker project (https://github.com/rocker-org/rocker), which has a base R install plus all the Hadley Wickham packages as well as a working TeX installation. I think the TeX stuff accounts for a lot of the bloat. Then I added pandoc and cURL and some extra LaTeX fonts. > >> One interesting use case for folks who don't want to run locally that this could help to solve could be to create a server image that runs Stan-as-a-service, potentially taking models and data via an HTTP request and returning a link to the results. > >>

> >>>>
> >>>> Hi Folks -
> >>>>
> >>>> Just wanted to put a small something I've been working on out there to see what folks think about it.
> >>>>
> >>>> This is a stab at making a template for a fully reproducible soup-to-nuts Stan-based project, that starts with input data and ends with a PDF containing figures and estimates derived from the model output. This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:
> >>>>
> >>>> https://gitlab.com/jzelner/reproducible-stan
> >>>>
> >>>> The ideas represented here are a crystallization of things that have been going on in a number of other projects of mine that rely on sensitive data and so can't be opened up in a way that is fully reproducible to anyone. There are three big reproducibility ideas in here, some newer than others, none of which are my own but instead represent a synthesis of some very powerful tools and ideas:
> >>>>
> >>>> 1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.
> >>>>
> >>>> 2) Docker: One of the challenges of reproducing any project (and Stan ones in particular for non-initiates) is having the relevant software installed locally to both run the Stan model and to do the requisite munging of model output. > >>>>
> >>>> 3) Continuous integration (CI): CI tools are commonly used in software engineering to make sure that small changes to a project don't break the whole thing. This project is hosted on Gitlab to take advantage of their easy-to-use and free Docker-based continuous integration service. This way, every time a commit is made to the repository, the Makefile is re-run and the model output (MCMC samples, figures and PDF writeup) are uploaded to the repository and are available for download.
> >>>>
> >>>> More information (and all the code and output) are available in the repository. It's very much a work-in-progress and is meant more as a prod for more thought and development than anything else, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks so much for showing me the way boosting the efficiency, as well as some problematic expressions! I was too focused on translating from the software to STAN line by line (to reduce the mismatches to minimal), and hadn't got to the phase of code optimization.

I'm still figuring out what STAN deems legal. I was able to print out the parameters in the "transformed parameters" block; didn't work very well when placing it inside "model". Now it seems that the major problem lies in drawing those deltas, latent variables in {0, 1}; even after change the inverse gamma prior to a uniform or normal.

To my best knowledge, this model is most similar to what was shown in the User's Guide (version 2.8.0) 9. Finite Mixtures. Instead of a mixture of K normals, this one is a mixture of a folded normal and a gamma, each distribution with hyper parameters. As pointed out in the manual, STAN doesn't support discrete parameter, but the simplex parameter theta to indicate mixing proportions.

In the paper, the authors have the mixing proportions (indicated as pi(x_i)) depend on the covariate matrix X (data). With no explicit example in the manual (maybe I missed it somewhere), I am not sure if I can model those mixing proportions the way the paper proposed. Do you have any comments or recommendation as how to work around it?

I had tried two naive ways, yet both got me the same error messages (code attached, uncommenting // in the code gives the second):
[476] "Initialization between (--2, -2) failed after 100 attempts. "
[477] " Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."

error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

1) Ignore the dependence of data, simply adopted the simplex parameter in the manual
2) First define a function to calculate theta -- parameter for the Bernoulli distribution; draw the latent indicator from Bernoulli; then calculate one mixing portion by sum(delta==1)/N

I can really use some help: can this model be coded in STAN at all? Thank you very much!!!

- Flora

Yes, the model can be coded in Stan.  At least in the
sense that you can make mixture out of anything.

What's legal is defined in the language reference
part of the manual, but it's about 90 pages of definitions.

What you're probably missing given the error is that every
value of the parameters that satisfies the declared constraints
should have a finite log density.

When you say the print statements didn't work in the model,
what I would recommend is removing all of the model, then
adding it back line-by-line --- there's a bug in the
current Stan or RStan that's ignoring print statements in
the model when the log density is illegal.

Betancourt,

I agree that with the simulate_gq_sq_exp.stan file you sent me, even with N = 300, that we see an ugly posterior. The chart I get for alpha vs. rho is here:

For some reason, when I switch to using:

real alpha;

instead of real<lower=0> alpha;

and use:

k(x_i, x_j) = exp(alpha - rho * abs(x_i - x_j)^2) + kronecker_delta_i_j * delta;

with:

alpha ~ normal(0, 1.5);

instead of:

Greetings,

I am a stan new user. Recently I have been trying to apply the hierarchical model (univariate changing settlement rate) in here: http://www.casact.org/pubs/forum/16wforum/Meyers.pdf on page 8.

                        chains = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2000, thin = 2, cores = 2)

A side question: when should I use stan and when should I use stan_model + sampling?

Thank you,
Ethan Kang

messages.subject_clean: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
messages.body_plain:
Yeah, part of the problem is probably the uniform priors with hard constraints. But even if those are great priors in this situation you'd need to fix a few things to implement them correctly. If you have a parameter x and in the model block you write x ~ uniform(-10, 0) then x needs to be declared with <lower=-10,upper=0>. That is, the support of the parameter as declared in the parameters block should match the constraints implied by the density function used in the model block. Fixing that might help. But, like Andrew says, it's worth thinking about whether the uniforms with hard constraints are logically necessary. If not, then priors that decay smoothly are usually better.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
My guess is that your use of the non-centered mean is
not getting adjusted for properly in the comparison.

   // a_0 should end up ~ 35, getting 65 days instead!

Did you mean a_sp here?

  y_hat[i] <- a_sp_ind[ind[i]] +
      b_warm_sp_ind[ind[i]] * warm[i] +
      b_photo_sp_ind[ind[i]] * photo[i]
      ;

  a_sp[k] <- a_0 + mu_a_sp[k];

This bit's not identified.  You can add a constant to a_0
and subtract it from all the mu_a_sp and get the same result.
Given that you let the scale of mu_a_sp vary:

  mu_a_sp ~ normal(0, sigma_a_sp);

and don't provide any prior whatsoever for a_0, this can
be a problem.  I'd check that you're recovering the a_sp
properly given that the a_0 isn't identified.

We always suggest starting simpler and building up models.
It's much harder to debug a complicated model than to build
up a simpler model a step at a time.

Another think to look at is whether your y_hat is right.  If
it is, but the components don't do what you think, it's probably
an identifiability problem.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
messages.body_plain:
We need to write up some Stan case studies to illustrate
the problems that arise.

The original BUGS default "diffuse" priors (like gamma(0.001, 0.001),
etc.) concentrate almost all of their prior mass away from 0.
That means if there's not much data, they will pull the
samples well away from 0 because the prior will dominate the
data.  Andrew's written about this extensively in books and
papers.

The later BUGS default priors (uniform(0, 100), etc.) concentrate
all of their mass in that interval.  The problem there is that
they essentially truncate.  So what'll happen is that if there's
any mass near the boundary, what happens is that it gets truncated
and it moves the posterior mean away from the boundary.   Consider
the case where the posterior would be something like normal(7, 2)
without the hard constraint and you add a (0, 10) constraint.  Then
the posterior mean will be below 7 because you've truncated above 10
even though it's only 1.5 sd away from the posterior mean.

Neither of these assumptions is going to matter much if there's
a lot of data and the posterior is sharp and doesn't violate the
prior constraints.  But that's not our usual operating conditions
with hierarchical models or other fine-grained statistical models.

- Bob

> Thanks for the suggestion. What kind of priors would you recommend? I always thought uniform prior is like a vague prior where you have no knowledge about the data.

> Yeah, part of the problem is probably the uniform priors with hard constraints. But even if those are great priors in this situation you'd need to fix a few things to implement them correctly. If you have a parameter x and in the model block you write x ~ uniform(-10, 0) then x needs to be declared with <lower=-10,upper=0>. That is, the support of the parameter as declared in the parameters block should match the constraints implied by the density function used in the model block. Fixing that might help. But, like Andrew says, it's worth thinking about whether the uniforms with hard constraints are logically necessary. If not, then priors that decay smoothly are usually better.

messages.subject: Estimating Derivatives
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Derivatives
messages.body_plain:
I'm relatively new to Stan, but have been really impressed with it. Thank you so much for making this excellent work available under a permissive open source license. I have been using command Stan 2.9.

Now my question: Is there a nice way to estimate derivatives in a Stan model?

Specifically, I have a financial portfolio valuation v = E[ f(x) ], and need to compute the derivative of v with respect to certain parameters of the distribution. (The vector x are basically prices and the function f is a payoff function that is continuous and piece-wise smooth.) There are two flavors of how to do this: First, the "path-wise" method looks at the prices x(t) as a function of the parameters t, and differentiates d(f(x(t))/dt using the chain rule (and takes its expectation). The other main flavor parameterizes the probability distribution p(x;t) with t, and computes

dv/dt = E[ f(x) d(log p(x;t))/dt ]

where the "score" or "likelihood ratio" (the derivative of the log likelihood) also requires a derivative.

Since Stan has automatic differentiation built in, can I access those to implement one of these methods in Stan without hand-coding derivatives into my Stan code? Is there an elegant way to express this? Any pointers to examples?

Thanks in advance for any help you can provide.
Gary

> On Jun 5, 2016, at 10:28 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> chswtch[s,t] ~ bernoulli_logit(valfun2);
>
> The question is that, wgtWith[s,t] always equals to (1 - wgtWith[s,t]),

Doesn't that mean wgtWith[s,t] is always 0.5?  Or was one of those
supposed to be wgtAgst?

Assuming your statement above was a typo and that

  wstAgst[s,t] == (1 - wgtWith[s,t])

You can just do the algebra to see what's going on when
you have predictors x and (1-x) and coefficients a and b:

  a * x + b * (1 - x) = a * x + b - b * x

In any case, you don't want to have a predictor that's
a linear function of other predictors.  And you usually want to
have an intercept.  What's happening here is that the b coefficient
is doing the work of a varying intercept.  I'd expect a and b here to
be positively or negatively correlated, so i'm not sure what's going
on, which is why I hoped someone better at regression than me
would answer this question.

If I wanted to answer this for myself, I'd do the simulations in
a simpler example than the one you present with just these predictors.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow convergence with a hierarchical model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow convergence with a hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

What Bob suggested is exactly what I would suggest:
1. Add tighter priors
2. Look at the non-centered reparameterization for your model.

If you know you have an additive or multiplicative non-identifiably, then you know your posterior distribution isn't proper, so you'll need to think about your model.

If synthetic data fits fine and real data doesn't, then I'd double check the model for misfit.

Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Slow convergence with a hierarchical model
messages.body_plain:
The general advice is

 * if possible, reparameterize so that the models are identifiable

 * if not (say, more predictors than data points in a regression),
   then control the behavior with priors (and accept the fact that
   it'll be relatively slow)

- Bob

> On Jun 5, 2016, at 7:09 AM, Jean-Baptiste SCHIRATTI <jean.baptis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> Can anyone, please, give me some advice regarding these identifiability questions ?
>
> Thank you !

>
> Le jeudi 2 juin 2016 12:04:23 UTC+2, Odile.S a écrit :

> Dear Bob,
>
> Thank you for your answer.
>
> I apologize, I should have mentioned that the dataset attached to the original post is indeed generated from the model. The data was generated using :
>
> p0 = 0.24, t0 = 70, v0 = 0.034, sigma_eta = 0.5, sigma_tau = 7, sigma = 0.01
>
> STAN estimated (with 5000 iterations and flat priors) the following values :
>
> p0 = 0.21, t0 = 68.8, v0 = 0.030, sigma_eta = 0.53, sigma_tau = 6.7, sigma = 0.099.
>
> I guess these estimates are not so bad. From these, I deduce that it is possible to fit the model on "synthetic data". Still, I followed your advice and tried the pairs() plot for parameters p0, t0 and v0. The point clouds are all oriented along the first diagonal, which suggest a strong positive correlation pairwise. In theory, the triplet (p,t,v) which defines the function gamma0 is not unique. This would clearly cause unidentifiability. Still, if t (for example) is fixed, the triplet becomes unique. Because of the definition
>
> gamma0(p0,t0,v0,eta[group[j]]*(t[j]-t0-tau[group[j]])+t0);
>
> where t0 plays a particular role, I thought that, in theory, the model is indeed identifiable. Am I mistaken ?
>
> I ran STAN on a sub-dataset of the one I attached to the original post. I included only the 50 first individuals (p=50). The performance of STAN seems better (see results below) even though the pairs() plots have not really improved.
>
>  Min.   :0.044   Min.   :0.0074   Min.   : 8.0   Min.   : 255   Min.   :0
>  1st Qu.:0.907   1st Qu.:0.0074   1st Qu.: 8.0   1st Qu.: 255   1st Qu.:0
>  Median :0.970   Median :0.0074   Median : 8.0   Median : 255   Median :0
>  Mean   :0.931   Mean   :0.0074   Mean   : 8.7   Mean   : 489   Mean   :0
>  3rd Qu.:0.993   3rd Qu.:0.0074   3rd Qu.: 9.0   3rd Qu.: 511   3rd Qu.:0
>  Max.   :1.000   Max.   :0.0074   Max.   :12.0   Max.   :4095   Max.   :0
>
> It seems that STAN converges more slowly as the size of the dataset increases. Is this due to identifiability issues ? What is a usual workaround for such identifiability issues ? Use priors ?
>
> Thank you
> Le jeudi 2 juin 2016 06:09:13 UTC+2, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> You're maxing out treedepth, which indicates a problem with
> the model (you probably get warnings about hitting max treedepth),
> and causes computational problems because you won't hit the U-turns
> and will wind up devolving to a simple diffusion.
>
> I would try simulating from the model and seeing if you can
> fit it.  If there's a bad misspecification (model doesn't fit
> data well), then sampling can be a problem.    It's also good
> to help debugging.
>
> If you look at the posterior, you shoudl be able to detect
> (for example, with the pairs() plot restricted to a subset
> of parameters), if there's non-identifiability (very highly
> correlated parameters).
>
> I have no idea what that gamma0 function is supposed to
> be doing and how it affects what's going on.  You don't need to assign
> to r and then return r by the way.  You can just return the
> expression directly.
>
> Some general suggestions:
>
> Non-centered parameterizations for the hierarchical parameters.  For
> example, instead of
>
> > tau ~ normal(0,sigma_tau);
>
>
> you can define a parameter tau_raw and set
>
>   tau <- tau_raw * sigma_tau;
>
> and take
>
>   tau_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>
> You can do this for lognormals, but it's trickier.
>
> I would also suggest more informative priors.  But you should
> look where your fit values go.  If values are running away into
> long tails, you definitely want priors.
>
> Use Stan's built-in random inits --- you shouldn't need to
> specify them yourself.
>
> - Bob
>

> >   real t[K];

> >   int<lower=1> group[K];
> > }
> >
> > parameters {

> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {

> >     mu[j] <- gamma0(p0,t0,v0,eta[group[j]]*(t[j]-t0-tau[group[j]])+t0);
> >   }
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >   eta ~ lognormal(0,sigma_eta);

> > }
> >
> > With these definitions, I assume uniform priors on the parameters p0, t0 and flat improper priors on the other parameters. eta and tau are random effects of the model. group is a grouping variable (a vector of integers) which allow to determine which element in the data vector y belong to a given individual.
> > I run the analysis using :

> >
> >  summary(do.call(rbind, args = get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup = FALSE)),digits = 2)

(This might be also because my code is not well-written). I also notice that the mean accept_stat__ is quite close to 1 (Is this a problem ?) The results are reported below.

> >  Max.   :1.00   Max.   :0.0029   Max.   :10   Max.   :1023   Max.   :0
> >
> > My question is the following : what can I change to make the convergence faster / reduce the number of leapfrog steps ?

messages.body_plain:
In any case, you don't want to build non-identifiability into
your likelihood.  Practically speaking, you should just drop the
wstAgst parameter that's a linear combo of other predictors.

- Bob

> On Jun 5, 2016, at 11:53 PM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks so much Bob.
>
> It was indeed a typo. I meant wstAgst[s,t] == (1 - wgtWith[s,t]). In terms of intercept, I do have an intercept parameter, which is beta[3,s] here, with being multiplied with no other predictors.
>
> I will follow your advice (do the algebra and run a simple simulation) to see if I could find out something.
>
> @ to all other users: I still appreciate other input from your experience.
>
> Thanks a lot.
>
> On Sunday, June 5, 2016 at 11:12:40 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jun 5, 2016, at 10:28 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > could somebody make some comments on this question? This indeed bugs me a lot.
> >
> > Many thanks!
> >
> >
> >
> > On Monday, May 30, 2016 at 5:56:06 PM UTC+2, Lei Zhang wrote:
> > Hi Stan,
> >
> > inside my model, I have a sampling statement where I use some features to predict choices (= 0 or 1) in an experiment, as shown below:
> >
> > valfun2 <- beta[3,s] + beta[4,s] * valdiff + beta[5,s] * wgtWith[s,t] + beta[6,s] * wgtAgst[s,t];
> > chswtch[s,t] ~ bernoulli_logit(valfun2);
> >
> > The question is that, wgtWith[s,t] always equals to (1 - wgtWith[s,t]),
>
> Doesn't that mean wgtWith[s,t] is always 0.5?  Or was one of those
> supposed to be wgtAgst?
>
> Assuming your statement above was a typo and that
>
>   wstAgst[s,t] == (1 - wgtWith[s,t])
>
> You can just do the algebra to see what's going on when
> you have predictors x and (1-x) and coefficients a and b:
>
>   a * x + b * (1 - x) = a * x + b - b * x
>
> In any case, you don't want to have a predictor that's
> a linear function of other predictors.  And you usually want to
> have an intercept.  What's happening here is that the b coefficient
> is doing the work of a varying intercept.  I'd expect a and b here to
> be positively or negatively correlated, so i'm not sure what's going
> on, which is why I hoped someone better at regression than me
> would answer this question.
>
> If I wanted to answer this for myself, I'd do the simulations in
> a simpler example than the one you present with just these predictors.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Python/Jupyter case study: hierarchical home radon model
messages.subject_clean: Python/Jupyter case study: hierarchical home radon model
messages.body_plain:
Chris Fonnesebck (of PyMC fame) kindly contributed a Jupyter notebook
he created as a demo for PyStan (for the short course Chris, Daniel, and
I just taught at Vanderbilt).  It's not only a good introduction
to PyStan and a good example of how to use Jupyter, it's a good
introduction to Stan and hierarchical modeling.  And it replicates
one of Andrew's favorite teaching examples---home radon level estimation
and prediction.

Here's the abstract I wrote for it:

  This case study replicates the analysis of home radon levels using
  hierarchical models of Lin, Gelman, Price, and Kurtz (1999).
  It illustrates how to generalize linear regressions to hierarchical
  models with group-level predictors and how to compare predictive inferences
  and evaluate model fits. Along the way it shows how to get data into Stan
  using pandas, how to sample using PyStan, and how to visualize the results
  using Seaborn.

You can find the link to the source repo and the rendered HTML
on our case studies page:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

Thanks, Chris!

- Bob

P.S. We are open for contributions at this point if anyone else has
anything.  I'm going to have to reorganize the home page.  I'm seeing
it doesn't scale from a handful to a dozen case studies.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reproducible research with Docker, Rstan, and Gitlab CI
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone -

Just wanted to let you know that the series of posts is complete, and that the last two show what I think is the coolest part, specifically getting RStan up and running in a Docker container and then using that to easily share and reproduce results for free on GitLab.

The series starts here:

http://www.jonzelner.net/statistics/make/docker/reproducibility/2016/05/31/reproducibility-pt-1/

And the post on making changes online and auto-updating results using GitLab's continuous integration service is here:

http://www.jonzelner.net/docker/gitlab/ci/reproducibility/2016/06/06/gitlab-ci/

Andrew - this last one may get at your interest in a Stan server, since it performs some of the same functionality, although via pushes to a git repository hosted on GitLab rather than via an HTTP request. But this approach has the benefit of being totally free and not requiring users to set up any kind of infrastructure (and will work just as well in a private repository as in the public one this project is built off of).

This is very much a work-in-progress, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated! Working on getting comments up and running on my blog, so in the interim email (j...@jonzelner.net) or stan-users is the best way to get in touch if you're interested!

-Jon

> Just in case it's of interest, here's a post on how to get started with Docker for RStan:
>
> http://www.jonzelner.net/docker/reproducibility/2016/06/03/docker/
>
> -Jon
>
> On Wednesday, June 1, 2016 at 8:13:04 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Let me repeat that I'd still love to have this as a demo feature, even if it requires a password so we are the only ones who can run it.
> >
> > > On Jun 1, 2016, at 1:04 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Well, at least 5GB is an upper bound.
> > >
> > > The only reason we haven't built servers for a Stan server
> > > is that we have no way to pay for the hosting.  It should be easy to
> > > set up a server-based version of Stan that operates via HTTP
> > > or some other form of socket.  We wouldn't need Docker for that,
> > > though that might be a dev ops friendly solution.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > >> On May 31, 2016, at 7:42 AM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >>
> > >> To answer Bob's question, the current rstan image is quite large at about 5gb.   It's built on top of the hadleyverse image from Dirk Eddelbuettel's rocker project (https://github.com/rocker-org/rocker), which has a base R install plus all the Hadley Wickham packages as well as a working TeX installation. I think the TeX stuff accounts for a lot of the bloat. Then I added pandoc and cURL and some extra LaTeX fonts. So there's definitely room to pare it down, especially for a stand-alone Stan-machine, particularly if it just ran cmdstan.
> > >>
> > >> Allen's point about running as privileged by default (b/c it needs direct access to the linux kernel) is definitely a sticking point, particularly for working in any kind of HPC environment.
> > >>
> > >> One interesting use case for folks who don't want to run locally that this could help to solve could be to create a server image that runs Stan-as-a-service, potentially taking models and data via an HTTP request and returning a link to the results. It might also be possible to link it to dropbox for something a bit more seamless from the user end? If it was well-packaged, a lab group could download it to a local server with minimal config.
> > >>
> > >> I was thinking it might be easiest for me to write up a 3-part series (Makefiles, Docker, and Gitlab CI) on my relatively lightly-trafficked blog, and then you guys can either link to or post a synopsis or carbon copy of those on the big blog?
> > >>
> > >> -Jon
> > >>
> > >>
> > >> On Monday, May 30, 2016 at 8:22:07 AM UTC-4, Allen B. Riddell wrote:
> > >> Docker support for Windows is new-ish.
> > >> https://docs.docker.com/engine/installation/windows/
> > >>
> > >> One issue with docker is that it runs as a privileged user by default.
> > >> By contrast, you can use a C++ compiler (and Stan) without being a
> > >> privileged user.
> > >>
> > >> A
> > >>
> > >> On 05/29, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > >>> Has anyone tried running this on Windows?
> > >>>
> > >>> How big are the docker images?  How big would it be without
> > >>> R, LaTeX, etc?  I'm wondering how feasible it would be to
> > >>> distribute a working Stan system this way and then communicate
> > >>> with it via protocol buffers.  Then we could have lightweight
> > >>> command-line, R, and Python wrappers.
> > >>>
> > >>> - Bob
> > >>>
> > >>>> On May 27, 2016, at 3:00 PM, Jon Zelner <jze...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >>>>
> > >>>> Hi Folks -
> > >>>>
> > >>>> Just wanted to put a small something I've been working on out there to see what folks think about it.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> This is a stab at making a template for a fully reproducible soup-to-nuts Stan-based project, that starts with input data and ends with a PDF containing figures and estimates derived from the model output. This repository contains all the code needed to re-generate a simple Stan example (fitting a 2-component finite mixture model) with a single command:
> > >>>>
> > >>>> https://gitlab.com/jzelner/reproducible-stan
> > >>>>
> > >>>> The ideas represented here are a crystallization of things that have been going on in a number of other projects of mine that rely on sensitive data and so can't be opened up in a way that is fully reproducible to anyone. There are three big reproducibility ideas in here, some newer than others, none of which are my own but instead represent a synthesis of some very powerful tools and ideas:
> > >>>>
> > >>>> 1) make: Everything is orchestrated using a Makefile that updates outputs as a function of their dependencies on each other. In some ways, this is the most powerful idea and a very old one.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> 2) Docker: One of the challenges of reproducing any project (and Stan ones in particular for non-initiates) is having the relevant software installed locally to both run the Stan model and to do the requisite munging of model output. Docker provides a way to create a portable environment that can run everywhere without forcing users to go through the relatively complicated install process. For example, the example presented here relies on: R, assorted R packages (readr, ggplot2, dplyr, gridExtra), RStan, pandoc, TexLive, etc. The provided Docker image makes it easy to just download the whole environment and re-generate the model results without a complicated local install.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> 3) Continuous integration (CI): CI tools are commonly used in software engineering to make sure that small changes to a project don't break the whole thing. This project is hosted on Gitlab to take advantage of their easy-to-use and free Docker-based continuous integration service. This way, every time a commit is made to the repository, the Makefile is re-run and the model output (MCMC samples, figures and PDF writeup) are uploaded to the repository and are available for download.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> More information (and all the code and output) are available in the repository. It's very much a work-in-progress and is meant more as a prod for more thought and development than anything else, so any feedback would be greatly appreciated!
> > >>>>
> > >>>> -Jon

messages.subject: Non-centered parameterization for standard deviations / variances?
messages.subject_clean: Non-centered parameterization for standard deviations / variances?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a regression model which includes a number of different hierarchical standard deviations for model parameters.

I have used a non-centered parameterisation for the model parameters, but I am wondering whether it is worth using a non-centered parameterisation for the hierarchical standard deviations as well.

Is this really just as simple as doing the standard non-centered parameterisation but constrain the values to be positive, ie
declare a bunch of N(0,1) variables but with <lower=0>, eg stdev_norms<lower=0>[n], and then
Set stdev[i] <- stdev_norms[i]*stdev_prior_width?

Is there a useful non-centered parameterisation of the gamma distribution that can be used in this case, rather than assuming that the stdev variables have a normal hierarchical prior?

Thanks

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Non-centered parameterization for standard deviations / variances?
messages.body_plain:
Non-centering works only for location-scale distributions.
The easiest thing to do would be to use a general linear
model, as in

theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1);
sigma = exp(mu + tau * theta_tilde)

This will limit you to log-normal distributions.  If you wanted
to use a Gamma distribution then you’d have to figure out
a new transform using the properties of the Gamma
distribution, for example https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution#Scaling.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] partially missing data in bivariate normal distribution
messages.body_plain:
Jaslene,

If everything is bivariate Gaussian then you can do everything analytically.

First, split your data into non-missing (which will be two-dimensional)
and missing the second component (which will be one-dimensional).

The non-missing data will be distributed according to the bivariate
Gaussian that you quoted

(y_1, y_2) ~ multi_normal( (mu_1, mu_2), Sigma ),

where Sigma is the 2x2 covariance matrix.

In order to construct the distribution of the missing data we have to
marginalize y_{2} out of the bivariate Gaussian.  Fortunately, this
is straightforward,

y_1 ~ normal(mu_1, sigma_1),

where sigma_1 is the square root of Sigma_{11}.

Your Stan model would then look _something_ like

data {
  int N_nonmiss;
  vector[2] y_nonmiss[N_nonmiss];
  int N_miss;
  real y_miss[N_miss];
}

parameters {
  vector[2] mu;
  cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
}

model {
  // Prior on mu
  // Prior on Sigma, see the manual for examples

  y_nonmiss ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
  y_miss ~ normal(mu[1], sqrt(Sigma[1, 1]);

}

it's actually the observed y[n,1], not the missing

  p(y[n,2] | y[n,1], mu, Sigma)

for maximum efficiency (both in per iteration time and
N_eff per iteration).  Or declare the y[n,2] as parameters if
you need to use them elsewhere.

messages.body_plain:
Indeed.

The default BUGS/JAGS approach is probably not the model of
missingness most people are after.  I had a nice discussion of
this with Merlise Clyde of Duke in the last plus one MCMCski --- she
was telling me about the lengths she went to coding up models for missing data
in BUGS/JAGS (but I don't have a reference) conditioned on other data.
When you do that and define a proper joint distribution, the code
looks much more like Stan code than the direct approach of just plugging
NA into a full-data model.

- Bob

P.S.  Thanks for the reference to the conditional y[n,2] | y[n,1] form.

On Wednesday, June 8, 2016 at 1:43:27 AM UTC-4, Stefano wrote:
> My knowledge in statistics is not enough to understand why a positively and neg correlated matrix is not suitable for multi_norm sampling. Unless the non-positiveness is related to some other property of my data.
> And why a positively defined matrix is required for multi_normal sampling?

It isn't related to any other property of the data. One definition of a positive definite covariance matrix is one that has all positive eigenvalues. You covariance matrix has 6 positive eigenvalues and 500 that are zero. This implies that if you knew any 6 genes for a person, you could figure out the other 500 with certainty. Does that seem reasonable?

The problem is that the maximum likelihood estimator of a covariance matrix is not very good unless the number of rows is large relative to the number of columns, whereas the opposite is true in your case once you transpose the matrix. You should look into shrunken covariance matrix estimators that do not suffer from this problem before attempting to use multi_normal in Stan.

Ben
