messages.body_plain:
Reading about shrinkage covariance estimation for matrices when "the sample size n is small and the number of considered variables p is large" I came across a solution that I adopted already "the diagonal matrix <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagonal_matrix> containing sample variances on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else". [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation_of_covariance_matrices <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation_of_covariance_matrices>]

In asking whether this is a meaningful solution for me, I briefly introduce my problem. I will limit the description to the part here this problem arises, so sorry if it's not as clear as it could be.

In a mixture model

PRODUCT_sample ( PRODUCT_cellType ( PRODUCT_gene (               proportion_cellType_sample ~ dir()    *     expression_gene_cell_type                 )  )  )

having SUM_genes (expression_cell_type) = 1

for expression_gene_cell_type  I could use:

1) a given number being the mean gene expression for cell_type; soft_max transformed
2) a parameter with prior dirichlet(..) with hyperparameter proportional to mean gene expression for cell_type
3) a parameter with prior multi_normal( .. , ..) soft_max transformed

The latter case (3) gives me opportunity to use the variance (of gene expression) information as well.

The question is: in the case I cannot estimate the covariances because the number of samples is small; would it make sense to assume all covariances are 0 (genes independent) and use the variances as diagonal?

messages.body_plain:
You can code it up just how you wrote it:

>    0<alpha, 0<beta<min(alpha,1)

You can code that up directly, but it's an odd constraint (not
differentiable at alpha = 1 and flat with alpha > 1):

  parameters {
    real<lower = 0> alpha;
    real<lower = 0, upper = min(alpha, 1)> beta;

So it might not work well with HMC if the value of alpha is near 1
and it has to cross over the boundary alpha = 1.

But I would suggest not trying to put a hard constraint on
the parameters, but rather something softer and then making sure
the data bears out your prior.

- Bob

enough data to estimate the covariance, you have to fall back
to a diagonal or use a strong prior (the latter being a generic
escape for non-identifiability in a Bayesian model).  In which
case, you'll probably be close to case (2).

messages.body_plain:
I'd suggest just keeping everything on the logit scale
and directly parameterizing alpha with a <lower=0> constraint
and gamma with a <lower=0, upper=1> constraint.

The 3PL model involves many degrees of freedom.  For instance,
a problem that all students answer correctly can be explained
by it being a very easy example or one that is easy to guess.
So I wouldn't expect the relevant parameters to be well defined.

Do the posterior intervals have the right coverage? If so, there's
probably nothing wrong with the model.

The logit scale doesn't upper-bound anything at 0, but I don't
think that's relevant here.  Your transforms look OK.

- Bob

> On Jun 8, 2016, at 4:40 PM, koenig...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Dear All.
>
> Currently I am trying to specify the following hierarchical 3PL Item Response model in Stan. It is an extension of the hierarchical 2PL model illustrated by Furr (in the Stan-Tutorials). The model itself is specified according to Glas & van der Linden (2003). Alpha (item discrimination), beta (item difficulties), and gamma (the pseudo-guessing parameter) are correlated draws from a multinormal distribution and are summarized in a vector ksi in the following way: xi = {log(a), b, logit(c)}.
>
> I specified the model in Stan as follows:
>
> model_3hpl <- '
> data {
>     int<lower=1> I;                 // # items
>     int<lower=1> J;                 // # persons
>     int<lower=1> N;                 // # observations
>     int<lower=1, upper=I> ii[N];
>     int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];
>     int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
>     vector[J] theta;          // # abilities
>     vector[3] xi[I];          // # alpha/beta/gamma vector
>     vector[3] mu;             // # alpha/beta/gamma means
>     vector<lower=0>[3] tau;   // # alpha/beta/gamma res.sds
>     cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Omega;  // # correlation matrix
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>      vector[I] alpha;
>      vector[I] beta;
>      vector[I] gamma;
>       for (i in 1:I) {          // # deriving alpha/beta/gamma from xi
>        alpha[i] <- exp(xi[i, 1]);
>        beta[i] <- xi[i, 2];
>        gamma[i] <- inv_logit(xi[i, 3]);
>       }
> }
>
> model {
>     xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));
>     L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
>
>     theta ~ normal(0,1);
>
>     mu[1] ~ normal(0,1);
>     mu[2] ~ normal(0,5);
>     mu[3] ~ normal(-1,1);
>
>     tau ~ exponential(.1);
>
>      for (n in 1:N)
>         y[n] ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii[n]]+(1-gamma[ii[n]])*inv_logit(alpha[ii[n]]*(theta[jj[n]]-beta[ii[n]])));
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>     corr_matrix[3] Omega;
>     Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
> }'
>
> The model runs, convergence is fairly well. However, I'm afraid there are some misspecifications, because parameter recovery for mu[3] and tau[3] are not that good. The prior on mu[3] is specified as normal(-1,1), since the pseudo-guessing parameter c is on the logit scale and thus is upward bound at zero.
>
> Are there any misspecifications, or do I miss something obvious?
>
> If somebody wants to replicate my results, here is the code for the data simulation, adapted from Furr(2016).

> # Set paramters for the simulated data

> J <- 500

> tau <- c(0.25, 1, 0.75)
> Omega <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 1, -0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 1), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE) #negative corr c & difficulty b
>

> xi <- MASS::mvrnorm(I, c(0, 0, -1.38), Sigma)

> beta <- as.vector(mu[2] + xi[, 2])
> gamma <- inv.logit(as.vector(xi[, 3]))
> theta <- rnorm(J, mean = 0, sd = 1)

> # Assemble data and simulate response

> delta <- alpha[data_list$ii] * (theta[data_list$jj] - beta[data_list$ii])

> Do we then
> need the Jacobian of qr_Q to allow us to put a prior
> on Q?  Or is there a way to put a sensible prior on

A standard normal prior on the elements of Z implies Q is jointly uniform among matrices where Q'Q = I, which is often reasonable. Yeah, I get tripped up by the names. Conceptually, Q * D * Q' is

messages.subject: On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.subject_clean: On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.body_plain:
I see (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments) that there has been discussion of replacing expressions like "y ~ normal(0,1)" with "target += normal(y|0,1)".

With as much humility as I can express while simultaneously questioning the devs' design decisions, I wanted to express that I'm really going to miss the current "~" format. I feel like it helped me, and others I've taught, understand the creation of stan code as an exercise of model expression. I like that with the "~" format you can simply replace characters with words and retrieve grammatical english ( "y~ normal(0,1)" means we're asserting that y is distributed as unit normal...").

I see that the argument was made that the use of "target +=" is more faithful to what Stan is doing behind the scenes computationally, and while I can't say I actually understand said background mechanics to see how the "~" format can lead to problematic misunderstanding, I have to wonder if the increased transparency to Stan's underlying mechanics is worth the more conceptually and visually cumbersome format.

It certainly looks like we'll all be making keyboard shortcuts for typing "target += " :O/

Presumably I'm wrong or an outlier?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject_clean: On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, June 9, 2016 at 3:27:28 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> I see (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-3-Density-Notation-and-Increments) that there has been discussion of replacing expressions like "y ~ normal(0,1)" with "target += normal(y|0,1)".
>
> With as much humility as I can express while simultaneously questioning the devs' design decisions, I wanted to express that I'm really going to miss the current "~" format. I feel like it helped me, and others I've taught, understand the creation of stan code as an exercise of model expression. I like that with the "~" format you can simply replace characters with words and retrieve grammatical english ( "y~ normal(0,1)" means we're asserting that y is distributed as unit normal...").

The '~' seems to get interpreted in two ways that I can tell: 1) "is distributed as"; and 2) "is drawn from ...".  Both of them are wrong since we frequently state priors as, for example, "theta ~ normal(0,1)" when the posterior we sample from is very much not normal... so neither "is distributed as" or "is drawn from" apply.  Both misinterpretations result in a fair bit of mailing list traffic so this is an attempt at making things better.

> I see that the argument was made that the use of "target +=" is more faithful to what Stan is doing behind the scenes computationally, and while I can't say I actually understand said background mechanics to see how the "~" format can lead to problematic misunderstanding, I have to wonder if the increased transparency to Stan's underlying mechanics is worth the more conceptually and visually cumbersome format.
>
> It certainly looks like we'll all be making keyboard shortcuts for typing "target += " :O/

Just replace the "_" shortcut for "<-"... :P

>
> Presumably I'm wrong or an outlier?

I'm pretty sure you have Andrew and Bob (or at least part of Bob) on your side so you could be doing worse.

Krzysztof

>
> Mike
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student
> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject_clean: On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, June 9, 2016 at 3:27:28 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:

> Presumably I'm wrong or an outlier?

Neither. But far too many people are reading theta ~ normal(0,1) as "theta is drawn from a standard normal distribution". Even interpreting theta ~ normal(0,1) as "theta is distributed standard normal" is only correct if you add "a priori" to it. It wasn't an unambiguous decision, and I don't think we have decided how long ~ will continue to be valid syntax. But those of us who supported the change wanted to avoid perpetuating the misunderstandings about how the Stan language relates to the Stan algorithms.

Ben

messages.subject: Is it possible to specify multiple models in a single STAN model file? If so, how?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to specify multiple models in a single STAN model file? If so, how?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am modeling some count data, and wish to try logistic, Poisson, and negative binomial (NB) regression using Bayesian approach. For negative binomial model, I am using gamma-Poisson re-parameterization (like here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/FRWFYxQmhKE>). My goal is to combine the three different model specification into one .stan file, and switch to different model based on a user-defined option, named "model_form" for example. "model_form = 1, 2, 3"  corresponds to logistic, Poisson and NB, respectively. I just use if-else clause in model block to switch to different models.

So far I can combine logistic and Poisson because the difference is just the link function and I can use if-else clause in model block and keep all other blocks the same. However, for NB model, there is an extra parameter. So the parameter block would be different. But the issue is that I cannot declare different parameters based on if-else conditions.

Would anyone encounter this kind of situation? Just wondering what's the best way to approach this. Any comments are highly appreciated! Thank you very much!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.body_plain:
If I understand correctly, the key problem with ~ is that by hiding the
fact that it increments the log density, it confuses people who don't
understand the basics of Bayesian inference.

The implicit hypothesis behind the removal of ~ as a solution seems to
be that by forcing things to be explicit, people who are unfamiliar with
Bayesian inference will be forced to understand what is going on.

While I have my priors about this, I don't have a strong opinion, so try
to keep an open mind --- essentially, this is an experiment in pedagogy,
and it will be interesting to see the outcome.

However, I hope that if things don't work out as expected, the question
will be revisited.

Best,

Tamas

Hi all,

I work for a ML R&D startup. We publish quarterly reports on cool stuff in ML, stats, and CS and build fully functional prototypes using (usually) public data. Currently, we're working on a report (and prototype) on probabilisitic programming. Needless to say, we've been working with stan a lot. Now, we're looking for companies, we'd get most excited about startups, that use probabilistic programming in interesting ways to solve industry problems (my apologies for this somewhat off-topic message).

We've found probabilisitic programming is widely used in academic settings (in a previous life, during a postdoc stint, I used Bayesian approaches to study human cognition). It seems like it's found fewer applications in the industry so far. Of course we believe there is tremendous potential, hence our excitement.

So, if you work with probabilistic programming in an industry setting (or if you know of people that do), I'd love to chat with you about the application of these approaches to real datasets (any experiences, good or bad). The goal is to highlight cool use cases in our report other than the one we'll demonstrate in our prototype (as well as giving some exposure to companies that do interesting work). Please reply to the thread and I'll reach out to you. Thanks! :)

- Friederike

messages.subject_clean: Save the Whole output of shinyStan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mahdi,

There are several possibilities:

1) Create a shinystan object (sso) from your stanfit object using the as.shinystan function:

sso <- as.shinystan(stanfit)
save(sso, file = "sso.rda")

You can then open "sso.rda" on any computer with shinystan installed.

2) A shinystan object is automatically created from a stanfit object when you call launch_shinystan, but to save it you need to assign it to an object, e.g.

sso <- launch_shinystan(stanfit)
save(sso, file = "sso.rda")

3) You can use the deploy_shinystan function to submit your model to RStudio's shinyapps (https://www.shinyapps.io) service and host it online. In the latest release of shinystan there's a bug in the deploy_shinystan function but it's already fixed on the develop branch of the shinystan github repository.

Hope that helps, but let me know if that doesn't answer your question or if any of those options don't work.

Jonah

I've been curious about progress on this as well.

Perhaps my curiosity is driven by my ignorance of CmdStan, but it doesn't seem like it is the the same as calling sample from within a C++ program. When thinking about C++ and Stan, I'm thinking about a similar workflow as R. Basically, I would load and modify some data, run the equivalent of the stan function from rstan in C++, and then do some followup analysis. For instance, suppose I read a large chunk of time series data from a database, I then do some processing on it, and want to do some estimation with Stan and then look at the results.

I'm not sure how easy that workflow is with CmdStan. I don't really see much guidance in the docs. My ignorant thought is that I would have to write the data to a file, but that would be some unnecessary overhead if the amount of data is large.

I'm not sure what the best practice is here. Is it possible to pipe the data? I see some questions from SO on calling exes from within C++ programs, has anyone tried this?

If CmdStan can handle this workflow, then I would be happy.

messages.body_plain:
Daniel's rewriting the services layer so that it will be
like calling CmdStan only from within C++.

All the I/O is handled through callbacks.  var_context
on the reading side, and various write wrappers on the output
side.  That is, there's no serialization format or files
indicated at the C++ API level.

Stanc generates the Stan model class, which has a constructor
which loads data into memory through a var_context.  This instantiated
model class is what's used as an argument to all the algorithms.

You can implement the writers to stream the output data wherever
you want.  It gets called one draw at a time.  CmdStan streams to
a file.

Let us know if you have more specific questions.

- Bob

messages.subject: No plans to remove ~
messages.subject_clean: No plans to remove ~
messages.body_plain:
Tamas:

I do not think there is any immediate plan to remove ~ from Stan.  My impression from recent discussions is that ~ will be kept along with the new notation.

A

> On Jun 10, 2016, at 1:39 AM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@GMAIL.COM> wrote:
>
> If I understand correctly, the key problem with ~ is that by hiding the
> fact that it increments the log density, it confuses people who don't
> understand the basics of Bayesian inference.
>
> The implicit hypothesis behind the removal of ~ as a solution seems to
> be that by forcing things to be explicit, people who are unfamiliar with
> Bayesian inference will be forced to understand what is going on.
>
> While I have my priors about this, I don't have a strong opinion, so try
> to keep an open mind --- essentially, this is an experiment in pedagogy,
> and it will be interesting to see the outcome.
>
> However, I hope that if things don't work out as expected, the question
> will be revisited.
>
> Best,
>
> Tamas
>
> On Thu, Jun 09 2016, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
>> In an ideal world I would love to keep the “~”, but we are not in
>> an ideal world and we have to deal with the reality of many peoples’

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] No plans to remove ~
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] No plans to remove ~
messages.body_plain:
The dev team is split on this one.   I think we understand
the tradeoffs:

* removing it will break backward compatibility and make
  Stan programs more verbose (as well as annoying most users
  and some developers)

* leaving it in will lead to continued misunderstandings
  about what a Stan program does (and annoy all the developers)

What we don't know is how annoyed which groups of people
will be.

In any case, it's not going to even be deprecated any time soon.
2.10 will have a bunch of language changes to support removing ~,
but we're not even all the way there yet (we still need explicit
function calls to log pmfs and log pdfs that drop constants).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Loglogistic distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Loglogistic distribution
messages.body_plain:
If it's this one:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-logistic_distribution

then you can define its log density yourself with a user-defined
function.

  functions {

    real loglogistic_log(real y, real a, real b) {
      return log(b) - log(a) + (b - 1) * (log(y) - log(a))
             - 2 * log1p_exp(b * (log(y) - log(a));
    }

  }

For more efficiency, you want to store and reuse repeated
subexpressions like log(b) and (log(y) - log(a)).
For example, I think that top term reduces to:

  log(b) - log(y) + b * (log(y) - log(a))

and then you can share the product term with the log1p_exp.
Oh, and log1p_exp(u) is log(1 + exp(u)), which allows us to
work on the log scale with u.

Once you know it works, you can put the functions block

messages.subject: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
messages.subject_clean: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
messages.body_plain:
As mentioned on a couple of other threads here, I'm working on using STAN for a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off. Since we are combining data from multiple studies, we try to account for uncertainty with some rigor, acknowledging both the reported errors (imputing them if they are not reported), and the number of repeated measurements taken for each experiment. To reflect these data in the model estimates, I'm using a t distribution to calculate the likelihood of the model given the data and their uncertainty, like so:

regression function: ln(Conc(t))=ln(Conc(0))-K*t

declaration in STAN with scaled data: Conc_s~student_t(df,mu_ln_Conc0-Klin_s*Time_s, sigma_C_s);

where df is set to the number of repeated observations at each time point minus one.

For experiments where pathogens die off in a biphasic pattern, the posterior estimates of K do not converge. Instead, the sampler seems to get stuck in a region that describes the fast rate of decay fairly well, occasionally jumping to the region that describes the line of best fit to all the data, but seeming not to explore the parameter space between these regions in a steady fashion. Is there some reason why this would be an expected behavior? I understand that using a t distribution with low degrees of freedom will make the data far less informative than using the standard normal distribution would (and indeed if I use the normal distribution instead, the model converges to the line of best fit), but I would have thought that the resulting posterior estimates would just be wider, rather than multi-modal.

On Friday, June 10, 2016 at 11:25:00 PM UTC-4, pcoll...@berkeley.edu wrote:
> As mentioned on a couple of other threads here, I'm working on using STAN for a meta-analysis of the effect of temperature on pathogen die-off. Since we are combining data from multiple studies, we try to account for uncertainty with some rigor, acknowledging both the reported errors (imputing them if they are not reported), and the number of repeated measurements taken for each experiment. To reflect these data in the model estimates, I'm using a t distribution to calculate the likelihood of the model given the data and their uncertainty, like so:
>
> regression function: ln(Conc(t))=ln(Conc(0))-K*t
>
> declaration in STAN with scaled data: Conc_s~student_t(df,mu_ln_Conc0-Klin_s*Time_s, sigma_C_s);
>
> where df is set to the number of repeated observations at each time point minus one.
>
> For experiments where pathogens die off in a biphasic pattern, the posterior estimates of K do not converge. Instead, the sampler seems to get stuck in a region that describes the fast rate of decay fairly well, occasionally jumping to the region that describes the line of best fit to all the data, but seeming not to explore the parameter space between these regions in a steady fashion. Is there some reason why this would be an expected behavior?

The distribution of the posterior mean if you have data assumed to be t-distributed is going to be multi-modal (this shows up in some examples in Christian Robert's Bayesian choice), particularly for small numbers of degrees of freedom and a small number of samples.  If you have a larger number of samples or larger degrees of freedom this gets masked unless you have severe "outliers".  .. there are a bunch of other situations with the t distribution where you can get multi-modality.  The intuition here is that with heavy tails there are multiple alternative explanations that are (in your case) equally good.  Unfortunately multi-modality with a deep trough (as in your case, indicated by rare switching) is not something that HMC solves all that well so you have very little information about the relative mass near each mode based on the rare switching.  One solution if you can code your posterior outside of Stan is to use the HMC samples as your importance sampling distribution in importance sampling to correctly re-weight the modes.  It might be less trouble to re-parameterize but I can't come up with the right thing to do at the moment.

messages.body_plain:
You almost always want to work on the log scale to prevent
underflow or overflow, and be careful about precision, so that'd
be:

  loglogistic_cdf_log(real y, real a, real b)
    return -log1p_exp(-b * (log(y) - log(a));
  }

and then you can use it with truncation notation, but you won't
need that if you only need the CDF.  Then you can calculate
the log of mu:

  log_mu[i] <- log(ult[origin[i]]) + loglogistic_cdf_log(dev[i], omega, theta);

You don't then indicate what you want to do with mu, but you
want to avoid going back to the linear scale exp(log_mu[i]) if you
can at all help it.

- Bob

log_sum_exp is critical for computational stats when
you want to avoid underflow to 0 or overflow to 1 in
probability calculations involving sums on the log scale.

  log_sum_exp(a, b) = log(exp(a) + exp(b))

                    = max(a,b) + log(exp(a - max(a,b)), exp(b - max(a, b))

You can see that the exp() now can't overflow since it gets an
argument less than or equal to 0 and you can see that the max(a,b)
term is going to get the leading digits of the result.

So to work with addition and multiplication on the log scale,
we have this

  log(a * b) = log(a) + log(b)

  log(a + b) = log(exp(log(a)) + exp(log(b))

             = log_sum_exp(log(a), log(b))

The first expression computes the log of a*b given the log of
a and the log of b, and the second expression does this for addition.

- Bob

messages.subject: Handling Outliers in Hierarchical Model with Two Parameters for which I estimate the Correlation
messages.subject_clean: Handling Outliers in Hierarchical Model with Two Parameters for which I estimate the Correlation
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have a hierarchical model for which the primary outcome is the relationship between the effect of attention on the following two parameters: Rho and PSS. (The code for .stan model can be found at https://github.com/ghislaindentremont/EndogenousVisualPriorEntry-BayesianHierarchicalModel/blob/master/Baseball/toj_color.stan.)

My model estimates the correlation between these effects (see violin plot of correlation parameter (r), attached). However, I was also interested at looking at the bivariate plot to get a better sense of the relationship of these effects. Therefore, I computed the participant-wise estimates of these effects by adding the estimate (median) of the mean of the effect to the product of the estimate (median) of the SD of the effect and the estimate (median) of the participant-wise deviation of the effect. If you look at the related scatterplot (attached), you'll see that there is at least one outlying point (bottom left) that appears to have a lot of leverage. Although I believe my model is fairly robust to such outliers, I believe that that one point may be having too much leverage on the estimate of the correlation parameter. However, I don't think I want to exclude that participant from the analysis all together...

Is there a way I can deal with this/these outlier(s) within the model to get what might be a better estimate of the correlation coefficient?

You will notice that in the linked code that I use bivariate normals as priors. I am currently running a full analysis (8 chains, 20,000 iterations each) with student_ts with nu = 3 as priors to see how that may effect the model's robustness to outliers. Although, I am not under the impression that it will change much given that the outlying values were within one SD of the normal priors.

If anything is unclear, let me know.

Looking forward to your responses,

Ghislain d'Entremont, BSc., Experimental Psychology Researcher

Hi John,

CmdStan has examples of how you can access the underlying Stan C++ from a C++ executable. We don't have this doc'ed because there hasn't been any real demand for it.

Ulf, to see how this is done, see stan-dev/cmdstan's src/cmdstan directory. See command.hpp (main.hpp just includes and calls command.hpp; this is going to be much simpler in the future). Daniel

On Friday, June 10, 2016 at 3:26:00 PM UTC-4, John Hall wrote:
> I'm not sure what the best practice is here. Is it possible to pipe the data? I see some questions from SO on calling exes from within C++ programs, has anyone tried this?

I don't know of anyone who has tried hard to get this to work, in part because it would be hard. But it is perhaps easier than it was a couple of weeks ago using the DLL sublibrary in Boost 1.61.0

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_61_0/doc/html/boost_dll.html

I speculate that if you compiled your Stan program without a main() function (like how rstan and pystan does it) into a shared object that you could import that using Boost DLL. But it would still be a challenge to do the I/O. In particular, unless you want a CSV file of output, you would have to do something to store the draws in memory. Maybe some of the new writers stuff would help with this.

If I were doing this, I would call R from C++ using the RInside package.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Krzysztof,

      Interesting that the t distribution behaves this way. Subjectively, it seemed to me like the model was choosing to omit the data from the tail of the die-off some of the time, which is exactly what you've described. I'm not sure why it wouldn't also sometimes choose to omit the data from the beginning of the curve and fit only to the tail, or why there is such a deep trough between fitting only the first data or fitting all the data - I would think that, since the likelihood around each data point is heavily tailed, multiple lines that would fit on a spectrum from matching the beginning of the curve extremely to matching the end of the curve extremely well. I guess that would happen if I didn't anchor the intercept, but with an anchored intercept, the density clumps around either the line that only matches the first data but has many residuals close to 0, or the line of best fit to all the data...

    There's a section in the STAN user manual about reparameterizing the t distribution as a normal distribution with gamma distributed standard deviation based on the degrees of freedom. I tried implementing this, but with low degrees of freedom, the scale of the gamma distribution is very large and I was getting lots of divergent transitions.

    The key problem here for what I'm trying to do, though, is that we are really only interested in the line of best fit to the data in this model - we have another model that explicitly fits the two different regions of biphasic data. So I will have to think about an acceptable compromise that will avoid this type of bimodal posterior but can account in some way for our knowledge about the degree of uncertainty in the various data sources as we try to integrate them.

  Phil

> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] On the coming deprecation of ~
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 10, 2016, at 1:39 AM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> If I understand correctly, the key problem with ~ is that by hiding the
> fact that it increments the log density, it confuses people who don't
> understand the basics of Bayesian inference.

The main issue is that we routinely see Stan code such as

  model {
    real y;
    y ~ normal(0, 1);  // rejects because y is not defined

where the author was expecting normal(0, 1) to act like a random number
generator.  Instead, they get a not-a-number warning.

We think it might be clearer if they had to write this:

    real y;
    target += normal_lpdf(y | 0, 1);  // also rejects

This latter syntax has been merged into the develop branch of Stan,
so will be in 2.10.

But we're not even deprecating ~ in 2.10.

Another alternative will be to make sure that variables are defined
before they are used.  The only way to define a variable in Stan is to have
it show up on the left-hand side of an assignment statement, so it
should be easy to detect.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, June 13, 2016 at 1:01:39 PM UTC-4, pcoll...@berkeley.edu wrote:
> Thanks Krzysztof,
>
>
>       Interesting that the t distribution behaves this way. Subjectively, it seemed to me like the model was choosing to omit the data from the tail of the die-off some of the time, which is exactly what you've described. I'm not sure why it wouldn't also sometimes choose to omit the data from the beginning of the curve and fit only to the tail,

Well, the model might have three modes HMC isn't necessarily going to find the third mode.  Another fun context where this comes up is partially observed t-distributed random walks with missing observations.  You can get 3+ modes per missing segment of observations.

> or why there is such a deep trough between fitting only the first data or fitting all the data

Think of the modes as alternative explanations.  The parameter space in between the modes doesn't make sense as an explanation (according to the model).  The other thing to check in this situation is whether the model does a good job of representing the data---when you have this kind of multi-modality sometimes it's just because the model explains so little of the data.

To simplify this have you tried fitting this model with normal distributions assumed all around? Do some model checking at that stage and make sure it says something sensible and you see the problem the t-distribution is needed for.  It's much easier to take a well-behaved model and drop something difficult like heavy tailed distributions into it rather than starting from there.

On Monday, June 13, 2016 at 3:46:08 PM UTC-4, Eric Buhle wrote:
> So at this point I have a few specific/algorithmic questions and a more general one:
>
> (1) I'm trying to understand the relationship between constraint violations and divergent transitions. Partly this reflects my fuzziness on what exactly causes divergences at a computational level, but suppose that somewhere along the NUTS tree, the integrator encounters a divergence. Which point gets retained for that iteration of the HMC chain? The last point (i.e., the chain doesn't move)? Or a slice sample from the points along the path before the divergence occurred? Or...? Ditto for the case when one of the points on the tree violates parameter constraints -- which point gets retained then?

A divergence is caused by the inability to numerically solve with sufficient accuracy the Hamiltonian differential equations for the next position. I believe in 2.9.0, a divergence causes the leapfrogging to stop, and it slices from the pre-divergent leapfrog steps. A constraint violation is different and causes the previous point to be retained.

> (2) Does a constraint violation necessarily (or usually) produce a divergence? If I know the divergences are just telling me about the infeasible holes in parameter space, should I feel reassured about treating them as innocuous?

No. A divergence happens while the constrains are being satisfied, albeit with a transformation from the constrained space to an unconstrained space.

> (3) Do you have any general guidance or best practices for situations like this, where reparameterizing to a dense set is either analytically cumbersome or computationally intractable?

You pretty much have to write a cumbersome Stan program. Can you make h be a vector of primitive parameters between 0 and 1 and define R as a transformed parameter that is equal to C ./ h?

messages.body_plain:
Deep down in the code, constraint violations actually do trigger divergences.
What happens when a constraint is violated is that an exception is thrown
and caught by the MCMC code which sets the log posterior density to
zero (potential to infinity) which the sampler then interprets as a divergence
(technically this _is_ a divergence, albeit an artificial one given the imposed
constraint).  We could potentially consider changing this behavior, although
it would require some changes to the architecture of the MCMC code.

But there are deeper problems here.  In particular, I can guarantee you that
you do not know C as well as you claim to do, because if you did then S would
guaranteed to be larger than C and none of this would be a problem!  What you
want to do is think _generatively_, with C a measurement of some background
rate, which itself is a parameter just the same as the rate for the total observation.  For
example, a very simple model would be

data {
  int<lower=0> C_meas;
  int<lower=0> S;
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> lambda_S;
  real<lower=0> lambds_C;
}

model {
  // priors
  …
  C_mean ~ poisson(lambda_C);
  N ~ poisson(lambds_C + lambds_S);
  … etc
}

_Anytime_ you’re subtracting a “background” you’re asking for trouble
and need to flip your model around to be generative to avoid these kinds
of issues.  Even when you have more complex covariate structure — it
will always be easier to implement generatively.

To get around (2) and (3), it's possible to declare a vector
of unconstrained parameters and do the transforms yourself
to a constrained vector.  These constraints can depend on
each other (as in a simplex) as long as you can compute the
transform and its Jacobian.  That can be a pain, though, even
when it is possible.

If you're dealing with an underlying simplex,
you might want to check if some of the components are collapsing
to zero and you definitely should check that the result is
identified;  if there are non-identifiabilities, Stan can try
really hard to explore a very large space of possibilities,
sometimes triggering numerical issues.

scientists make when trying to build probabilistic models and it leads to no end of
common problems.  If you build up everything generatively then any constraints will
be straightforward to implement and the complexly structured data modeled implicitly
by the forward model that combines all of those simple constraints together.

subtraction”.  In your case you wouldn’t want to follow this exactly but rather replace
the likelihood for C_meas with your complex generative model.

Hi Masih -

Another approach would be to convert the model into discrete time and estimate it directly.

If you normalize the time period to 1 (so that your volatility measures will be interpreted
as volatility over that time period), dt = 1 and dW ~ normal(0, 1). After a bit of re-arranging,
it is a fairly simple model. The trick is coding the dW terms as latent variables which you assign
distributions. If you want to go to higher frequencies, you should appropriately scale the
innovations.

I've provided a worked example here. Please don't follow my bad example: save the model
file in its own .stan file. I've only included the model as a string so that you can run the entire
script and it will work:

https://gist.github.com/khakieconomics/cc085366707388936eb8f7d40ad7b5e7

The model seems to be able to recover known parameters _reasonably_ well, with the
exception of alpha, beta and gamma. gamma in particular doesn't seem to be very strongly
identified. The model seems to be capable of recovering known volatility quite well.

Cheers,
Jim

about the measurement process.  (1) assumes that the signal and
background (or baseline or whatever) is additive, which is consistent
with most data generating processes.  (2) assumes that the signal is

messages.body_plain:
We can’t do anything but speculate without seeing the entire model, and given
what you imply about the model we won’t have time to look at it in the necessary
detail.

But I’ll just add a few comments.

1) There’s a difference between expected background and actual background —
if if you know the expected background exactly you can get substantial variation
from measurement to measurement.  In other words, there’s a huge difference
between

R_meas ~ Poisson(C + S)

and

C_meas ~ Poisson(C)
S_meas ~ Poisson(S)
R_meas = C_meas + S_meas.

Conflicts such as R_meas - C > S_meas almost always come form assuming
the former when it’s really the latter that is appropriate.

2) All of this carries over to time-series or space-time models.  In fact a state-space
perspective is very helpful here — the model is of the underlying rates, both for
signal and background, and the measurement model is how those rates manifest
as an explicit measurement.  The second model above is a very simple example
of this idea, and you can imagine extending it where C and S are time series (or
C is a constant assumed known and S is a time series).

In the end it’s hard to beat the Folk Theorem — if you’re having computational
problems then you’re not really fitting the right model.

data {
  vector[K] theta_lb;
  ...

parameters {
  vector[K] theta_raw;
  ...

transformed parameters {
  vector[K] theta;
  theta <- exp(theta_raw) + theta_lb;
  increment_log_pob(sum(theta_raw));  // log Jacobian of theta_raw -> theta

Now you have theta with varying lower bounds.

messages.subject_clean: Bimodal posterior when using t-distributed errors for linear regression
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, June 13, 2016 at 4:01:30 PM UTC-7, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:

> That's particularly un-cooperative data! Yes I would expect a bi-modal posterior with that.  If you're

> that sure about that initial point I think you will be stuck re-weighting the two modes HMC finds.
>

> I assume this means there will be more data involved too? In that case the bi-modality may just resolve but it really depends on the data and the model.  I would keep both models in the mix just to sort out the computational problems as you build up.
>
> Krzysztof
>

Yes, this is essentially an incorrect model for the data, but we're interested in fitting it because it is common practice to impose an assumption of monophasic die-off in environmental models and risk assessment frameworks because expressions for multiphasic decay are much more difficult to work with, because the proper way to relate the parameters of such expressions to external factors, such as temperature is unclear, and because the mechanisms of multiphasic decay are poorly understood, so it is unclear how to evaluate monophasic and multiphasic data in the same framework.

I don't expect the model integrating data across experiments will resolve the multimodal posteriors, because it adds to the complexity by including a relationship between K (the slope) and temperature, and also because there seems to be a lot of noise in the K~temperature relationship for this particular pathogen, maybe even to the point where there is no K~temperature relationship below 45 degrees C.

I've found an ad hoc way to approximate the uncertainty associated with small numbers of repeated observations by using an empirical function to relate mean standard deviations of the normal distributions of best fit to t distributions, given the degrees of freedom:

sigma_C_t<-(1+1060950*exp(-5.524948*df)).*sigma_C_s;

This seems to do the trick in terms of avoiding multi modality, although there are a handful of divergent transitions in each run.

messages.subject_clean: Imprecise Dirichlet in Stan (for Bayesian rank-sum & signed-rank instead of Wilcoxon/Friedman)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan list/users,

Has anyone implemented something similar to the so called Imprecise Dirichlet Process in Stan?
The authors of a set of papers describing the use of this "IDP" describes it like this on the home page:
"IDP is based on a Prior Near-Ignorance Dirichlet Process. This is the class of all Dirichlet Processes obtained by fixing the prior strength of the Dirichlet Process and letting the normalized base measure vary in the set of all probability measures."
http://ipg.idsia.ch/software/IDP.php

and they provide R (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/IDPSurvival/index.html) and Matlab source code. However it seems the license is GPL so I'd rather have Stan implementations that are fully free and not look at their code.

>From their related papers I found this which seems to describe the general idea ( http://arxiv.org/pdf/1402.2755v2.pdf ):

"...the use of an almost vacuous model which they
call “near-ignorance” or “imprecise” model. This is a model that behaves a priori as a vacuous
model for some basic inferences (e.g., prior mean, prior credible regions) but it always provides
non-vacuous posterior inferences"

and then:

"The main aim of this
paper is to derive a prior near-ignorance DP, called Imprecise DP (IDP). This is the class T of all
DPs obtained by fixing the prior strength of the DP and letting the normalized base measure vary
in the set of all probability measures. We will show that the IDP behaves a priori as a vacuous
model for all predictive inferences. This, together with the fact that it is a nonparametric model,
allows us to start a statistical analysis with very weak assumptions about the problem of interest.
However, contrarily to a full vacuous model, we will show that the IDP can learn from data"

Has anyone seen this or related models implemented in Stan or is there something hindering their implementation?

Any pointers or advice appreciated.

Thanks,

Robert Feldt

messages.body_plain:
Stan requires a fixed parameter set, so the bestyou can
do is approximate a DP with a large-K Dirichlet.

We recommend completely the opposite approach to
priors, which incorporate as much information you have.
There's a wiki page on prior recommendations and also
a long discussion in the manual.

And be careful.  Many purportedly "vague" and "noninformative"
priors usually don't behave the way people expect them to in practice.
For instance, in an LDA model, the scale of the prior has
an enormous impact on the topics found and how many topics
are assigned per document.  Because it's a Dirichlet, the
uniform distribution is Dirichlet(1).  Then when you go
Dirichlet(epsilon) for epsilon << 1, the prior's focusing
increasing weight on there being a sparse solution.

And just a heads up:  RStan and PyStan are under GPL.
It's only the math library, core Stan library, and CmdStan
that are BSD licensed.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Non-Identified Random Effects
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Non-Identified Random Effects
messages.body_plain:
This comes up in IRT (Rasch) models all the time, which
are built up from exactly that structure (with an added
multiplicative invariance).

Given the vectorized multilevel density

  y ~ N(alpha0 + alpha1[group1] + alpha2[group2], sigma)

I'm assuming you have something like these hierarchical priors:

  alpha0 ~ normal(0, const);

  alpha1 ~ normal(0, tau1);

  alpha2 ~ normal(0, tau2);

The priors being centered at 0 will already weakly identify
everything, but not as strongly as if you literally force
the alpha1 and alpha2 to be centered:

  alpha1[1:(K - 1)] <- alpha1_raw;
  alpha1[K] <- -sum(alpha1_raw);

I wasn't sure whether Krzysztof was suggesting that, or
another common approach, which sets

  alpha1[K] <- 0
  alpha2[K] <- 0

The latter will force alpha0 (albeit weakly) to be the right thing
so that alpha0 + alpha1[K] + alpha2[K] is correct.  This approach is also
recommended in Gelman and Hill around the discussion of ideal point models
(a kind of IRT-like voting model).  But I've found it doesn't work so
well in practice if K is large.

Gelman and Hill also recommend subtracting the mean, but as
Krzysztof points out, that produces an improper posterior, so won't
work in HMC (I doubt it actually works in BUGS for the same reason, though
it'll get close because Gibbs doesn't move very fast with correlations).

The problem I often run into if the alpha2 really all should be
roughly zero is numerical, because then you're way down in the neck
of the funnel and need small movements for alpha2 and large movements
for sigma (on the unconstrained scale), thus building in a kind of
ill-conditioning for adaptation.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
That truncation calculation looks right to me.

log(1 / (1 - poisson_cdf(0 | theta[n])))
= -log(1 - poisson_cdf(0 | theta[n]))
= -log(1 - poisson(0 | theta[n]))
= -log(1 - exp(-theta[n]))
= -log1m_exp(-theta[n])

What kind of systematic bias are you seeing?   Are
the intervals right?  Does the limit as you get
more data do the right thing?  Are multiple chains converging
OK as measured by r-hat and are you getting reasonable n_eff
estimates?

- Bob

> On Jun 15, 2016, at 7:56 AM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I have trouble with this simple model:
>
> data {
>   int N;
>   int freqs[N];
> }
> parameters {
>   real mu;
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>   vector<lower=0>[N] theta;
>
> }
> model {
>   theta ~ lognormal(mu, sigma);
>   freqs ~ poisson(theta);
>   for (n in 1:N) increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-theta[n]));
>   //  mu ~ normal(-1, 6);
>   //  sigma ~ lognormal(1, 6);
> }
>
> It is supposed to be a compound lognormal-Poisson model, for frequency data (freqs) with zero frequencies not observed.
> So data typically looks like this:
>     80 69 39 31 29  9  7  7  6  5  4  4  3  3  3  2  2  2  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1
> .. but is longer, so that its length (N) is around 1000-2000.
>
> I see a systematic bias with real data if I make a posterior check by generating draws from (mu, sigma). Also the estimates are clearly off for simulated data, and different from ML estimates from R package sads.
>
> The problem seems to be the censoring and the likelihood correction, as I tried simulated data with vanilla lognormal-Poisson and got good estimates. I have tried to write the likelihood correction with poisson_ccdf as well, and directly without log1m_exp(), with no change.
>
> There is probably something obviously wrong with the model or the approach to correct for missing zeros that I don't see, but what is it? :)
>
> (An equivalent censored gamma-Poisson model with theta integrated out seemed to work fine, although I didn't test it very thoroughly. My Stan is from 2.9.0 from CRAN, installed today, and the compiler is clang.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Noah,

First, which Stan interface are you using? I'd try running CmdStan first to get rid of the interaction with any of the computing platforms.

How do the effective sample sizes look? Are they similar?

I'd try these things:
- change compiler optimization level
- change compiler version
- change compiler (OS X now defaults to clang++)
- make sure to time only the run and not the compile time (compile times vary widely with compilers, versions, and optimization levels)

And I would be very careful about measuring N_eff / s and using that as my comparison instead of wall time. Seeds aren't going to reproduce the same results across platforms (it will reproduce the same results on the same platform with the same compiler, compiler settings, and version of Stan), so comparing behavior for particular seeds isn't a great comparison.

Can you let us know if you find anything useful? (Or even if you dont?)

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, June 17, 2016 at 10:31:56 AM UTC-4, Brandon Whited wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I've read some other discussions about weighting a Bayesian model and it seems that weights are not really valid in a Bayesian sense. I don't understand why and I'm hoping someone can help me with the context of my problem. The situation I am modeling is crop yield. We are measuring yield from varying sizes of fields and would like to put more importance on larger fields. The crop experts' agree that larger fields provide a better estimate of yield and that information should be taken into account. If weights don't exactly make sense from the Bayesian perspective, is there an alternative way of incorporating this information, or could you help me with the intuition about why we don't need weights?

Others have thought more about this but: assume the observation is yield/(m^2 of field), assume you observe only the field-level average yield/(m^2 of field) (or whatever resolution you have), build the model from there.  If one field1 is much larger than field 2, it will have more units where you measured yield in field1 and therefore show up more times in the likelihood. Then you add an observation model that says that you only observe the field-level sum and fit the whole thing in Stan. That's fully coherent but maybe difficult to fit b/c the field sub-unit parameters are going to be completely unidentified without further modeling (has within-field yield variation been quantified?)

 The ad-hoc weighting alternative is skip the observation model and just assume explicitly that the exact field1 observation appears multiple times based on how much bigger the field is.  That's wrong and mis-represents the variance of the field1 measurement but depending on the model there would be approximations that don't do such a rotten job of that.  I don't know that I've seen simulation studies that really get into this but we could do a Stan case study about it.

That's the sketch...

>
> Many thanks!
>

messages.body_plain:
Comments below.

On Thursday, June 16, 2016 at 7:39:37 PM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What kind of systematic bias are you seeing?

Like with data generated from mu=-1, sigma=3, I get estimates mu≈1.37±0.05 (sd)  and sigma=2.06±0.04, while ML from the sads package are for example -0.60±0.25 and 2.78±0.11 (My impression is that even the ML estimates are off the ±2sd limits more than 5% of the time, but they are on the right ballpark at least, and better with larger data.)

Compared to the ML estimates, Intervals from the Stan model seem overly tight.

Making data smaller in the sense of number of counts (N) leads to wider intervals and maybe a bit better estimates, but the intervals are still maybe too narrow. (And mixing gets poor, so it's hard to see what's happening near the prior.)

Increasing data tightens the intervals, but keeps the estimates off (pretty much where they were, so with increasing N it converges into wrong estimates with overly tight intervals).

Making the true sigma smaller makes the estimates closer to true values (which is understandable for the lognormal then kind of vanishes), but mixing gets worse so I can't take the sigma very small. I haven't played with the true mean much.

Posterior means of theta are probably ok, with a downward bias when freq is one or small. (This is ok I guess, for then the lognormal prior gives more evidence than data. At larger values of freq, data totally overrides the prior as it should with Poisson.)

(It somehow it feels like the lognormal is the culprit, but I'm mostly just baffled...)

Chains are ok as far as I can see, in terms of trace plots, r-hat and n_eff. A few (≈ 1–5) numerical problems or divergent transitions are reported.

I tested with bare Poisson, the theta removed but censoring left in, and then the estimates are right. I even tested a lognormal with data and the Poisson thing left out, and it also seems to be fine. :)

All this is with my Mac, but there's an AWS instance available where I could try to run the model later.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero-truncated lognormal-Poisson
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Zero-truncated lognormal-Poisson
messages.body_plain:
You could try translating poisson-lognormal to a regular
normal scale and transforming the result.  That'd at least
verify that all the coding is right.

In your model, it'd be

parameters {
  real mu;
  real log_sigma;
  real log_theta[N];
  }
model {
  log_theta ~ normal(mu, exp(log_sigma));
  freqs ~ poisson_log(log_theta);

  for (n in 1:N) increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-theta[n]));

  mu ~ normal(-1, 6);
  log_sigma ~ normal(3, 6);
}

That should be the same model, only ith the parameters now expressed
on the unconstrained scale.

And to double check the increment_log_prob version, I'd try

  for (n in 1:N)

    freqs[n] ~ poisson_log(log_theta) T[1, ];

I used poisson_log(log_theta), which is equivalent to
poisson(exp(log_theta)).

Are those posterior sd or MCMC std error?  We usually try
to calibrate with 80% or 90% intervals, or even 50% intervals
if there are enough values.

I always get confused on where the logs are happening in the
lognormal, so I'd check that;  the inner term for the
lognormal log density is

  ((log y - mu) / sigma)^2

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It's just like Andrew's eight-schools example (where
you measure test score improvement with standard error
per school).  The data is the measurement plus error.

The kinds of objections people have to weighting
is when it's something like adjusting for population
proportions and there's not a generative model behind
the data collection process.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving warmup adaptation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Improving warmup adaptation
messages.body_plain:
The bonus and pitfall are the same:  increased
adaptation speed.

We haven't really done systematic tuning of those
window parameters across models, so would actually be
interested in what you're observing.

In particular, you want to check that you get to the
same adaptation parameters (step size and mass matrix).
Adaptation converges when it's generated a good enough
set of draws to estimate (co)variance of the typical
set (where most of the posterior mass is and where MCMC
visits).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Weighted LDA - a weight for every pair word-topic
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Weighted LDA - a weight for every pair word-topic
messages.body_plain:
What's detrimental to what goal?

Weighting destroys the generative nature of the model, which is
usually a very bad idea as it makes the results hard to
interpret and it makes the model hard to generalize or combine
with other models.

The log density only matters up to a constant, so your
entire expression doesn't do anything because there aren't any
pareters in it.  Could you say a bit more specifically what
you're going to do?

If you have fixed topic probabilities, then you only need
to estimate the theta for each document (and also the prior,
either a Dirichlet or logistic normal as in the correlated
topic model).  For that, you won't get any effect whatsoever
from a word that has the same probability in each topic.  So
if you have things that feel like stopwords ("the", "is", etc.),
then what you probably want to do is think about a stronger prior
on them in estimating the phi (topic-word probabilities).

- Bob

Hi Stan development team members:

I have been trying to get my toy example running using rstan. I have previously fitted the model in WinBUGS and it works fine but now I would like to converted to stan version as I have heard numerous good things about it.

the model I try to fit is a hierarchical model on 7 categories of species where I model their species abundance estimates recorded as interval (a,b) and parameterised as a bivariate vector (midpoints=(a+b)/2, log (range)=log(b-a)) and fit a multivariate normal distribution to each category of species with its own mean vector and variance and covariance matrix.

However, there is an inherent hierarchical structure within the species and thus I impose constraints on midpoints of each species category.
ie: mu_g[1] (midpoints for global species)= mu_cr[1] (midpoints for coral reefs)+mu_m[1] (midpoints for marine) +mu_t[1] (midpoints for terrestrial) +mu_other[1] (midpoints for all other unobserved species). In addition, mu_t[1]=mu_ar[1](midpoints for arthropods) +mu_insects[1] (midpoints for insects).

In addition, we assume a global correlation matrix for all categories of species and the variance covariance matrix is parameterised to be species-specific diagonal matrix containing standard deviation*global correlation matrix*species-specific diagonal matrix containing standard deviation.

In each category, there are some missing values of log(range).

I use LKJ distribution on cholesky factor of global correlation matrix and fit a multi_normal_cholesky( mean vector, cholesky factor of the covariance matrix) and basically use the most conventional priors on my parameters.

The model did run but it took ages to return the output (much longer comparing to WinBUGS) and unfortunately my results are not converged either.

I think my model is relatively simple and it should not take such a long time for HMC to run, I have attached my stan code and dataset, could someone please suggest me how I can improve the model? Perhaps I overlook some of the aspects?

Thanks so much for your help and advice.

>
> ok. I doubt the mass matrix and step size are 'the same' for the 500 iteration case, but why is the slower adaptation version necessarily the better one?

If everything's working, the adaptation in all chains should
hit roughly the same step size and mass matrix.  Getting to the
right answer faster is better.

> It seems so far the opposite is the case.
> Testing on a more complex model this took fitting time from days or weeks to hours, with good neff in output and no divergences... is there some concern that even with apparently good output results according to all checks, they may be in some way biased by the faster adaptation approach?

It is possible to adapt too quickly and get stuck outside
of the typical set you want to visit for sampling. So we tend to
be conservative in our approach in the hopes that more models adapt
properly.

But as I said last time, we've tried to be conservative with
adaptation and haven't done a lot of testing on different window sizes
or alternative adaptation strategies.

> The manual speaks of 'expanding windows' during slow adaptation - does this mean that if I specify a window of 5, that this is the first window and later windows are larger? how much larger?

Yes.  They double each time up until the final window.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hard to say without more details.  Stan requires
the log density function that you define to be differentiable
with respect to the parameters.  So if you have an
iterative algorithm, Stan will just autodiff that iterative
algorithm.  It can work in some cases, but isn't ideal
in terms of efficiency or arithmetic accuracy and stability
when compared to working out a second iterative algorithm
for the derivatives.  That is, the accuracy guarantees for
iterative approximations of functions don't automatically carry
over to their derivatives.

I'd suggest you try it and see what happens.  Do you have
a way to simulate data according to the model and see if you
can recover the parameters?

- Bob

messages.subject: Missing binomial data in a meta-analytic epidemiological model
messages.subject_clean: Missing binomial data in a meta-analytic epidemiological model
messages.body_plain:
Hey Everyone!

Background

I am developing an epidemiological model to estimate the prevalence of a series of eight separate but related mental disorders. The available data represent published studies measuring two or more of those disorders – although the number of disorders measured by a given study varies (e.g., some studies measure only 2 disorders, a few measure all 8). The estimated prevalence for any given disorder is quite rare in the target population (some are as low as 1%) although there is considerable heterogeneity across estimates. The data itself is structured as follows within R:

head(dat)

#   studyid disorderid samplesize count
# 1       1          1        453     6
# 2       1          2        453     4
# 3       1          3        453     1
# 4       1          4        453     4
# 5       1          5        453    12
# 6       1          6        453    90

In this respect, studyid represents the study identifier (e.g., studyid=1 means Study 1); disorderid represents the disorder identifier (e.g., disorderid=1 means Disorder 1); samplesize represents the size of the relevant sample; and, count represents the number of patients found to suffer from a given disorder in a given sample.

Model Summary

The model applies a binomial likelihood function to each value of count with N equal to samplesize and theta equal to the estimated prevalence for each disorder within a given study. To account for between-study variability, I adopt a random-effects/hierarchical approach whereby the prevalence for a given study is modelled as a multivariate normal distribution with unknown means and a covariance matrix representing the combination of the between-study SDs and the between-study correlations amongst the disorders. I have implemented several optimizations (e.g., using a Cholesky factorization) recommended in the manual to improve convergence. The present model converges quickly with acceptable effective N values. Application to simulated data also reveals this model to perform quite well. The Stan code is appended. If needed, I could provide some R code to simulate data suitable to test the model.

Problem

My question has to do with missing data. Despite the model performing well in its current form, it occurs to me that any disorders unmeasured by a given study represent a case of missing data that should be incorporated into the model. I already estimate the logit-transformed prevalence for each disorder within each study (in the study_estimates parameter) – including the missing values; however, I do not model a corresponding count estimate for those missing values. I understand how this would be accomplished for a continuous dependent measure – but I understand this is not so simple for discrete measures. Instead, the recommendation appears to be marginalizing out the missing data. I was hoping someone could advise me on how to do so for a binomial measure – or point me in the direction of an example dealing with a binomial likelihood function. Just to be clear, I have the samplesize, studyid and disorderid for each missing value.

Of course, any advice on further improvements (or cautions on things I may have done wrong) are also most welcome. This message board (and the excellent documentation for Stan itself) has already proven invaluable!

Cheers,
Jon

messages.subject: Solving the 1D diffusion equation (a PDE) using Stan
messages.subject_clean: Solving the 1D diffusion equation (a PDE) using Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have been playing around with Stan's ``integrate_ode'' functionality - really nice by the way! I was wondering - how easy would it be to do inference for a PDE model in Stan?

As an example, I have been trying to infer the diffusion parameter for a 1D diffusion equation:

du/dt = D d^2 u / dx^2

where u=u(x,t) measures a population density of some species, and D is the diffusion coefficient. Further, suppose that we know the initial conditions: u(0,t) = f(x), as well as (Dirichlet) boundary conditions: u(x,0) = 0, and u(x,L) = 0. Finally if we assume a normal sampling model about the mean u(x,t), then we have an inference problem.

Typically we would solve this equation by some sort of finite difference method, where we discretise in both x and t. However, if we have a decent integrator, then we should be able to just discretise in distance, and then use the time integrator for each grid point in x. If we use a centralised finite difference approximation for x, then this amounts to integrating:

d v(i,t) / dt = D [v(i+1,t) - 2 v(i,t) + v(i-1,t)] / 2h

where v(i,t) is the approximate solution at grid point i at time t, and h is the step size.

Ideally I was hoping we could use Stan's integrate_ode function for each of the grid points i, to calculate the mean v(i,t), and then use that to increment the log probability by: ~ normal(v(i,t), sigma). At the moment however, I am a little unclear as to how to do this.

My thoughts were that we could essentially do the following at each time step:

vector[T] yHat;
for(i in 1:N){
    real y_hat_individual[T,1];
    y_hat_individual <- integrate_ode()
}

However, I'm not sure how to write the derivative function (that takes three values of v, and returns a single derivative as per the above finite difference approximation.)

Does anyone have an idea as to how I would do this?

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Solving the 1D diffusion equation (a PDE) using Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Solving the 1D diffusion equation (a PDE) using Stan
messages.body_plain:
ODEs, while by no means trivial, are relatively straightforward
and hence admit general solvers like CVODE that we can plug
into the Stan Math Library.  PDEs, however, are much, much
more complicated and don’t admit such generic solvers, hence
we cannot hope to have anything like a generic “integrate_pde”
solver.  Unfortunately PDEs require expert-motivated, bespoke
solvers and the methods are evolving so quickly that there aren’t
the generic libraries we would need to easily be able to integrate
even these bespoke methods into Stan.

That means you’ll have to make approximations and argue their
validity on a case by case basis.  Discretizing over space is one
such approximation which can be okay in some cases and
disastrous in others.  You can also discretize over space and
time, giving you something equivalent to a (hopefully sparse)
spatial model — see any of the INLA doc for much more on this
approach.

I know, and I second my initial response.  A good discretization, both in
terms of design and implementation, requires expert knowledge of the

messages.body_plain:
Change to normal() and log_sigma did not change anything. The likelihood correction term needed an extra exp(),
 for (n in 1:N) increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(exp(-log_theta[n])));
that was not in your changes.

The truncation syntax then: it destroys any mixing of the chains (5000 iterations):

(I have actually tried truncation syntax before, but didn't mention it, because it is a bit separate issue.) Does this mean that the likelihood correction is wrong? Well, the same likelihood correction term works with a bare Poisson model without the normal/lognormal layer. I haven't tried truncation syntax there.

BTW, these are the chains with the manual correction term (500 iterations):

My sd's are posterior standard deviations, and they were there to compare with the ML estimate which gives approximate sd's. The (false) posteriors seem normal enough to make the sd estimates robust.

On Friday, June 17, 2016 at 10:11:32 PM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You could try translating poisson-lognormal to a regular

> In your model, it'd be
>
> parameters {

>   real log_sigma;
>   real log_theta[N];
>   }
> model {
>   log_theta ~ normal(mu, exp(log_sigma));
>   freqs ~ poisson_log(log_theta);
>   for (n in 1:N) increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-theta[n]));
>   mu ~ normal(-1, 6);
>   log_sigma ~ normal(3, 6);
> }
>
>
> That should be the same model, only ith the parameters now expressed
> on the unconstrained scale.
>
> And to double check the increment_log_prob version, I'd try
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     freqs[n] ~ poisson_log(log_theta) T[1, ];
>
> I used poisson_log(log_theta), which is equivalent to
> poisson(exp(log_theta)).
>
> Are those posterior sd or MCMC std error?  We usually try
> to calibrate with 80% or 90% intervals, or even 50% intervals
> if there are enough values.
>
> I always get confused on where the logs are happening in the
> lognormal, so I'd check that;  the inner term for the
> lognormal log density is
>
>   ((log y - mu) / sigma)^2
>
> - Bob

I had a similar problem recently and 'hanging' was caused by the integrator getting stuck for high parameter values. To solve this I put upper bounds on parameters which helped. I know this isn't ideal since we want to avoid using these sorts of ``cutoff'' priors, but thought I'd let you know what helped me.

I see that you have quite a few parameters that have no upper bounds; perhaps try putting upper limits on them?

I think this issue is going to be fixed for the next release of Stan (2.10.0); however someone in the know please correct me if I'm wrong.

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] overestimated standard deviation of random effect
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] overestimated standard deviation of random effect
messages.body_plain:
Let’s assume that you’re using a uniform prior on
the standard deviation of the hierarchical distribution.
For sd = 0.1, there is finite mass below but infinite
mass above, hence the prior will bias the fit high.
For sd = 1 the same thing happens.  In fact, for
any finite value of sd there is infinite mass above
that value which can bias the fit high.  In other
words, “diffuse” priors aren’t actually uninformative,
they actually impose a huge amount of information
that large values are okay.

What you are seeing in an issue of incoherency
where that prior bias towards large values is
inconsistent with your prior knowledge that the
sd has a reasonable value.  So you’ll need a
prior that is consistent with that knowledge,
for example a half Cauchy or half Normal
with scale on the order of the variation you’d
expect in the population.

messages.subject: NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.subject_clean: NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.body_plain:
The notebook in this repository shows the results of a very simple one parameter Bernoulli model with NUTS and ADVI.

https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/blob/master/stanadvi.ipynb

The trivial model is taken from the cmdstan manual (although the for loop has been replaced with a vectorized version).

The notebook only uses pystan to write the data in R format. The stan compilation and execution is handled by an up to date pull of the develop branch of cmdstan. You should be able to reproduce the results by doing `git clone --recursive https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/` <https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/> then doing `make stan-update` in the cmdstan directory, then running the notebook.

The NUTS results are great: the MAP estimate of p pretty much exactly matches the true value nine times out of nine, and the width of the posterior is within 2 signifiant figures of the expected (frequentist) width sqrt(p*(1-p)/N).

The ADVI results are not as good. Agreement with the true value is rare, and the posterior mean and variance varies from run to run.

I have a bunch of questions:
 1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
 2) what's a good ELBO score? The larger the better? Are the values seen here (-6e3) a sign of a problem?
 3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
 4) is ADVI simply not appropriate for this problem? If so, given the trivial nature of the model (and that it is the first example in the cmdstan model), what kind of model would be OK with ADVI?
 5) or is ADVI as implemented in (cmd)stan not ready for public consumption without great care over convergence/initialization? NUTS seems pretty idiot proof, but is that less true of ADVI?

And a bonus question, which is I think unrelated to this problem: why isn't the example listing on p9 of the the cmdstan manual vectorized? What's with the for loop? :-)

Thanks,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've slowly been expanding a complicated hierarchical model: I evaluate the effects of three between-subject and one within-subject variables on four outcome variables. Initially, I included no interaction terms and the model ran fine, giving sensible results (as per intuition + PPC). However, as I've been adding interaction terms - the model attached includes four-way interactions (full factorial) - the model has been throwing more errors when I try to run it. Namely: "Error in function boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<double>(double,double): numeric overflow" and "Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value", and, fatally, "Initialization between (--2, -2) failed after 100 attempts".

Does anyone have any immediate ideas as to what the problem might be and/or potential solutions to it? Or, does anyone have any suggestions about how to troubleshoot this?

I am really hoping someone can provide some insight without having to dive into the details of the model, since, understandably, it is rather elaborate at this point.

Cheers,

Ghislain d'Entremont

> > Hello all,
> >
> > I am working on a problem where we track animal paths over time. In particular we track animal's angle of motion relative to their previous path, and want to build a model for angle of motion. Our initial thoughts were to use the Von Mises distribution.
> >
> > However, the distribution of angles moved by the animals has much fatter tails than the Von Mises (itself basically a circular normal.) Data that looks similar to our real data can be generated via the following in R:
> >
> > library(CircStats)
> > phi <- rwrpcauchy(1000000,pi,rho = 0.7)-pi
> > hist(phi,100)

> > Basically what we would ideally like to do is to use a more robust version of the Von Mises; equivalent to replacing the normal by a Student t or Cauchy in non-circular statistics. There is a circular version of the distribution I describe: it is called the wrapped Cauchy distribution (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrapped_Cauchy_distribution) - the same distribution I used to generate the above.
> >
> > My question is - how can I fit a similar distribution in Stan? I was thinking that basically I could do something like:
> >
> > phi ~ von_mises(0,kappa);
> >
> > kappa ~ gamma(a,a);

> > So basically use a mixture of Von Mises to yield something like a wrapped Cauchy. (This is through analogy of representing a Student T as a mixture or normals).

> > I have tried the above however, and it doesn't seem to work; the posterior predictive distribution for phi looks pretty much the same as for the vanilla Von Mises.

That is confusing.  Why doesn't anyone indent?  That's
a serious question --- we just get file after file from
people with no indentation at all and no spacing, which
makes these programs really hard to scan.

I'd recommend:

* just defining LGC3 directly rather than by constructing J
  full of zeroes and multiplying (lots of useless multiply adds,
  which are relatively slow).

* vectorizing the definitions of mu (just over i if that's
  all that's possible --- I didn't slog through the actual definitions).

* don't use N and n as constants and then define N x n structures
  (this is taste more than anything else)

* and speaking of taste, please, please, indent --- I don't know how
  anyone can read or work with all this non-indented code --- it's
  very hard to scan

* vectorize

for(j in 1:N){
X[j] ~ normal(mu[j], sd_x );
}

as

  to_vector(X) ~ normal(to_vector(mu), sd_x);

by definining X to be a matrix.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.body_plain:
NUTS doesn't provide a MAP estimate.  Optimization provides
the MAP estimate.  You also don't get the frequentist posterior
interval.  The posterior for the simple Bernoulli is a beta
distribution, and it's not even symmetric unless alpha = beta.

Your question (1) is the key thing we've been asking ourselves.

Alas, NUTS isn't completely robust, but we've tagged ADVI
as experimental (I hope that's clear in the interfaces), precisely
because we don't know how to characterize when it will work or
how to make it signal that it's gone wrong.

- Bob
