You need to track down where your program runs into errors.
That's why we included print() statements, but there's a hitch.
I think all of our interfaces are broken in that they don't print
if the model block rejects---you only see the rejected message.
And I'm afraid this didn't get fixed in 2.10 because we never
created an issue with a 2.10 milestone.  I'm going to fix that.

So you need to remove everyting in your model and build it up
a bit at a time to see where the numerics go bad.

messages.subject: Bayesian principal component analysis in STAN and JAGS using LOO as comparison
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian principal component analysis in STAN and JAGS using LOO as comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi every,

motivation
the motivation was to run a bayesian PCA and compare the
performance via the LOO Package with JAGS and STAN.

results
1. The good news is that STAN and JAGS performing similar considering the looic, et al.
when using cholesky decomposition in STAN and wishart distribution in JAGS.
2. The QR factorization of Ben to gain the eigenvalues/eigenvectors didn't performed well.
The looic value doubled.
3. JAGS execution time is <1s, whereas STAN about order 20-30 times slower.

sources
The JAGS/BUGS model based about code by Petr Keil.
http://www.petrkeil.com/?p=2316

can be downloaded directly from:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/petrkeil/bPCA/master/man/PCA.bugs

I didn't included it.

I also did a variante using QR decomposition based upon the idea of Ben Goodrich
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/JAD/stan-users/1-kJN4pu3vg/yyaaJF8kOAAJ

The JAGs parallel calling was inspired by Andrew Gelmann using the lecuyer module.

Questions
1. Can the PCA.stan be improved to match JAGS execution speed?
2. Did I make a mistake in coding PCA_qr.stan?

Thank you so much,
Andre

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.

So for now it seems like ADVI can't be used for very simple problems that appear in the documentation. Do you happen to know if that's an inherent limitation of the algorithm, or of Stan's implementation?

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.body_plain:
Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
designed.

You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical
understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan
was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical
understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early
results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough
to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.

This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
against its use in production analysis.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.body_plain:
Variational inference is a very general technique that arguably
includes EP as well as the various forms of hand-tuned VB (custom
approximations to go with the models).

ADVI uses a multivariate normal (diagonal or dense covariance)
approximation to the posterior and some other approximations for
computing (Alp's paper is super clear on all this).  As far
as we know, there aren't bugs in the implementations and we don't
suspect implementations are an issue.

So this doesn't say anything much about how other variational
inference schemes might or might not work.

- Bob

> On Jun 22, 2016, at 6:45 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
> is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
> becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
> particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
> and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
> it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
> designed.
>
> You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
> a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
> beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
> NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical
> understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan
> was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical
> understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early
> results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough
> to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
> are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
> any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.
>
> This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
> against its use in production analysis.
>
> On Jun 22, 2016, at 3:25 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Hi Bob,
>>
>> Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.
>>
>> So for now it seems like ADVI can't be used for very simple problems that appear in the documentation. Do you happen to know if that's an inherent limitation of the algorithm, or of Stan's implementation?
>>
>> Mike
>>
>> On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 03:10:22 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> NUTS doesn't provide a MAP estimate.  Optimization provides
>> the MAP estimate.  You also don't get the frequentist posterior
>> interval.  The posterior for the simple Bernoulli is a beta
>> distribution, and it's not even symmetric unless alpha = beta.
>>
>> Your question (1) is the key thing we've been asking ourselves.
>>
>> Alas, NUTS isn't completely robust, but we've tagged ADVI
>> as experimental (I hope that's clear in the interfaces), precisely
>> because we don't know how to characterize when it will work or
>> how to make it signal that it's gone wrong.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>> > On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:27 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> >
>> > HI, Mike.  It's good to have this sort of example.  My quick answer is that the way to check that ADVi is giving reasonable results is by simulating fake data from the fitted model.  We are currently working on general guidelines for this idea.
>> > Andrew
>> >
>> >> On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:21 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>
>> >> The notebook in this repository shows the results of a very simple one parameter Bernoulli model with NUTS and ADVI.
>> >>
>> >> https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/blob/master/stanadvi.ipynb
>> >>
>> >> The trivial model is taken from the cmdstan manual (although the for loop has been replaced with a vectorized version).
>> >>
>> >> The notebook only uses pystan to write the data in R format. The stan compilation and execution is handled by an up to date pull of the develop branch of cmdstan. You should be able to reproduce the results by doing `git clone --recursive https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/` <https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/> then doing `make stan-update` in the cmdstan directory, then running the notebook.
>> >>
>> >> The NUTS results are great: the MAP estimate of p pretty much exactly matches the true value nine times out of nine, and the width of the posterior is within 2 signifiant figures of the expected (frequentist) width sqrt(p*(1-p)/N).
>> >>
>> >> The ADVI results are not as good. Agreement with the true value is rare, and the posterior mean and variance varies from run to run.
>> >>
>> >> I have a bunch of questions:
>> >>  1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
>> >>  2) what's a good ELBO score? The larger the better? Are the values seen here (-6e3) a sign of a problem?
>> >>  3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
>> >>  4) is ADVI simply not appropriate for this problem? If so, given the trivial nature of the model (and that it is the first example in the cmdstan model), what kind of model would be OK with ADVI?
>> >>  5) or is ADVI as implemented in (cmd)stan not ready for public consumption without great care over convergence/initialization? NUTS seems pretty idiot proof, but is that less true of ADVI?
>> >>
>> >> And a bonus question, which is I think unrelated to this problem: why isn't the example listing on p9 of the the cmdstan manual vectorized? What's with the for loop? :-)
>> >>
>> >> Thanks,
>> >> Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian principal component analysis in STAN and JAGS using LOO as comparison
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian principal component analysis in STAN and JAGS using LOO as comparison
messages.body_plain:
I looked at PCA Cholesky and it's about as good as you're going to
be able to code this in Stan.

We don't care about execution time---we care about n_eff/second (or
its inverse, second/n_eff) and to a lesser extent, convergence rate.
And you want to use Stan's posterior analysis, because it's much more
conservative about convergence than the techniques currently built into
JAGS/Coda.

Some of the issue is that if you have good conjugate priors and
the problem's not that hard, Gibbs can be really fast.

Also, those predictive computations in generated quantities are
going to kill you speed-wise, because each of those
multi_normal_log things requires factoring the matrix.  We really
need to vectorize these.  You should also be able to use the
multi_normal_cholesky() directly for the multi_normal_log calls.

- Bob

P.S.  You don't seem to be using all your data in that program, but Stan's
OK with that.

messages.subject: multiplicities in STAN
messages.subject_clean: multiplicities in STAN
messages.body_plain:
Quick question ...

In the HMC STAN uses, there is a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance criteria applied to new proposal points.  Normally, if rejected, the current point is repeated in the M-H acceptance algorithm.  Usually, this is specified by assigning a multiplicity to the points -- e.g. the number of times a point is repeated.  In the STAN output (via the "extract()" member method in pystan) there seems to be neither multiplicity values nor are points repeated in the chain.  I'm confused why multiplicities are not specified ... Could you please explain? -- Thank you.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Priors for spatial lengthscale
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for spatial lengthscale
messages.body_plain:
Christopher, have you tried using an inverse-lengthscale parameterization? You simply change this:

    Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2));

to

    Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist*(2*spatialScale^2));

I find this a more intuitive parameterization as values from 0-1 imply near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1), making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for simpler functions.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

On Tue, Jun 21, 2016 at 6:12 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The length scale shrinking to zero does not give
> you an identity covariance but rather a covariance
> where all entries are unity, which is not positive-definite
> and hence will frustrate the Cholesky decomposition.
>
> A prior will still be helpful, but you really need to add
> a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another
> possible parameter, to Sigma_spatial to regularize the
> covariance.
>
> On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I'm trying to model the mean values of data collected from a number of sites where means at each site can be spatially autocorrelated.  I used a squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough for me to think that it's a substantial problem.
> >
> > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation) while still having sufficient mass in the tail to allow for substantial spatial signal.  I've tried a variety of options (half Cauchy, half student_t, exponential), but none seem to have improved anything.
> >
> > Is there something else wrong with this model?  Should I be using a different covariance function? Does anyone have any suggestions or advice for the prior?
> >
> > Thank you
> >
> > /* Model Objectives:
> > Estimate the mean value at each site and the grand mean.
> > Allow for standard deviation to vary among sites
> > Account for spatial autocorrelation of means among sites
> > */
> > data{
> >   int n; // observations
> >   int nSite; // sites
> >   int siteID[n]; // which site belongs to each obs.
> >   vector[n] x;
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] Dist; // Distance matrix, pre-scaled so the minimum distance is 1
> > }
> > transformed data{
> >   real xScale; // the range of x divided by 4, to establish a reasonable scale for priors
> >   real xMean;
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] sqDist; // pre-compute squared distance matrix
> >   xMean <- mean(x);
> >   xScale <- (max(x) - min(x))/4;
> >   for(i in 1:nSite) for(j in 1:nSite)
> >     sqDist[i,j] <- Dist[i,j]^2;
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<lower=0> spatialScale; // spatial lengthscale;
> >   real grandMean; // overall mean of x
> >
> >   // Non-central parameterizations; use is defined in next block
> >   vector[nSite] raw_siteMean;
> >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_siteSD;
> >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_indSDHier;
> >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[nSite] raw_indSD;
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   vector[nSite] siteMean; // mean of x at each site
> >   real siteSD; // stdev of siteMean
> >   real indSDHier; // overall stdev of x around the sitemeans
> >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> >
> >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential covariance
> >   L_Sigma_spatial <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_spatial);
> >
> >   siteSD <- tan(raw_siteSD) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> >   siteMean <-  siteSD *
> >     L_Sigma_spatial * // comment out this line to remove spatial dependence
> >     raw_siteMean + grandMean; // ~ MVN_chol(grandMean, siteSD*L_Sigma_spatial);
> >   indSDHier <- tan(raw_indSDHier) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> >   for(i in 1:nSite)
> >     indSD[i] <- indSDHier * tan(raw_indSD[i]); // ~half-cauchy(0, indSDHier)
> > }

> >   raw_siteMean ~ normal(0,1);
> >   spatialScale  ~ cauchy(0, 1); // A variety of other priors have been attempted, including student_t and exponential

> > }

messages.body_plain:
There's no Metropolis step in NUTS.  See the Hoffman
and Gelman JMLR paper.

In basic HMC, if you simulate the Hamiltonian accurately, the
acceptance probability is 100%, but that's not usually
a good tradeoff for speed (because you need a low step
size).

In either algorithm, you can get repeated draws.

Just dumping out all the draws is more conventional in
my experience, as it feeds more neatly into things like
the autocorrelation algorithm we use for computing effective
sample size.  We could do counts when there are repeats, but
then we'd have to change all of our downstream algorithms.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multiplicities in STAN
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] multiplicities in STAN
messages.body_plain:
I have never seen a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm specified
by such a multiplicity so I can’t claim that I fully understand
your question.  Almost every Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
coming out of statistics is specified by the average acceptance
probability.

The NUTS sampler in Stan is more subtle as it’s not a
straightforward Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.  Instead of
trying to jump to just one point we try to jump to all points
in the trajectory, and when those trajectories are nontrivially
long the probability of staying at the initial point is very small.
Of course this is what you want, as many repeats of a single
state indicate very low acceptance probabilities and hence
very large autocorrelations.

messages.body_plain:
I think he meant that rather than repeating draws in the
output, you'd just record how many times each one was seen.
That can be more compact and more efficient for calculating
expectations, especially if the number of repeats is high
compared to the number of parameters.

- Bob

> On Jun 23, 2016, at 12:04 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> by such a multiplicity so I can’t claim that I fully understand
> your question.  Almost every Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
> coming out of statistics is specified by the average acceptance

> The NUTS sampler in Stan is more subtle as it’s not a
> straightforward Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.  Instead of
> trying to jump to just one point we try to jump to all points
> in the trajectory, and when those trajectories are nontrivially
> long the probability of staying at the initial point is very small.
> Of course this is what you want, as many repeats of a single
> state indicate very low acceptance probabilities and hence

On Wed, Jun 22, 2016, at 09:58 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Christopher, have you tried using an inverse-lengthscale
> parameterization?
> You simply change this:
>
>     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2));
>
> to
>
>     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist*(2*spatialScale^2));
>
> I find this a more intuitive parameterization as values from 0-1 imply
> near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1),
> making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for
> simpler functions.
>
>
> --
> Mike Lawrence
> Graduate Student
> Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> Dalhousie University
>
> ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
>
>
> On Tue, Jun 21, 2016 at 6:12 PM, Michael Betancourt
> <betan...@gmail.com>
> wrote:
>
> > The length scale shrinking to zero does not give
> > you an identity covariance but rather a covariance
> > where all entries are unity, which is not positive-definite
> > and hence will frustrate the Cholesky decomposition.
> >
> > A prior will still be helpful, but you really need to add
> > a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another
> > possible parameter, to Sigma_spatial to regularize the
> > covariance.
> >
> > On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <
> > christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm trying to model the mean values of data collected from a number of
> > sites where means at each site can be spatially autocorrelated.  I used a
> > squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation
> > matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it
> > also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough
> > for me to think that it's a substantial problem.
> >
> > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I
> > think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the
> > spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to
> > near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation)
> > while still having sufficient mass in the tail to allow for substantial
> > spatial signal.  I've tried a variety of options (half Cauchy, half
> > student_t, exponential), but none seem to have improved anything.
> >
> > Is there something else wrong with this model?  Should I be using a
> > different covariance function? Does anyone have any suggestions or advice
> > for the prior?
> >
> > Thank you
> >
> > /* Model Objectives:
> > Estimate the mean value at each site and the grand mean.
> > Allow for standard deviation to vary among sites
> > Account for spatial autocorrelation of means among sites
> > */
> > data{
> >   int n; // observations
> >   int nSite; // sites
> >   int siteID[n]; // which site belongs to each obs.
> >   vector[n] x;
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] Dist; // Distance matrix, pre-scaled so the minimum
> > distance is 1
> > }
> > transformed data{
> >   real xScale; // the range of x divided by 4, to establish a reasonable
> > scale for priors
> >   real xMean;
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] sqDist; // pre-compute squared distance matrix
> >   xMean <- mean(x);
> >   xScale <- (max(x) - min(x))/4;
> >   for(i in 1:nSite) for(j in 1:nSite)
> >     sqDist[i,j] <- Dist[i,j]^2;
> > }
> > parameters{
> >   real<lower=0> spatialScale; // spatial lengthscale;
> >   real grandMean; // overall mean of x
> >
> >   // Non-central parameterizations; use is defined in next block
> >   vector[nSite] raw_siteMean;
> >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_siteSD;
> >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_indSDHier;
> >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[nSite] raw_indSD;
> > }
> > transformed parameters{
> >   vector[nSite] siteMean; // mean of x at each site
> >   real siteSD; // stdev of siteMean
> >   real indSDHier; // overall stdev of x around the sitemeans
> >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> >
> >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential
> > covariance
> >   L_Sigma_spatial <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_spatial);
> >
> >   siteSD <- tan(raw_siteSD) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> >   siteMean <-  siteSD *
> >     L_Sigma_spatial * // comment out this line to remove spatial dependence
> >     raw_siteMean + grandMean; // ~ MVN_chol(grandMean,
> > siteSD*L_Sigma_spatial);
> >   indSDHier <- tan(raw_indSDHier) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> >   for(i in 1:nSite)
> >     indSD[i] <- indSDHier * tan(raw_indSD[i]); // ~half-cauchy(0,

> > }

> > > you an identity covariance but rather a covariance

> > > a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another

> > > squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation
> > > matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it
> > > also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough
> > > for me to think that it's a substantial problem.

> > > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I
> > > think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the
> > > spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to
> > > near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation)

> > >   int nSite; // sites

> > > }
> > > parameters{
> > >   real<lower=0> spatialScale; // spatial lengthscale;
> > >   real grandMean; // overall mean of x
> > >
> > >   // Non-central parameterizations; use is defined in next block
> > >   vector[nSite] raw_siteMean;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_siteSD;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_indSDHier;
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[nSite] raw_indSD;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters{
> > >   vector[nSite] siteMean; // mean of x at each site
> > >   real siteSD; // stdev of siteMean
> > >   real indSDHier; // overall stdev of x around the sitemeans
> > >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> > >
> > >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> > >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential
> > > covariance
> > >   L_Sigma_spatial <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_spatial);

> > >   siteSD <- tan(raw_siteSD) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)

> > >     L_Sigma_spatial * // comment out this line to remove spatial dependence

> > > siteSD*L_Sigma_spatial);

> > > indSDHier)
> > > }

> > > attempted, including student_t and exponential

> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > If it helps, I can provide some data and a set-up script.
> > >
> > >

given the inspiration of the original question and we (the
dev team and other common answerers) really are the
worst to judge what’s useful for users of various background
and what’s not.  But it would be great if users would collate
what they found useful to make it easier for others to find
and give us feedback as to what explainations/recommendations
worked well.  And it would be doubly great if someone built
some site or forum to facilitate users identifying/sharing
anything they find useful.

> On Wed, Jun 22, 2016, at 09:58 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > Christopher, have you tried using an inverse-lengthscale
> > parameterization?
> > You simply change this:
> >
> >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2));
> >
> > to
> >
> >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist*(2*spatialScale^2));
> >
> > I find this a more intuitive parameterization as values from 0-1 imply
> > near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1),
> > making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for
> > simpler functions.
> >
> >
> > --
> > Mike Lawrence
> > Graduate Student
> > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > Dalhousie University
> >
> > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Jun 21, 2016 at 6:12 PM, Michael Betancourt
> > <betan...@gmail.com>
> > wrote:
> >
> > > The length scale shrinking to zero does not give
> > > you an identity covariance but rather a covariance
> > > where all entries are unity, which is not positive-definite
> > > and hence will frustrate the Cholesky decomposition.
> > >
> > > A prior will still be helpful, but you really need to add
> > > a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another
> > > possible parameter, to Sigma_spatial to regularize the
> > > covariance.
> > >
> > > On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <
> > > christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > I'm trying to model the mean values of data collected from a number of
> > > sites where means at each site can be spatially autocorrelated.  I used a
> > > squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation
> > > matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it
> > > also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough
> > > for me to think that it's a substantial problem.
> > >
> > > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I
> > > think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the
> > > spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to
> > > near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation)
> > > while still having sufficient mass in the tail to allow for substantial
> > > spatial signal.  I've tried a variety of options (half Cauchy, half
> > > student_t, exponential), but none seem to have improved anything.
> > >
> > > Is there something else wrong with this model?  Should I be using a
> > > different covariance function? Does anyone have any suggestions or advice
> > > for the prior?
> > >
> > > Thank you
> > >
> > > /* Model Objectives:
> > > Estimate the mean value at each site and the grand mean.
> > > Allow for standard deviation to vary among sites
> > > Account for spatial autocorrelation of means among sites
> > > */
> > > data{
> > >   int n; // observations
> > >   int nSite; // sites
> > >   int siteID[n]; // which site belongs to each obs.
> > >   vector[n] x;
> > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] Dist; // Distance matrix, pre-scaled so the minimum
> > > distance is 1
> > > }
> > > transformed data{
> > >   real xScale; // the range of x divided by 4, to establish a reasonable
> > > scale for priors
> > >   real xMean;
> > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] sqDist; // pre-compute squared distance matrix
> > >   xMean <- mean(x);
> > >   xScale <- (max(x) - min(x))/4;
> > >   for(i in 1:nSite) for(j in 1:nSite)
> > >     sqDist[i,j] <- Dist[i,j]^2;
> > > }
> > > parameters{
> > >   real<lower=0> spatialScale; // spatial lengthscale;
> > >   real grandMean; // overall mean of x
> > >
> > >   // Non-central parameterizations; use is defined in next block
> > >   vector[nSite] raw_siteMean;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_siteSD;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_indSDHier;
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[nSite] raw_indSD;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters{
> > >   vector[nSite] siteMean; // mean of x at each site
> > >   real siteSD; // stdev of siteMean
> > >   real indSDHier; // overall stdev of x around the sitemeans
> > >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> > >
> > >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> > >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential
> > > covariance
> > >   L_Sigma_spatial <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_spatial);
> > >
> > >   siteSD <- tan(raw_siteSD) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> > >   siteMean <-  siteSD *
> > >     L_Sigma_spatial * // comment out this line to remove spatial dependence
> > >     raw_siteMean + grandMean; // ~ MVN_chol(grandMean,
> > > siteSD*L_Sigma_spatial);
> > >   indSDHier <- tan(raw_indSDHier) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> > >   for(i in 1:nSite)
> > >     indSD[i] <- indSDHier * tan(raw_indSD[i]); // ~half-cauchy(0,
> > > indSDHier)
> > > }
> > > model{
> > >   grandMean ~ normal(xMean,xScale);
> > >   raw_siteMean ~ normal(0,1);
> > >   spatialScale  ~ cauchy(0, 1); // A variety of other priors have been
> > > attempted, including student_t and exponential
> > >   x ~ normal(siteMean[siteID], indSD[siteID]);
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > If it helps, I can provide some data and a set-up script.
> > >
> > >

1. Mind creating a new thread for separate discussion topics? One of the difficulties in finding things is due to threads getting hijacked.
2. Yes, we've considered discourse and flarum. There just hasn't been enough expertise / benefit / time to move from what sort of works to another system that has different flaws. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NUTS vs ADVI comparison, ADVI giving wrong/unstable results
messages.body_plain:
Just to tune in on the discussion, I also think fake data simulations is useful! It will be a practical solution to checking approximate inferences and also make a step in the right theoretical direction about assessing finite-sample bias.

Dustin

> On Jun 22, 2016, at 7:23 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks all! Some of this discussion went a little over my head, but I'm glad to know I wasn't doing anything stupid, and this is work in progress!
>
> Mike
>
> On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 17:26:27 UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > And this is why we're excited about the research project of developing methods to use targeted fake-data simulation to detect problems with ADVI and other approximations!
> >
> > > On Jun 22, 2016, at 9:45 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
> > > is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
> > > becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
> > > particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
> > > and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
> > > it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
> > > designed.
> > >
> > > You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
> > > a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
> > > beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
> > > NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical
> > > understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan
> > > was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical
> > > understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early
> > > results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough
> > > to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
> > > are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
> > > any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.
> > >
> > > This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
> > > against its use in production analysis.
> > >
> > > On Jun 22, 2016, at 3:25 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi Bob,
> > > >
> > > > Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.
> > > >
> > > > So for now it seems like ADVI can't be used for very simple problems that appear in the documentation. Do you happen to know if that's an inherent limitation of the algorithm, or of Stan's implementation?
> > > >
> > > > Mike
> > > >
> > > > On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 03:10:22 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > NUTS doesn't provide a MAP estimate.  Optimization provides
> > > > > the MAP estimate.  You also don't get the frequentist posterior
> > > > > interval.  The posterior for the simple Bernoulli is a beta
> > > > > distribution, and it's not even symmetric unless alpha = beta.
> > > > >
> > > > > Your question (1) is the key thing we've been asking ourselves.
> > > > >
> > > > > Alas, NUTS isn't completely robust, but we've tagged ADVI
> > > > > as experimental (I hope that's clear in the interfaces), precisely
> > > > > because we don't know how to characterize when it will work or
> > > > > how to make it signal that it's gone wrong.
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > > On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:27 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > HI, Mike.  It's good to have this sort of example.  My quick answer is that the way to check that ADVi is giving reasonable results is by simulating fake data from the fitted model.  We are currently working on general guidelines for this idea.
> > > > > > Andrew
> > > > > >
> > > > > >> On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:21 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> The notebook in this repository shows the results of a very simple one parameter Bernoulli model with NUTS and ADVI.
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/blob/master/stanadvi.ipynb
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> The trivial model is taken from the cmdstan manual (although the for loop has been replaced with a vectorized version).
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> The notebook only uses pystan to write the data in R format. The stan compilation and execution is handled by an up to date pull of the develop branch of cmdstan. You should be able to reproduce the results by doing `git clone --recursive https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/` <https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/> then doing `make stan-update` in the cmdstan directory, then running the notebook.
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> The NUTS results are great: the MAP estimate of p pretty much exactly matches the true value nine times out of nine, and the width of the posterior is within 2 signifiant figures of the expected (frequentist) width sqrt(p*(1-p)/N).
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> The ADVI results are not as good. Agreement with the true value is rare, and the posterior mean and variance varies from run to run.
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> I have a bunch of questions:
> > > > > >>  1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
> > > > > >>  2) what's a good ELBO score? The larger the better? Are the values seen here (-6e3) a sign of a problem?
> > > > > >>  3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
> > > > > >>  4) is ADVI simply not appropriate for this problem? If so, given the trivial nature of the model (and that it is the first example in the cmdstan model), what kind of model would be OK with ADVI?
> > > > > >>  5) or is ADVI as implemented in (cmd)stan not ready for public consumption without great care over convergence/initialization? NUTS seems pretty idiot proof, but is that less true of ADVI?
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> And a bonus question, which is I think unrelated to this problem: why isn't the example listing on p9 of the the cmdstan manual vectorized? What's with the for loop? :-)
> > > > > >>
> > > > > >> Thanks,
> > > > > >> Mike

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben!

On Wednesday, June 22, 2016 at 12:43:39 PM UTC-7, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, June 22, 2016 at 3:29:17 PM UTC-4, Alireza RG wrote:
> > I also figured that
> >
> > 1) I need to use neg_binomial_2 instead of neg_binomial_2_log since I'm using mu,
> > 2) since 'b' can be negative, mean of NB can get negative too, so I changed to formulation a bit
>
> neg_binomial_2 with log(mu) is better numerically.
>
> > But still lambda becomes really small, which results in really large mu values. Will reparametrizing this using poisson-gamma decomposition help?
>
> I doubt it. Perhaps you have stronger prior beliefs about alpha than standard uniform?
>
> > Also, what prior should I use for shape? Shape should be always positive, that's why I used gamma.
>
> The gamma distribution is decent but not with very small shape and rate hyperparameters. Figure out what mean and mode seem reasonable and then back out what the shape and rate should be.
>
> > I get a few of these warnings too:
> >
> >              Exception thrown at line 32: neg_binomial_2_log: Precision parameter is inf, but must be finite!     1
>
> One instance of that is nothing to worry about.
>
> > And how can I exclude Y[1]? Rhat value for mu[1] is NaN. This shouldn't cause problems, right?
>
> The problem is that you are doing mu[1] <- Y[1] and then modeling Y[1] with mu[1].  You could either put a marginal prior on mu[1] or omit Y[1] from the likelihood.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: CmdStan v2.10.0 released!
messages.subject_clean: CmdStan v2.10.0 released!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

CmdStan v2.10.0 has been released: https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/tag/v2.10.0

Most of the changes in CmdStan are due to improvements in the Stan library. Below are the user-facing changes in Stan v2.10.0. For more information, see the full release notes for Stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.10.0

New User-Facing Features
--------------------------------------------------
* introduction of = for assignment; deprecating <- (#1819)
* _lpdf, _lpmf, _lcdf, _lccdf and vertical bar notation
  for probability mass, density, and cumulative distribution
  functions; update user-defined function syntax;
  deprecate older forms (#1811)
* target += lp to replace increment_log_prob(lp); target() to rpelace
  log_prob() function;  remove lp__ variable access (#1800)
* conditional (ternary) operator (#1125)
* stiff diff eq solver CVODES from Sundials
* add control parameters (tolerance, max iteraitons) to ODE solvers
* rename ODE solvers based on algorithm, integrate_ode_rk45
  for existing non-stiff Runge-Kutta solver and integrate_ode_bdf
  for the stiff backward differentiation form;  deprecate
  the unmarked integrate_ode function (#1886)
* limiting diff eq iterations in solvers (Boost/CVODES)
* unit_vector as parameter (#1713) [it never worked in the past]
* rename multiply_log and log_binomial_coefficient
  to lmultiply and lchoose (also part of #1811)
* incomplete beta function as inc_beta (#1540)

Daniel

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] (Logistic growth) ODE model in Stan getting stuck before sampling begins
messages.body_plain:
Ben, I was able to recover the parameters fine with RStan v2.9.0. I'm guessing there's something going on with how you generated data. Can you post your script? I'll try to replicate and figure out what's going on.

Here's mine:

theta <- c(0.5, 0.05)
sigma <- 2
y0 <- 5

N <- 10
T <- 20

library(deSolve)
t0 <- 0.0
ts <- 1:T

logistic_diff <- function(t, state, parameters) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parameters)), {
    dy <- theta_1 * y * (1 - theta_2 * y)
    list(c(dy))
  })
}
parameters <- c(theta_1 = theta[1], theta_2 = theta[2])
out <- ode(y = c(y = y0), times = c(t0, ts), func = logistic_diff, parms = parameters)

out <- out[-1, 2]

y <- matrix(out, T, N)
y <- y + matrix(rnorm(T * N, 0, sigma), T, N)

data <- list(T = T, N = N, t0 = t0, ts = ts, y = y)

library(rstan)
fit <- stan("ode_example.stan", data = data)

messages.body_plain:
I suppose we could pay someone to archive these discussions, but if in the meantime one of you could add something to the wiki on priors, that would be great!
As Alan said, it's' here:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
Andrew

> On Jun 23, 2016, at 9:56 AM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Honestly, there are so many gems sprinkled through these hundreds of threads, that it may pay for someone to collate and archive them.
>
> Anyone interested in editing the inaugural issue of "Proceedings of the General Bayesian Discussions & Friends of Stan"? 8-)
>
> Avi
>
> On Thursday, June 23, 2016 at 8:41:46 AM UTC-4, a...@ariddell.org wrote:
> > It would be wonderful to capture some of this discussion and put it on
> > the Stan Wiki, somewhere on
> > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations .
> > Right now the page does not have any discussion of priors for GPs.
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > A
> >
> > On Wed, Jun 22, 2016, at 09:58 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > Christopher, have you tried using an inverse-lengthscale
> > > parameterization?
> > > You simply change this:
> > >
> > >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2));
> > >
> > > to
> > >
> > >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist*(2*spatialScale^2));
> > >
> > > I find this a more intuitive parameterization as values from 0-1 imply
> > > near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1),
> > > making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for
> > > simpler functions.
> > >
> > >
> > > --
> > > Mike Lawrence
> > > Graduate Student
> > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > Dalhousie University
> > >
> > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tue, Jun 21, 2016 at 6:12 PM, Michael Betancourt
> > > <betan...@gmail.com>
> > > wrote:
> > >
> > > > The length scale shrinking to zero does not give
> > > > you an identity covariance but rather a covariance
> > > > where all entries are unity, which is not positive-definite
> > > > and hence will frustrate the Cholesky decomposition.
> > > >
> > > > A prior will still be helpful, but you really need to add
> > > > a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another
> > > > possible parameter, to Sigma_spatial to regularize the
> > > > covariance.
> > > >
> > > > On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <
> > > > chr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I'm trying to model the mean values of data collected from a number of
> > > > sites where means at each site can be spatially autocorrelated.  I used a
> > > > squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation
> > > > matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it
> > > > also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough
> > > > for me to think that it's a substantial problem.
> > > >
> > > > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I
> > > > think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the
> > > > spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to
> > > > near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation)
> > > > while still having sufficient mass in the tail to allow for substantial
> > > > spatial signal.  I've tried a variety of options (half Cauchy, half
> > > > student_t, exponential), but none seem to have improved anything.
> > > >
> > > > Is there something else wrong with this model?  Should I be using a
> > > > different covariance function? Does anyone have any suggestions or advice
> > > > for the prior?
> > > >
> > > > Thank you
> > > >
> > > > /* Model Objectives:
> > > > Estimate the mean value at each site and the grand mean.
> > > > Allow for standard deviation to vary among sites
> > > > Account for spatial autocorrelation of means among sites
> > > > */
> > > > data{
> > > >   int n; // observations
> > > >   int nSite; // sites
> > > >   int siteID[n]; // which site belongs to each obs.
> > > >   vector[n] x;
> > > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] Dist; // Distance matrix, pre-scaled so the minimum
> > > > distance is 1
> > > > }
> > > > transformed data{
> > > >   real xScale; // the range of x divided by 4, to establish a reasonable
> > > > scale for priors
> > > >   real xMean;
> > > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] sqDist; // pre-compute squared distance matrix
> > > >   xMean <- mean(x);
> > > >   xScale <- (max(x) - min(x))/4;
> > > >   for(i in 1:nSite) for(j in 1:nSite)
> > > >     sqDist[i,j] <- Dist[i,j]^2;
> > > > }
> > > > parameters{
> > > >   real<lower=0> spatialScale; // spatial lengthscale;
> > > >   real grandMean; // overall mean of x
> > > >
> > > >   // Non-central parameterizations; use is defined in next block
> > > >   vector[nSite] raw_siteMean;
> > > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_siteSD;
> > > >   real<lower=0,upper=pi()/2> raw_indSDHier;
> > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[nSite] raw_indSD;
> > > > }
> > > > transformed parameters{
> > > >   vector[nSite] siteMean; // mean of x at each site
> > > >   real siteSD; // stdev of siteMean
> > > >   real indSDHier; // overall stdev of x around the sitemeans
> > > >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> > > >
> > > >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> > > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> > > >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential
> > > > covariance
> > > >   L_Sigma_spatial <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma_spatial);
> > > >
> > > >   siteSD <- tan(raw_siteSD) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> > > >   siteMean <-  siteSD *
> > > >     L_Sigma_spatial * // comment out this line to remove spatial dependence
> > > >     raw_siteMean + grandMean; // ~ MVN_chol(grandMean,
> > > > siteSD*L_Sigma_spatial);
> > > >   indSDHier <- tan(raw_indSDHier) * xScale; // ~half-cauchy(0, xScale)
> > > >   for(i in 1:nSite)
> > > >     indSD[i] <- indSDHier * tan(raw_indSD[i]); // ~half-cauchy(0,
> > > > indSDHier)
> > > > }
> > > > model{
> > > >   grandMean ~ normal(xMean,xScale);
> > > >   raw_siteMean ~ normal(0,1);
> > > >   spatialScale  ~ cauchy(0, 1); // A variety of other priors have been
> > > > attempted, including student_t and exponential
> > > >   x ~ normal(siteMean[siteID], indSD[siteID]);
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > If it helps, I can provide some data and a set-up script.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > --

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mixed effect model: ADVI and Maximum Likelihood results are very different
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] mixed effect model: ADVI and Maximum Likelihood results are very different
messages.body_plain:
Don't do this:
 sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) ;

Instead, just put a prior on sigma directly, for example a half-normal or half-Cauchy with peak at 0.

A

> On Jun 23, 2016, at 3:17 PM, Kayhan Batmanghelich <batman...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you Bob for your reply and sorry for my late reply (I was in a conference).
>
> Thank you for your points, those were very helpful. My model here is a basic mixed effect model (see below), I believe that ML and posterior mean values should be close. For improper prior for beta, we expect MAP and ML to be the same. Plus the values have real meaning (here height of the individuals) and from experimental results and other independent studies study we know the approximate inferred heritability of height (h^2: heritability of height). Unfortunately ML and the posterior mean are orders of magnitudes different. While infrared ML for $h^2$ is > 0.5 (close to what we expect) the posterior mean is 0.015 using ADVI. I feel either I am missing something or ADVI is not working. Another sign is that y (height) is in centimeter, so the intercept (beta_1) should be > 100cm while the mean value on intercept is around 8cm . One more sign that ADVI is not working is that I have tried this model in pymc3 and if I wait long enough NUTS in pymc3 almost produces ML value (very slow). So far, I have not been able to get NUTS working in RStan. It stays in the in iteration 1 in the warm up stage for many hours without moving while CPU seems occupied.
>
> An idea how to get this to work?
>
> I modified the code (vectorized as you suggested) and looked into the data to make sure that the intercept is not added. Here is the updated code (any further improvement):
> ###### READ DATA
> # read y
> infile <- "/home/batmanghelich/Projects/CgGi/data/y.data.bin"
> con <- file(infile, "rb")
> dim <- readBin(con, "integer", 2)
> y <- matrix( readBin(con, "numeric", prod(dim)), dim[1], dim[2])
> close(con)
>
> # read K
> infile <- "/home/batmanghelich/Projects/CgGi/data/K.data.bin"
> con <- file(infile, "rb")
> dim <- readBin(con, "integer", 2)
> K <- matrix( readBin(con, "numeric", prod(dim)), dim[1], dim[2])
> N <- dim[1]
> close(con)
>
> # read X
> infile <- "/home/batmanghelich/Projects/CgGi/data/X.data.bin"
> con <- file(infile, "rb")
> dim <- readBin(con, "integer", 2)
> X <- matrix( readBin(con, "numeric", prod(dim)), dim[1], dim[2])
> M <- dim[2]
> close(con)
>
> ####### MODEL
> heritability_code<-'
>   data {
>      int<lower=1> N;  // number of subjects
>      int<lower=1> M;  // number of covariates
>      vector[N]  y;   // phenotype
>      matrix[N,M]  X;  // covariates
>      cov_matrix[N]   K; // GRM matrix
>   }
>
>   transformed data {
>     cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;
>     vector[N]  mu0 ;
>     matrix[N,N] eye;
>
>     L <- cholesky_decompose(K) ;
>
>     for (j in 1:N) {
>        mu0[j] <- 0;
>     }
>   }
>
>   parameters {
>   // Define parameters to estimate
>
>   // coefficient of the fixed effect
>   vector[M]  beta ;
>
>   // variance of the Population standard deviation
>   real<lower=0> sigma2 ;
>
>   // heritability (h2)
>   real<lower=0,upper=1>  h2 ;
>
>   // random genetic effect
>   vector[N]  g;
>
>   }
>
>   transformed parameters  {
>   // combination of the intercept and the fixed effect
>   vector[N]  mu;
>
>   // Individual mean
>   mu <- X * beta  ;
>
>   }
>
>   model {
>
>   sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(0.001,0.001) ;
>   h2 ~ uniform(0,1) ;
>
>   // data generation
>   g ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu0, sqrt(h2*sigma2) * L) ;
>
>
>   // observation
>   y  ~ normal(mu + g, sqrt( (1 - h2) * sigma2 ) );
>
>   }
> '
>
> ########## RUN the model
> library(rstan)
>
> # to run ADVI
> #rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
> #options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
> model <- stan_model(model_code = heritability_code)
> data <- list(N=N, M=M, y=c(y), K=K, X=X)
> fit <- vb(model, data=data, algorithm='fullrank', iter=5000 )
> save(fit, file='/scratch/users/batmanghelich/fit.vb.RDATA')
>
>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-wqziS7SQzkM/V2w1Wi9jA7I/AAAAAAAAPB0/WlNCOmjZ_IIwiqR6_B1KV7LigKn3o6LxACLcB/s1600/h2.png>
>
>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-fZlcZwIbKiE/V2w1QmYC8PI/AAAAAAAAPBs/xr5koRNzsk8xqqLPzx4Xz1g2JgIbGQVqgCLcB/s1600/sigma2.png>
>
>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-eCvefhu5IOA/V2w1MqBpF0I/AAAAAAAAPBk/EUJwiWk3Lz0IRwopR9gNq-QuVDrknXtvwCLcB/s1600/beta.png>
>
> On Tuesday, 7 June 2016 15:25:58 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> > You don't have an intercept in that X matrix, do you?  If
> > so, the model's not going to be identified and it can cause
> > serious slowdowns if not outright failures (see the manual chapter
> > on problematic posteriors).  You might also want to add a prior
> > to beta --- in fact, it'll be necessary if there are strong
> > collinearities in the columns of X.
> >
> > I don't know about your particular model, but the posterior mode
> > can be very far away from the posterior mean in general, and both can
> > be far away from the MLE.  With improper priors,
> > you get infinite prior mass in the tails, so they're not no-ops in
> > the sense you might expect.  In the asymptotic limit, with a fixed
> > prior, the posterior mean (and mode) will approach the MLE.
> >
> > You can define a unit-diagonal (NxN) matrix as diag_matrix(rep_vector(1, N))
> > without the loops (that's just for convenience --- it won't be any faster).
> >
> > This
> >
> > > for (j in 1:N) {
> > >      y[j] ~ normal( mu[j] + g[j], (1-h2)*sigma ) ;
> > >   }
> >
> > can be vectorized as
> >
> >   y ~ normal(mu + g, (1 - h2) * sigma);
> >
> > You should just define sigma as a parameter, not sigma_inv, though
> > the implied improper priors will differ by a Jacobian (doesn't affect
> > the MLE, which isn't based on a full probabilty modle, but it does affect
> > the Bayesian posterior and poterior mode).
> >
> > Also be careful that our multi-normal is based on co*variance* whereas
> > our univariate normal is parameterized by scale (std dev).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Jun 7, 2016, at 2:45 PM, Kayhan Batmanghelich <batman...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear Stan users,
> > >
> > > I am trying to develop a mixed effect model using rstan. Given that beta_0 and beta (intercept and the coefficient of the fixed effect) are treated as parameters (improper prior), I expect the results to be very close to maximum likelihood estimation. I want to estimate $h^2$ which is basically the variance explained by the random effect. Using maximum likelihood estimation (more specifically Restricted maximum Likelihood estimation), I expect values around 0.5 for $h^2$ with standard error of around 0.07. Sure, SE is not the same as posterior of variance but at least the posterior mean should be close to ML.
> > > I couldn’t get NUTS to run for this because; it stopped at the warm up step for about 8 hrs; perhaps due to the size of the problem. So I switched to ADVI. The results is very different than ML. Estimated $h2$ is around 0 and intercept does not look correct either. Any idea? Am I missing something?
> > >
> > > (N is around 4500 and M is 8)
> > >
> > >         mean   sd  10%   50%   90%
> > > beta_0 11.21 1.13 9.74 11.23 12.71
> > > h2      0.03 0.00 0.02  0.03  0.03
> > >
> > > This is the code:
> > >
> > > ####### MODEL
> > > mixed_model<-'
> > >   data {
> > >      int<lower=1> N;  // number of subjects
> > >   int<lower=1> M;  // number of covariates
> > >   vector[N]  y;       // height of subjects
> > >   matrix[N,M]  X;  // covariates
> > >   cov_matrix[N]   K;
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   transformed data {
> > >   cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;
> > >   vector[N]  mu0 ;
> > >   matrix[N,N] eye;
> > >
> > >   L <- cholesky_decompose(K) ;
> > >
> > >   for (j in 1:N) {
> > >   mu0[j] <- 0;
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   for (j in 1:N) {
> > >     for (i in 1:N) {
> > >     eye[i,j] <- 0.0;
> > >     }
> > >       eye[j,j] <- 1.0;
> > >     }
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   parameters {
> > >
> > >   real beta_0;
> > >   // coefficient of the fixed effect
> > >   vector[M]  beta ;
> > >   // Inverse of the Population standard deviation
> > >   real<lower=0> sigma_inv;
> > >
> > >   // proportion of variance (h2)
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1>  h2 ;
> > >
> > >   vector[N]  g;
> > >
> > >   // environment noise
> > >   //vector[N]  epsilon;
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   transformed parameters  {
> > >   // combination of the intercept and the fixed effect
> > >   vector[N]  mu;
> > >   real<lower=0> sigma;
> > >
> > >   // Individual mean
> > >   mu <- X * beta + beta_0 ;
> > >
> > >   // get the Population standard deviation from its inverse
> > >   sigma <- 1 / sigma_inv ;
> > >
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   model {
> > >
> > >   sigma_inv ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ;
> > >   h2 ~ uniform(0,1) ;
> > >
> > >   // data generation
> > >   g ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu0, sqrt(h2*sigma) * L) ;
> > >
> > >   // noise generation
> > >   //epsilon ~ normal( 0, (1 - h2)*sigma  ) ;
> > >
> > >   // observation
> > >   //y ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu + g , sqrt( (1 - h2)*sigma )*eye ) ;
> > >   for (j in 1:N) {
> > >      y[j] ~ normal( mu[j] + g[j], (1-h2)*sigma ) ;
> > >   }
> > >
> > >   }
> > > '
> > >
> > > ########## RUN the model
> > > library(rstan)
> > >
> > > model <- stan_model(model_code = mixed_model)
> > > data <- list(N=N, M=M, y=c(y), K=K, X=X)
> > > fit <- vb(model, data=data, algorithm='fullrank', iter=5000 )
> > >
> > >         mean   sd  10%   50%   90%
> > > beta_0 11.21 1.13 9.74 11.23 12.71
> > > h2      0.03 0.00 0.02  0.03  0.03
> > >
> > > ​

messages.body_plain:
Yes, and also, as we've discussed, it's a nontrivial problem to do targeted or adaptive fake-data checking because then we're no longer drawing the parameters from their prior so the results of Cook, Gelman, Rubin (2006) don't directly hold.
A

> On Jun 23, 2016, at 12:47 PM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Just to tune in on the discussion, I also think fake data simulations is useful! It will be a practical solution to checking approximate inferences and also make a step in the right theoretical direction about assessing finite-sample bias.
>
> Dustin
> > On Jun 22, 2016, at 7:23 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks all! Some of this discussion went a little over my head, but I'm glad to know I wasn't doing anything stupid, and this is work in progress!
> >
> > Mike
> >
> > On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 17:26:27 UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > And this is why we're excited about the research project of developing methods to use targeted fake-data simulation to detect problems with ADVI and other approximations!
> > >
> > > > On Jun 22, 2016, at 9:45 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Intuitively, ADVI works best when the target distribution (i.e. your posterior)
> > > > is Gaussian without too many correlations.  How is degrades as the target
> > > > becomes less Gaussian or the correlations grow is an open question.  In
> > > > particular, there are low-dimensional models where ADVI works poorly
> > > > and high-dimesnional models where ADVI works okay.  In general, however,
> > > > it can struggle on the kinds of complex models for which Stan was originally
> > > > designed.
> > > >
> > > > You hit on an even more important, point, however, in that we don’t yet have
> > > > a strong theoretical understanding of how to check whether ADVI will work
> > > > beforehand or how to verify that ADVI worked after the fact (unlike HMC/
> > > > NUTS where we’ve been developing a wealth of theoretical and empirical
> > > > understanding).  One of the strong motivations for including ADVI in Stan
> > > > was to do simulation tests like yours to build up a preliminary empirical
> > > > understanding of when ADVI might work and when it might not.  The early
> > > > results are consistent with the above intuition, but still not quite generic enough
> > > > to really inform practice (at least in my opinion).  Also in my opinion, the limitations
> > > > are more to do with the limitation of the assumed variational distributions than
> > > > any of the particulars in the ADVI implementation itself.
> > > >
> > > > This lack of understanding is why we list ADVI as “experimental” and warn
> > > > against its use in production analysis.
> > > >
> > > > On Jun 22, 2016, at 3:25 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > Hi Bob,
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks! My point in mentioning "MAP" (which I misused: I just meant the mean and width of the posterior) was to note that the NUTS posteriors are stable from run to run, and in approximately the right place, which is not true of the ADVI estimates.
> > > > >
> > > > > So for now it seems like ADVI can't be used for very simple problems that appear in the documentation. Do you happen to know if that's an inherent limitation of the algorithm, or of Stan's implementation?
> > > > >
> > > > > Mike
> > > > >
> > > > > On Wednesday, 22 June 2016 03:10:22 UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > > NUTS doesn't provide a MAP estimate.  Optimization provides
> > > > > > the MAP estimate.  You also don't get the frequentist posterior
> > > > > > interval.  The posterior for the simple Bernoulli is a beta
> > > > > > distribution, and it's not even symmetric unless alpha = beta.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Your question (1) is the key thing we've been asking ourselves.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Alas, NUTS isn't completely robust, but we've tagged ADVI
> > > > > > as experimental (I hope that's clear in the interfaces), precisely
> > > > > > because we don't know how to characterize when it will work or
> > > > > > how to make it signal that it's gone wrong.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > - Bob
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:27 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > HI, Mike.  It's good to have this sort of example.  My quick answer is that the way to check that ADVi is giving reasonable results is by simulating fake data from the fitted model.  We are currently working on general guidelines for this idea.
> > > > > > > Andrew
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >> On Jun 21, 2016, at 6:21 PM, Michael Williams <mjwil...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> The notebook in this repository shows the results of a very simple one parameter Bernoulli model with NUTS and ADVI.
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/blob/master/stanadvi.ipynb
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> The trivial model is taken from the cmdstan manual (although the for loop has been replaced with a vectorized version).
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> The notebook only uses pystan to write the data in R format. The stan compilation and execution is handled by an up to date pull of the develop branch of cmdstan. You should be able to reproduce the results by doing `git clone --recursive https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/` <https://github.com/williamsmj/stanadvi/> then doing `make stan-update` in the cmdstan directory, then running the notebook.
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> The NUTS results are great: the MAP estimate of p pretty much exactly matches the true value nine times out of nine, and the width of the posterior is within 2 signifiant figures of the expected (frequentist) width sqrt(p*(1-p)/N).
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> The ADVI results are not as good. Agreement with the true value is rare, and the posterior mean and variance varies from run to run.
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> I have a bunch of questions:
> > > > > > >>  1) in situations where I don't know the right answer, how would I be able to tell something has gone wrong here? Is the ELBO score a clue? Is the eta adaptation weird? Is it strange that it converges after a couple of hundred iterations?
> > > > > > >>  2) what's a good ELBO score? The larger the better? Are the values seen here (-6e3) a sign of a problem?
> > > > > > >>  3) are there command line parameters I could use to fix this particular problem?
> > > > > > >>  4) is ADVI simply not appropriate for this problem? If so, given the trivial nature of the model (and that it is the first example in the cmdstan model), what kind of model would be OK with ADVI?
> > > > > > >>  5) or is ADVI as implemented in (cmd)stan not ready for public consumption without great care over convergence/initialization? NUTS seems pretty idiot proof, but is that less true of ADVI?
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> And a bonus question, which is I think unrelated to this problem: why isn't the example listing on p9 of the the cmdstan manual vectorized? What's with the for loop? :-)
> > > > > > >>
> > > > > > >> Thanks,
> > > > > > >> Mike

messages.body_plain:
I added some recommendations regarding GP parameters, including the one I made in this thread, to the bottom of the wiki earlier today. Given my own novice standing with regards to GPs, it might be beneficial for someone to check my reasoning/understanding.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

On Thu, Jun 23, 2016 at 6:34 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> I suppose we could pay someone to archive these discussions, but if in the meantime one of you could add something to the wiki on priors, that would be great!
> As Alan said, it's' here:
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations
> Andrew

> > On Jun 23, 2016, at 9:56 AM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

> > Honestly, there are so many gems sprinkled through these hundreds of threads, that it may pay for someone to collate and archive them.
> >
> > Anyone interested in editing the inaugural issue of "Proceedings of the General Bayesian Discussions & Friends of Stan"? 8-)
> >
> > Avi
> >
> > On Thursday, June 23, 2016 at 8:41:46 AM UTC-4, a...@ariddell.org wrote:

> > > It would be wonderful to capture some of this discussion and put it on
> > > the Stan Wiki, somewhere on
> > > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations .
> > > Right now the page does not have any discussion of priors for GPs.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > >
> > > A
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jun 22, 2016, at 09:58 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> > > > Christopher, have you tried using an inverse-lengthscale
> > > > parameterization?
> > > > You simply change this:
> > > >
> > > >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2));
> > > >
> > > > to
> > > >
> > > >     Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist*(2*spatialScale^2));
> > > >
> > > > I find this a more intuitive parameterization as values from 0-1 imply
> > > > near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1),
> > > > making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for
> > > > simpler functions.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > --
> > > > Mike Lawrence
> > > > Graduate Student
> > > > Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
> > > > Dalhousie University
> > > >
> > > > ~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tue, Jun 21, 2016 at 6:12 PM, Michael Betancourt
> > > > <betan...@gmail.com>
> > > > wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > The length scale shrinking to zero does not give
> > > > > you an identity covariance but rather a covariance
> > > > > where all entries are unity, which is not positive-definite
> > > > > and hence will frustrate the Cholesky decomposition.
> > > > >
> > > > > A prior will still be helpful, but you really need to add
> > > > > a multiple of the identity matrix, with the scaling another
> > > > > possible parameter, to Sigma_spatial to regularize the
> > > > > covariance.
> > > > >
> > > > > On Jun 21, 2016, at 9:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <

> > > > > christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm trying to model the mean values of data collected from a number of
> > > > > sites where means at each site can be spatially autocorrelated.  I used a
> > > > > squared-exponential covariance function to build the spatial correlation
> > > > > matrix.Unfortunately, the model has a large number of diverging errors; it
> > > > > also fails with the cholesky decomposition of the matrix frequently enough
> > > > > for me to think that it's a substantial problem.
> > > > >
> > > > > This model has no difficulties if the spatial component is removed. I
> > > > > think the most likely source of the error would be the prior for the
> > > > > spatial lengthscale.  I'd like for this parameter to be able to shrink to
> > > > > near-0 (which result in an identity matrix for the spatial correlation)
> > > > > while still having sufficient mass in the tail to allow for substantial
> > > > > spatial signal.  I've tried a variety of options (half Cauchy, half
> > > > > student_t, exponential), but none seem to have improved anything.
> > > > >
> > > > > Is there something else wrong with this model?  Should I be using a
> > > > > different covariance function? Does anyone have any suggestions or advice
> > > > > for the prior?
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you
> > > > >
> > > > > /* Model Objectives:
> > > > > Estimate the mean value at each site and the grand mean.
> > > > > Allow for standard deviation to vary among sites
> > > > > Account for spatial autocorrelation of means among sites
> > > > > */
> > > > > data{
> > > > >   int n; // observations
> > > > >   int nSite; // sites
> > > > >   int siteID[n]; // which site belongs to each obs.
> > > > >   vector[n] x;
> > > > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] Dist; // Distance matrix, pre-scaled so the minimum
> > > > > distance is 1
> > > > > }
> > > > > transformed data{

> > > > >   vector[nSite] indSD; // each site's scaling of indSDHier
> > > > >
> > > > >   matrix[nSite, nSite] Sigma_spatial; // Spatial matrix
> > > > >   matrix[nSite,nSite] L_Sigma_spatial; // cholesky of spatial matrix
> > > > >   Sigma_spatial <- exp(-sqDist/(2*spatialScale^2)); // squared exponential
> > > > > covariance

> > > > > indSDHier)
> > > > > }

messages.body_plain:
Regarding the original question:

I'm a bit confused as to how that would work.  Given the squared-exponential covariance function Cov[i,j] = sigma^2 * exp(-D[i,j]^2 / l^2), where D[i,j] is the fixed distance between points i and j and l is the length-scale parameter, I was under the impression that as l^2 approached 0,  exp(-D[i,j]^2 / l^2) would also approach 0 for the off-diagonals (while the diagonals, with 0 distance, remained at 1).  Thus, a prior that shrunk l towards 0 should reduce the correlation to an identity matrix.  Is this mistaken?  I know I must be screwing something up somewhere, but I don't see how this is it.

Thank you for your help, everyone.

messages.body_plain:
Here's some R code to help intuition:

  library(MASS)
  inv_rho = .001 #contrast .001 & 10
  eta = 1
  sigma = 1
  N = 1e2
  s = matrix(NA,nrow=N,ncol=N)
  for(i in 1:N){
    for(j in 1:N){
      s[i, j] = eta * exp(-((i-j)^2)*inv_rho) + sigma
    }
  }
  out = MASS::mvrnorm(1,rep(0,times=N),s)
  plot(out,type='l',ylim=c(-10,10))

As has been pointed out in other threads here, inv_rho & eta play somewhat similar roles in areas of the parameter space, but generally you should observe that for a given value of eta, you get more wiggly plots with larger values for inv_rho.

messages.body_plain:
I think that informative priors on lenghscale can make a lot of sense.  To start with:  at the extremes of lengthscales near 0 or infinity, there will be no info to learn about this hyperparameter.  And, a lot of the time, you can get some (soft) bounds on reasonable lenghtscale based on the nature of the problem.  For example if we're modeling annual economic data, we probably wouldn't want a lenghtscale less than 2 years.  And so on.
A

messages.subject: One posterior evaluation in HMC takes longer when sampling with stan than in external evaluation?
messages.subject_clean: One posterior evaluation in HMC takes longer when sampling with stan than in external evaluation?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

we tackle two models that seem to present a challenge to NUTS especially, which is why we use Stan to perform MALA sampling.
The first model is a simpler model, called the independent model (mdl.indep), the second imposes some additional dependencies among RVs, called the dependent model (mdl.dep).
Now a possible strategy for inference is to sample from the independent model using Stan and then compute importance weights for the dependent model which we are actually interested in:

> fit.indep  <- sampling(mdl.indep.marg, data = xdat.indep, iter = nsamps/nchains, chains = nchains, algorithm = 'HMC', control = list(int_time=1))
> e.indep <- extract(fit.indep, permuted=T)
> lp.dep <- apply(e.indep$shIn, 1, function(a) return(log_prob(fit.dep, unconstrain_pars(fit.dep, list(shIn=a)))))

another is to use stan directly with the dependent model:

> fit.dep  <- sampling(mdl.dep.marg, data = xdat.dep, iter = nsamps/nchains, chains = nchains, algorithm = 'HMC', control = list(int_time=1))

What is strange to me is the following: If I'm not mistaken the computations of lp.dep <- apply() and fit.dep  <- sampling(..., control = list(int_time=1)) should use exactly the same number of posterior evaluations (as int_time=1). However, the importance sampling variant uses 50 secs, the direct stan variant 12 mins. Any suggestions on why that might be and how it might be possibly improved?

Thanks!
Ingmar

>

messages.subject: Censored Data - User Manual Page 107 !
messages.subject_clean: Censored Data - User Manual Page 107 !
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wanted to ask for some clarification on how stan works with survival (censored) data. Before asking my question, I think it would be helpful that I start with the likelihood in survival analysis:

Likelihood contribution of subject i = L_i = f(t_i)^{d_i} S(t_i)^{1 - di}

where :

t_i = either the event time or the time the subject got censored

d_i = observing indicator (if the event observed is 1, and 0 if we didn't get to see the event (censored))

f(t_i) = probability density of death at t_i

S(t_i) = 1 - CDF(t_i)

The likelihood above means that:

1) if subject i dies at t_i ----> we increment the log likelihood by log(f(t_i))

2) if subject i gets censored at t_i (he dies later but we don't get to see it) ----> we increment the log likelihood by log(S(t_i))

The logic above is what exactly explained on page 108 and 109 of the user manual. In specific, the code on the top of page 109, explains that :

y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma) ---> i.e. incrementing log likelihood by log of density at observed times

increment_log_prob(N_cens*normal_cdf_log(U, mu, sigma)); -----> incrementing log likelihood by log survival for censored subjects.

Here is the question: on page 107, there is a piece of code where its model block reads as:

y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma) ------> as before, this is equivalent to increment log likelihood by log density at observed times

y_cens ~ normal(mu, sigma) -----> Is this equivalent to incrementing log likelihood by log(s(t)) ?

Why I'm asking this?

We know S(t) = 1 - CDF = 1 - \int f(z) dz. Suppose evaluating S(t) requires the actual integration, then incrementing log likelihood by log (s(t)) for censored observations is difficult as it requires integration. However, the trick on page 107 where censored data are treated as parameters with a lower bound of their censoring times, can help us avoid dealing with S(t). Maybe by defining censored times as parameters, STAN by itself deals with S(t) under the hood without users interference?

If instead of computing S(t), I could use this trick, then dealing with cases with more complicated S(t) would become very handy. One such example is when we have covariates that are functions of time in our survival analysis.

Thanks very much for your help,

messages.subject: 1D GP analytical inference with direct sum kernel
messages.subject_clean: 1D GP analytical inference with direct sum kernel
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

To all the GP experts, would really appreciate if you can shed some light to this direct kernel sum problem.

Let X and Y be a set of 1-D predictor and observation respectively

y(x_i) = n(x_i) + s(x_i) + err_i

where  n(x) is GP with a neural network kernel, s(x) is a GP with a SE kernel and e_i ~ N(0, sigma).

Following R&W,

k(x, x’) = k_n(x, x’) + k_s(x, x’)

where k, k_n, k_s are the kernel for y, n and s respectively and I is the identity matrix

Let A = [k_n(X, X) + k_s(X, X) + sigma^2 * I]^(-1)

I can implement the analytical solution for y in STAN with:

mu(y) = (k_n(X_tilde, X) + k_s(X_tilde, X)) * A * y

cov(y) = (k_n(X_tilde, X_tilde) + k_s(X_tilde, X_tilde)) – (k_n(X_tilde, X) + k_s(X_tilde, X)) * A * t((k_n(X_tilde, X) + k_s(X_tilde, X)) + sigma^2*I

And the estimate for y looks reasonable.

Now, I want to find the analytical solution for n(X_tilde) and s(X_tilde) assuming n(x) and s(x) to be independent.

>From above, the means seem to be clear:

mu(n) = k_n(X_tilde, X) * A * y

mu(s) = k_s(X_tilde, X) * A * y

But, how about cov(n) and cov(s)?

Let N_tilde = k_n(X_tilde, X) and S_tilde = k_s(X_tilde, X)

cov(y)

= (k_n(X_tilde, X_tilde) + k_s(X_tilde, X_tilde)) – (N_tilde + S_tilde) * A * t((N_tilde + S_tilde)) + sigma^2*I

= k_n(X_tilde, X_tilde) – N_tilde * A * t(N_tilde) +

   k_s(X_tilde, X_tilde) – S_tilde * A * t(S_tilde) +

   sigma^2 * I +

   N_tilde * A * t(S_tilde) + S_tilde * A * t(N_tilde)

Following the logic of this (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.00566.pdf), it seems to me that:

cov(n) = k_n(X_tilde, X_tilde) – N_tilde * A * t(N_tilde)

cov(s) = k_s(X_tilde, X_tilde) – S_tilde * A * t(S_tilde)

If this is true, the following needs to hold?

N_tilde * A * t(s_tilde) + S_tilde * A * t(N_tilde) = 0

such that cov(y) = cov(n) + cov(s) + sigma^2 * I

My questions are:

1.     1. am I missing something with my maths?

2.     2. if not, how can I supply a prior to enforce this constrain in STAN?

Many thanks,

Andy
