messages.subject: Re: 1D GP analytical inference with direct sum kernel
messages.subject_clean: 1D GP analytical inference with direct sum kernel
messages.body_plain:
It seems you want something similar as in R&W Section 5.4.3 Manua Loa example where there are four covariance functions (eq 5.19), and Figure 5.7 shows different components (or the birthday example in BDA3).
You can think of your model as
 y = f + e
where you can have
1) f=n+s, e=err
 or if you want to focus on one of the components
2a) f=n, e=s+err
2b) f=s, e=n+err
Then you can use the usual equations (which you know already) to compute mu(f) and cov(f) for these different choices.
In a way when making predictions you choose which part is the interesting signal (f) and which part is the nuisance parameter (e).

Aki

messages.subject: Re: no matches for normal(real, real)
messages.subject_clean: no matches for normal(real, real)
messages.body_plain:
On a given trial, a subject is presented with sensory cues that tell them the probability of reward on the right side (real rprob). Because of the particular sensory cues we are using, there is some noise in their estimate of real rprob, and so on a given trial, their estimate of real rprob (perceived_rprob) can be described as a random draw from a normal distribution with mean=real rprob, and with st. dev.=real rprob*m_prob +prob_offset.

I have made a model in stan that accounts for the trial by trial choice data of subjects based on real probabilities and real reward amounts.  But we know that there is noise in subjects' estimate of probabilities and reward amounts, and that the noise scales in a particular way (i.e., the st. dev. increases linearly with the magnitude), based on previous psychophysical data.  I was hoping to have a model that could account for the trial by trial choice data while simultaneously accounting for the perceptual noise, which we know exhibits a linear relationship.

Does that make sense?  If this is impossible in stan, or completely misguided, please let me know.  I previously tried to do this using gradient descent, but introducing rngs is problematic for such a model.  That was my main motivation for building the model in stan instead.

Thanks again,
Christine

On Monday, June 27, 2016 at 9:08:51 PM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:

messages.body_plain:
Christine,

I believe this would be simplified if you think more generatively.  The idea is to
build your model to mimic the data generating process itself.  For example, in
a simple Binomial experiment we have some latent “true” probability of success
that we measure in a finite number of trials,

k ~ Binomial(N, p);

and we infer p from k and N.  This can be made much more complicated, with
different p for many different individuals or trials, or having p be a function of
covariates (leading to logistic regression), etc.

I don’t fully understand the model that you are trying to build, but it sounds like
there are some data censoring issues.  For example, having just (k / N) instead
of k and N separately makes this drastically more complicated because you
can’t exactly recover the likelihood.

Having some empirical p = k / N, call it p_hat, along with some estimate of the
standard deviation also runs into problems because the Gaussian approximation
is valid only for true p away from the 0 and 1 boundaries.  To avoid issues we
recommend treating such convolutions on the logit scale, for example

logit_obs_prop ~ normal(logit_latent_prob, m * log_latent_prob + offset).

That said, I would be very hesitant in this particular model as it is very hard to
derive from any reasonable generative model (I understand the psycophysical
literature might support it, but statistical misunderstandings are rampant in
many, many fields).

So long story short, the kind of model you want (latent parameters that aren’t
directly observed with hierarchical structure) is very much appropriate for Stan
but at the moment you’re likely being limited by some of the assumptions in
your model.

It would help if you could simplify your model to just the essence of what
you’re trying to fit and then it would be much easier for us to comment and
make more explicit recommendations.

Thank you Ben and Michael.  I apologize for the confusion, I have not done a good job of describing the model.

According to some economic theories, humans choose between two prospects, or gambles, based on the relative value of those prospects (in my case, Rval and Lval), where the value is the product of a nonlinear subjective function relating true probability and perceived probability (in my case, exp(-(-log(p))^alpha)), and a nonlinear function relating true reward amount and perceived reward amount (in my case, vol^rho).  My primary interest is in inferring the parameters alpha and rho from many thousands of choices between different gambles.

However, in my experiment, I am using certain sensory cues to convey reward probability and reward amount to the subject (e.g., # light flashes conveys the true probability).  It is known that subjects' estimates of such stimuli can be noisy.  Specifically, the standard deviation in the subjects' estimate of # flashes grows linearly with the # flashes presented.

My concern is that if I don't account for this sensory noise, it could mess up my estimates of alpha and rho.  So I was hoping to compare the alpha and rho parameters before accounting for noise (that model already works in stan) and afterwards, to see if it is something I should worry about.

Does that make sense?  Please let me know if I should clarify anything, and thanks so much for your feedback!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] no matches for normal(real, real)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] no matches for normal(real, real)
messages.body_plain:
> Thank you Ben and Michael.  I apologize for the confusion, I have not done a good job of describing the model.

No worries, just for future reference we can help much better
with short, simple examples that capture your problem.

>
> According to some economic theories, humans choose between two prospects, or gambles, based on the relative value of those prospects (in my case, Rval and Lval), where the value is the product of a nonlinear subjective function relating true probability and perceived probability (in my case, exp(-(-log(p))^alpha)), and a nonlinear function relating true reward amount and perceived reward amount (in my case, vol^rho).  My primary interest is in inferring the parameters alpha and rho from many thousands of choices between different gambles.
>
> However, in my experiment, I am using certain sensory cues to convey reward probability and reward amount to the subject (e.g., # light flashes conveys the true probability).  It is known that subjects' estimates of such stimuli can be noisy.  Specifically, the standard deviation in the subjects' estimate of # flashes grows linearly with the # flashes presented.
>
> My concern is that if I don't account for this sensory noise, it could mess up my estimates of alpha and rho.  So I was hoping to compare the alpha and rho parameters before accounting for noise (that model already works in stan) and afterwards, to see if it is something I should worry about.
>
> Does that make sense?  Please let me know if I should clarify anything, and thanks so much for your feedback!

Yeah, that’s conceptually no problem for Stan, you just have
to be careful in how you build the model.  You start with
some latent p_true and then some observer-specific p_true_obs
that gets corrected for the observer-dependent environment,
and then some data generated from each p_true_obs.
p_true and all of the p_true_obs would be parameters that
you fit jointly.

The problem with working with probabilities is that they
have to stay within 0 and 1, so you can’t apply a correction
that gives p_true_obs outside of these ranges.  I _highly_
recommend reformulating your model in terms of logit(p),
which is unconstrained and then constraining back to
a probability with a logistic only when constructing the
measurement part of the likelihood.

So, as a very informal example, you might have something
like

logit_p_true ~ normal(0, 5); // covers the bulk of the probabilities

// alpha quantifies how easily logit_p_true is conveyed to each observer
// beta1 and beta1 quantifies how much the rewards bias the observer-specific probability
mu_logit_p_obs[i] = alpha * logit_p_true + beta1 * positive_reward_strength - beta2 * negative_reward_strength;

logit_p_obs[i] ~ normal(mu_logit_p_obs[i], sigma);

k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], logit_p_obs[i]);

And you could make sigma depend on the latent probability,
too.  I’m sure the model would become very complicated
very quickly, but by starting with something simple and adding
complexity bit by bit you should be able to develop a robust,
principled model.

On Tuesday, June 28, 2016 at 2:13:06 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > Thank you Ben and Michael.  I apologize for the confusion, I have not done a good job of describing the model.
>
> No worries, just for future reference we can help much better
> with short, simple examples that capture your problem.
>
> >
> > According to some economic theories, humans choose between two prospects, or gambles, based on the relative value of those prospects (in my case, Rval and Lval), where the value is the product of a nonlinear subjective function relating true probability and perceived probability (in my case, exp(-(-log(p))^alpha)), and a nonlinear function relating true reward amount and perceived reward amount (in my case, vol^rho).  My primary interest is in inferring the parameters alpha and rho from many thousands of choices between different gambles.
> >
> > However, in my experiment, I am using certain sensory cues to convey reward probability and reward amount to the subject (e.g., # light flashes conveys the true probability).  It is known that subjects' estimates of such stimuli can be noisy.  Specifically, the standard deviation in the subjects' estimate of # flashes grows linearly with the # flashes presented.
> >
> > My concern is that if I don't account for this sensory noise, it could mess up my estimates of alpha and rho.  So I was hoping to compare the alpha and rho parameters before accounting for noise (that model already works in stan) and afterwards, to see if it is something I should worry about.
> >
> > Does that make sense?  Please let me know if I should clarify anything, and thanks so much for your feedback!
>
> Yeah, that’s conceptually no problem for Stan, you just have
> to be careful in how you build the model.  You start with
> some latent p_true and then some observer-specific p_true_obs
> that gets corrected for the observer-dependent environment,
> and then some data generated from each p_true_obs.
> p_true and all of the p_true_obs would be parameters that
> you fit jointly.
>
> The problem with working with probabilities is that they
> have to stay within 0 and 1, so you can’t apply a correction
> that gives p_true_obs outside of these ranges.  I _highly_
> recommend reformulating your model in terms of logit(p),
> which is unconstrained and then constraining back to
> a probability with a logistic only when constructing the
> measurement part of the likelihood.
>
> So, as a very informal example, you might have something
> like
>
> logit_p_true ~ normal(0, 5); // covers the bulk of the probabilities
>
> // alpha quantifies how easily logit_p_true is conveyed to each observer
> // beta1 and beta1 quantifies how much the rewards bias the observer-specific probability
> mu_logit_p_obs[i] = alpha * logit_p_true + beta1 * positive_reward_strength - beta2 * negative_reward_strength;
>
> logit_p_obs[i] ~ normal(mu_logit_p_obs[i], sigma);
>
> k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], logit_p_obs[i]);
>
> And you could make sigma depend on the latent probability,
> too.  I’m sure the model would become very complicated
> very quickly, but by starting with something simple and adding
> complexity bit by bit you should be able to develop a robust,
> principled model.
>
>

2. For k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], logit_p_obs[i]), what is N[i]?  I couldn't find this in the manual/documentation.  Does it correspond to that particular trial number?  Or the total number of trials?

Thank you so much!
Christine

On Tuesday, June 28, 2016 at 8:52:45 PM UTC-4, Christine C wrote:
> Thank you so much for your help!  I apologize again for not explaining the model clearly enough.
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, June 28, 2016 at 2:13:06 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >
> > > Thank you Ben and Michael.  I apologize for the confusion, I have not done a good job of describing the model.
> >
> > No worries, just for future reference we can help much better
> > with short, simple examples that capture your problem.
> >
> > >
> > > According to some economic theories, humans choose between two prospects, or gambles, based on the relative value of those prospects (in my case, Rval and Lval), where the value is the product of a nonlinear subjective function relating true probability and perceived probability (in my case, exp(-(-log(p))^alpha)), and a nonlinear function relating true reward amount and perceived reward amount (in my case, vol^rho).  My primary interest is in inferring the parameters alpha and rho from many thousands of choices between different gambles.
> > >
> > > However, in my experiment, I am using certain sensory cues to convey reward probability and reward amount to the subject (e.g., # light flashes conveys the true probability).  It is known that subjects' estimates of such stimuli can be noisy.  Specifically, the standard deviation in the subjects' estimate of # flashes grows linearly with the # flashes presented.
> > >
> > > My concern is that if I don't account for this sensory noise, it could mess up my estimates of alpha and rho.  So I was hoping to compare the alpha and rho parameters before accounting for noise (that model already works in stan) and afterwards, to see if it is something I should worry about.
> > >
> > > Does that make sense?  Please let me know if I should clarify anything, and thanks so much for your feedback!
> >
> > Yeah, that’s conceptually no problem for Stan, you just have
> > to be careful in how you build the model.  You start with
> > some latent p_true and then some observer-specific p_true_obs
> > that gets corrected for the observer-dependent environment,
> > and then some data generated from each p_true_obs.
> > p_true and all of the p_true_obs would be parameters that
> > you fit jointly.
> >
> > The problem with working with probabilities is that they
> > have to stay within 0 and 1, so you can’t apply a correction
> > that gives p_true_obs outside of these ranges.  I _highly_
> > recommend reformulating your model in terms of logit(p),
> > which is unconstrained and then constraining back to
> > a probability with a logistic only when constructing the
> > measurement part of the likelihood.
> >
> > So, as a very informal example, you might have something
> > like
> >
> > logit_p_true ~ normal(0, 5); // covers the bulk of the probabilities
> >
> > // alpha quantifies how easily logit_p_true is conveyed to each observer
> > // beta1 and beta1 quantifies how much the rewards bias the observer-specific probability
> > mu_logit_p_obs[i] = alpha * logit_p_true + beta1 * positive_reward_strength - beta2 * negative_reward_strength;
> >
> > logit_p_obs[i] ~ normal(mu_logit_p_obs[i], sigma);
> >
> > k[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], logit_p_obs[i]);
> >
> > And you could make sigma depend on the latent probability,
> > too.  I’m sure the model would become very complicated
> > very quickly, but by starting with something simple and adding
> > complexity bit by bit you should be able to develop a robust,
> > principled model.
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
I'd like to model a fraction in the range 0 to 1. One component of the mixture is well described by a beta distribution. The problem is the other component is a delta function at 1.

To be concrete, imagine the fraction represents something like how full gas tanks are in cars leaving a gas station. Some fraction theta are exactly 100% full. The remainder, 1-theta are somewhere between 0 and 100% full, perhaps beta(a, b). The parameters theta, a and b could be linear functions of the observed features (model of car, time of day, etc.)

Can I solve this in a single model in stan, where the parameters theta, a and b are correlated?

Or do I need to decompose it into two problems (1) a bernoulli model to infer the posterior on theta, for the binary question: is the tank full or not? and separately (2) for the subset of observations with non-full tanks, the beta distribution model for the fraction?

Or am I missing some other approach?

And does this class of problems have a name? Pointers most welcome!

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi, is this is a hierarchical model, or do you have direct data?  If it's direct data (i.e., you observe the gas tank level directly), then there is a simple solution.  Let y be your data, numbers between 0 and 1 representing tank level.
Define z = 1 if y=1 or 0 otherwise.
First, run a logistic regression to predict z given your predictors.  That's your first model.
Second, fit a model for y, but just on the data for which z=0 (that is, the non-full tank) to estimate your continuous model.  Rather than a beta distribution, you might want to use a lognormal as then the parameters are easier to interpret.
You can fit the models together in one Stan program.
A

messages.body_plain:
No, it's simpler than a zero-inflation model.  With the classic zero-inflated Poisson, the challenge is that data zeroes can come from the regular Poisson model (which can produce values of 0, 1, 2, etc) or from the zero-inflated part.  Mike W's example is a mixture of a discrete and continuous distribution:  _all_ his 1's come from the discrete "full tank" component of the model, and all his non-1's come from the continuous part of his model.  The separation is clean.
A

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm reading the Dynamic Linear Models with R <http://www.springer.com/us/book/9780387772370> book, where most of chapter 4 is devoted to Bayesian estimation of parameters. They code most of it manually though, and it can get quite tricky for complicated models. I'm trying to reproduce the example on p.186 in Stan, where the model to be estimated consists of local linear trend and AR(2) components

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-uPliCAqgWrQ/V3Wl0HpwJqI/AAAAAAAABwE/TMWZQ9oV3q0oriZDNg6QUVVFl3TEVrshACLcB/s1600/question.JPG>
Priors for (ϕ1ϕ2) are N(0,(2/3)^2) and N(0,(1/3)^2) and the inverses of variances are assumed to be independent with Gamma priors g(a2/b,a/b) where a = 1 and b =1000.
I found some discussions here before on constraining parameters to be stationary <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/dlm/stan-users/h7XLPDwLE-M/wKyX5nh0qx4J>, so that part has been partially resolved.
However, the estimation fails because "error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done" after a ton of messages that complain "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue: validate transformed params: W is not positive definite".

I'm a beginner in Stan and I'm certain that I've messed up somewhere in the code. Any help is appreciated!

Thanks,
Peyman
